articles.title_orig: Nike Debuts Locally Designed Line for China
articles.title_zh: Nike Debuts Locally Designed Line for China
articles.content_orig:
After appointing a new head of China , severing ties with local e-commerce distributors and launching NikeSkims in China , Nike is making another big move as part of its China turnaround plan with the launch of its first dedicated local line, developed by its newly formed Local Product Creation team.
Dubbed Local Creation Collections, the launch marks Nike ’s 45th anniversary in China and takes a “designed in China” approach that moves beyond merely telling Chinese stories, according to Nike.
Co-creating with local manufacturers, the team was swiftly formed just over 120 days ago and based in Shanghai. Rather than “merely adding more Chinese elements” such as mandarin collars and qipao accents to sporty garments, the new collection — which spans the Nike Sportswear and Jordan Streetwear brands — is meant to reflect the local team’s on-the-ground lifestyle research.
“Grounded in Nike’s sport DNA, we bring consumer insight closer to every stage of creation — from design and development to production. Inspired by the lives, evolving needs and aspirations of young people across China, we are creating products shaped by the people who live here,” said Cathy Sparks, Nike’s new China head, in a statement.
“Sometimes the product doesn’t have to be super loud to create this emotional value,” added Flavia Cervantes, vice president of Local Creation for Greater China, who recently relocated to Shanghai.
“Through silhouette, material, tailoring and styling, we design to fit the contemporary Chinese rhythm,” Cervantes continued during a showcase at Shanghai Fashion Week.
To inform the design, Nike’s local team joined local running crews, attended art events, took part in trail races, visited local communities and spoke with people known for their street style. The team sought firsthand insight into “a generation unwilling to choose between quality, performance, aesthetics and personal style,” Nike explained.
The 20-plus-piece collection adopts a modular system and adjustable silhouettes. Defined by smooth, clean materials, it uses technical insulation and natural-fiber blends to create lightweight pieces with a relaxed, clean structure that can easily fit into a “quiet luxury” wardrobe.
Tapping into the new generation’s interest in nostalgia, Cervantes’ team looked at old images of Michael Jordan ’s off-court style, including his well-tailored suits, leather bombers and other tailored pieces. The result is the new Jordan Tailored Sport Collection, which marries the GOAT’s bold off-court style with Chinese street style.
“We see significant opportunity to serve consumers more holistically, with a stronger head-to-toe product experience across sport and everyday life,” Cervantes explained, adding that the collection includes five new materials developed specifically for the local market.
The collection, which launches on Nov. 12, will hit shop floors in key cities and at selected retailers, including SKP-S in Beijing and the multibrand retailer SND , whose latest Westbund door is next to Adidas and Lululemon’s new China headquarters.

articles.title_orig: These common infections can cause cancer. Here’s what can lower your risk.
articles.title_zh: These common infections can cause cancer. Here’s what can lower your risk.
articles.content_orig:
President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.
Less than a month before the midterm elections , the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll .
The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.
At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.
Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel.
"It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.
Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."
He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."
The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News.
"The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.
The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.
"A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.
For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices.
The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon.
"Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."
Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.
"Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.
Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA .
Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.
Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
"By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.
Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout.
Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs .
A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office.
Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.
"Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.
Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February.
Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions.
"Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.
"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.

Speaking at the Canton Fair’s 70th anniversary, the premier defended China’s role in global trade and invited foreign firms to invest in the country
Premier Li Qiang said on Wednesday that China stands ready to import more high-quality goods, particularly high-value-added products, as part of efforts to promote more balanced trade.
“International trade is not merely figures on a ledger, but a voluntary choice to enhance well-being,” Li said during the keynote speech, according to a readout from state news agency Xinhua.
“As both a ‘super seller’ and a ‘super buyer’, China delivers predominantly ‘neighbour-benefiting’ and ‘neighbour-enriching’ positive spillovers to all partners,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying
articles.title_zh: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying
articles.content_orig:
FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of spying, in the latest sign of rising tensions between Moscow and Tokyo.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai, from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, adding that he had been accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s foreign ministry summoned the Russian ambassador in Tokyo, Nikolay Nozdrev, over the arrest later on Wednesday.
Imai, a reporter at the newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin, was reportedly preparing to return to Japan when he was arrested for allegedly collecting information on Russia’s defence capabilities, according to Russia’s Tass news agency.
Russia’s FSB security agency claimed the journalist had intended to pass the information on to Japanese intelligence.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Japan’s foreign ministry urged Moscow to extend “fair and impartial treatment” to the detained journalist. “The Japanese embassy … in Moscow and the consulate general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk lodged a request with the Russian authorities for the prompt provision of information, as well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” an official told Agence France-Presse.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the announcement by Russian authorities but it was “still confirming the details”.
“Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” it said.
Imai’s arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over sovereignty of islands belonging to the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war ⁠in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap .
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kurils have been under Russian control since the end of the second world war, when Soviet forces seized the islands in the final days of the conflict, forcing about 17,000 Japanese citizens to leave and, over time, replacing them with a similar number of Russians.
In 2022, Moscow scrapped a programme that allowed former residents to travel to the islands to visit the graves of their ancestors in protest at Japan’s support for Ukraine.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an ​uproar in Japan . Tokyo has ‌said it would continue ​implementing sanctions against ​Russia and supporting Ukraine.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title_orig: Bank of America Q3 profit tumbles 17% as deals, trading revenue fall
articles.title_zh: Bank of America Q3 profit tumbles 17% as deals, trading revenue fall
articles.content_orig:
Third largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earnings
Bank of America (BAC.N), has been fined $1.21bn by US regulators for widespread failures to detect ‌potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings.
The treasury department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank’s failure to report more than $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, including $1bn that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks.
“Financial institutions are on the ​front lines of protecting our economic and national security,” the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said in a statement. “When a bank of this size ​fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the ⁠entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”
The treasury said the bank “prioritized its revenues” in building compliance programs, and overly relied on inquiries ​from outside parties such as law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.
The consent order requires Bank of America to hire an ​independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that the bank failed to detect at the time, and report those transactions to FinCen.
“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” said a Bank of America spokesperson in a statement. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of ​employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised ​by our regulators.”
The spokesperson added that the bank’s third-quarter results due for release on Wednesday would include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2bn, which will reduce quarterly net income ‌by approximately ⁠17 cents a share.
Analysts have estimated adjusted EPS of $1.10, according to mean estimates compiled by LSEG, but that excludes one-offs like this fine.
Shares were down 2.7% in after-hours trading after closing the day down 1.1%.
The penalty is likely to add to negative investor sentiment and raise concerns about higher expenses and whether Bank of America can maintain its roughly $6bn quarterly share buyback pace, the UBS analyst Erika Najarian said in a note.
With earnings due ​on Wednesday, “we think shares likely underperforming at ​open,” she said.
She noted there ⁠was no asset cap, a regulatory penalty that would limit how large the bank could grow.
As part of the fine, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency levied a $750m civil ​penalty against the lender, the largest ever for the regulator, citing failures to address shortcomings in its anti-money ​laundering programs that were ⁠identified as part of a 2024 cease-and-desist order from the watchdog.
The regulator said the bank’s compliance program was “deficient and ineffective”, and its transaction monitoring system caused the bank to delay filing suspicious activity reports on billions of dollars of transactions.
In addition, the bank paid an $11.6m fine to the Office of Foreign ⁠Assets Control ​for over 400 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The treasury said the bank mistakenly ​processed millions of dollars in payments that violated sanctions programs targeting countries including Russia and Iran.
The fine comes days after American Express was also hit with a $350m penalty for similar anti-money ​laundering shortcomings.

articles.title_orig: What does the historic Bank of America fine mean for US-China capital streams?
articles.title_zh: What does the historic Bank of America fine mean for US-China capital streams?
articles.content_orig:
Analysts say penalties signal tighter scrutiny over cross-border financial flows
As the US Treasury imposed historic fines on Bank of America over compliance failures involving Chinese money-laundering networks, analysts see the action as a signal that could prompt Western banks to tighten scrutiny of Chinese clients and cross-border transactions.
The penalties, announced on Tuesday and totalling more than US$1.21 billion, included what the US Treasury described as its third-largest penalty on record and the largest in the history of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bank of America had failed to report more than US$5 billion in suspicious transactions in a timely manner, including more than US$1 billion involving national security-related and other priority risks such as “suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese money-laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money-laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border”, according to a Treasury statement.
The bank had also processed millions of dollars in payments “in apparent violation of sanctions programmes”, including those targeting Russia, Iran and narcotics and global terrorism networks, the Treasury added.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo spends a peaceful night in the hospital after cancer surgery
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo spends a peaceful night in the hospital after cancer surgery
articles.content_orig:
VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV spent a calm night in the hospital after successful surgery that saw part of his right lung removed and a confirmed cancer diagnosis , the Vatican said early Wednesday.
It said more information would follow later in the day.
The 71-year-old American pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer that accounts for 80% of all cases, according to the American Lung Association.
The 90-minute operation to remove a malignant lung nodule was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned,” the Vatican said Tuesday. Leo was in the operating theater for nearly three hours, it said.
The Vatican did not offer details on planned treatment moving forward or whether the cancer might have spread.
The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli hospital as he entered Tuesday.
The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.
The surgery saw the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung removed using a “video-assisted technique,” according to the Vatican.
Following his surgery, the pontiff “woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor,” the Vatican said. The room is next to the usual papal apartment, complete with private chapel, which is currently undergoing renovations.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.
The cancer diagnosis could complicate his busy schedule.
Just weeks earlier, hundreds of thousands of people packed the streets of Paris for an outdoor mass on a visit that saw Leo warn about the risks of artificial intelligence.
He was planning to take a historic two-week visit to South America next month, although it is unclear if that will still go ahead.
Messages of support and sympathy flowed in after the news.
Dr. Fernando Daniels III, a 67-year-old physician from Maryland  was among many praying for Leo’s swift recovery in the Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square.
“I’ve seen miracles in medicine. I’ve seen people told with terminal illnesses they wouldn’t live and they did,” he told NBC News.
“Prayers of all should heal him,” said Daniels, who was traveling as part of a group.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife, Jeanette Rubio, were praying for the pope, who was born in Chicago.
“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X.
“We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation,” New York City’s Archbishop Ronald Hicks said in a statement.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, the German Catholic news agency KNA reported.
“The pope‘s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” Steinmeier was quoted as saying.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Vatican City, and Mithil Aggarwal reported from Hong Kong.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of crippling drone missions as ties with US worsen
articles.title_zh: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of crippling drone missions as ties with US worsen
articles.content_orig:
Outage of terminals managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX comes as Russia launches ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from US
Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The terminals, which are distributed and managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine . Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.
SpaceX did not confirm any changes to Starlink’s functionality and it was not immediately clear why the restrictions had been put in place. Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded their engines to jet power in the early summer.
But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals has been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk, an ally of Trump, had previously cut off Starlink service to Ukrainian soldiers during an offensive that took a small amount of Russian territory. Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader – an extraordinary act of political interference against a wartime ally – as a personal feud between the two presidents has burst into the open.
The reports that Starlink was being throttled on the frontlines were interpreted by some as further pressure on Ukraine to end the fighting and make a deal with Russia at any cost.
Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
after newsletter promotion
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five major power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” he said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed by either side. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”
Ukraine is observing a short-term moratorium on striking Russian refineries while Kyiv seeks to show that it is ready for talks with Russia. Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday to meet Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister. He will also be received by King Charles.
Zelenskyy is seeking new negotiations with the US. He has sent proposals to the Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, saying Ukraine was ready to work towards a ceasefire and “Russia must also be part of this agreement”.

articles.title_zh: Strong Patient Outcomes Earns Holy Cross Health High Performing Recognition in U.S. News & World Report’s 2026-2027 Best Hospitals Rankings - Florida Hospital News and Healthcare Report
articles.source: Florida Hospital News and Healthcare Report
articles.content_orig:
Posted by cfelixcpa | Oct 14, 2026 | SF STAT! | 0 |
October 13, 2026 – Cardiovascular and orthopedic issues are two of the most common reasons patients seek hospital care. Holy Cross Health earned High Performing ratings for five conditions and procedures—heart failure, pacemaker implantation, hip fracture, hip replacement and knee replacement—in U.S. News & World Report’s 2026-2027 Best Hospitals rankings.
For most patients, health care isn’t defined by one specialty. It’s defined by confidence that they’ll receive high-quality care, regardless of why they walk through the door. Holy Cross Health’s five High Performing ratings reflect strong performance across a broad range of procedures and conditions, offering patients another independent measure to consider when choosing where to receive care.
“Every patient who walks through our doors deserves exceptional care,” said Pierre Monice, FACHE, President and CEO of Holy Cross Health. “Patients place an incredible amount of trust in us, often during some of the most difficult moments of their lives. Recognition like this is meaningful because it reflects the commitment our physicians, nurses and colleagues bring to earning that trust every day.”
For the 2026-2027 Best Hospitals rankings, U.S. News & World Report evaluated nearly 4,500 hospitals across 14 adult specialties and 23 procedures and conditions. Hospitals earning a High Performing rating performed significantly better than the national average for a specific procedure or condition based on objective measures, including patient outcomes, complication rates, nursing care and other indicators of clinical performance. Only 16% of evaluated hospitals earned a Best Hospitals designation.
This year’s recognition highlights two of Holy Cross Health’s clinical programs:
“High-quality care doesn’t happen by chance,” said Jason Boren, Chief Operating Officer of Holy Cross Health. “It’s built decision by decision, patient by patient. Whether someone comes to us for heart failure, joint replacement or a pacemaker, every member of the care team plays a role. That’s what these ratings recognize.”
U.S. News & World Report recognizes the physicians, nurses, technicians and many other providers who shape each patient’s experience from the first evaluation through recovery and highlights the depth of expertise across Holy Cross Health’s cardiovascular and orthopedic programs.
A member of Trinity Health, Fort Lauderdale-based Holy Cross Hospital, dba Holy Cross Health, is a full-service, not-for-profit, Catholic, teaching hospital operating in the spirit of the Sisters of Mercy for more than 70 years. Holy Cross Health earned High Performing ratings for five Types of Care in U.S. News and World Report’s 2026-2027 Best Hospital rankings ; received the American Heart Association’s Commitment to Quality award for achieving high performance across three or more clinical areas in the Get With The Guidelines® program for two years running in 2025 and 2026; received “LGBTQ+ Healthcare Equality High Performer” designation from the Human Rights Campaign Foundation’s 2026 Healthcare Equality Index; and received four out of five stars in the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Overall Hospital Quality Star Ratings for two consecutive years in 2025 and 2026. Additionally, Holy Cross Wound Healing and Hyperbarics program earned the 2025 Center of Distinction award by Healogics®, Physicians Outpatient Surgery Center at Holy Cross HealthPlex landed a spot on Newsweek’s list of America’s Best Ambulatory Surgery Centers 2025 and Holy Cross Health Foundation is designated as a High Performer from the Association for Healthcare Philanthropy. Holy Cross Health was also named among the 2024 America’s Best-In-State Hospitals by Newsweek and selected as a Forbes America’s Best Employers for Healthcare Professionals in 2025 and 2026. Through strategic collaborations and a commitment to being a patient-centered, transformative and healing presence, the 557-bed hospital offers progressive inpatient, outpatient and community outreach services and clinical research trials to serve as the community’s trusted health partner for life. Holy Cross Health also includes the new Holy Cross Health Center & Emergency Care — Deerfield Beach, which opened in May 2026; Holy Cross HealthPlex outpatient facility; The Holy Cross Health Family Health Center in Oakland Park; urgent care centers; and more than 40 Holy Cross Medical Group offices, a multi-specialty physician-employed group of 200+ physicians providing services throughout Broward County. Holy Cross Health Center & Emergency Care – Fort Lauderdale at Sunrise is currently under construction and is expected to open in August 2027. To learn more about Holy Cross Health, visit holy-cross.com , and connect with them on Facebook , LinkedIn , Instagram and YouTube .

articles.title_orig: Consumer prices rose at 3.7% annual rate in September as gas costs skyrocket
articles.title_zh: Consumer prices rose at 3.7% annual rate in September as gas costs skyrocket
articles.content_orig:
September brought little relief to the accelerating cost of living, as consumer prices increased again and kept the inflation rate well above the Federal Reserve's goal.
The consumer price index , a broad measure of goods and services costs across the U.S. economy, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month, putting the 12-month rate at 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected respective gains of 0.6% and 3.6%.
Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, the so-called core CPI rose 0.3% for the month and was up 2.6% on an annual basis, compared with respective estimates for 0.2% and 2.5%.
The annual rate for headline inflation was 3.4% in August while the core rate was 2.4%.
Surging energy costs were again the primary culprit in the inflation picture. The energy index jumped 5.2% as tensions continued between the U.S. and Iran in a war launched in late February that shows no signs of ending anytime soon.
Gasoline prices soared 9.1%, accounting for about half the gain in headline CPI, according to the BLS. Over the past year, gas has posted a 34.2% rise while fuel oil has roared higher by 74.2%.
Food prices were flat on the month and up 2.5% from a year ago. However, shelter prices increased 0.4% and used car and truck prices jumped 0.7%. Apparel prices, which are sensitive to tariffs, increased 0.3% and are up 3.4% on an annual basis.
Stock market futures turned negative following the release while bond yields were sharply higher. Futures traders also raised the odds of a rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Oct. 27-28 to about 54%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds for a rate rise before the end of the year increased to better than 96%, with a near 50-50 chance of the Fed boosting rates by half a percentage point by December.
This is the final CPI reading that FOMC officials will get before that meeting. The BLS on Thursday will release the September reading on the producer price index, a measure of wholesale costs.
"CPI came in hot and it wasn't just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years," said Sonu Varghese, chief macro strategist at Carson Group. "The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we've yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom."
Inflation as measured by the CPI has surpassed the Fed's 2% benchmark since March 2021. The gauge had been trending lower at the start of 2026, but then spiked following the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran.
Over the past few months, the year-over-year trend has moderated but still has held well above target.
Fed officials responded in September by approving their first interest rate hike in more than three years, a quarter percentage point move that took the benchmark funds rate to a target range of 3.75%-4%. Markets expect the Fed to skip an October increase but to hike again in December.
The type of supply shocks that have driven the energy surge generally are considered temporary, and policymakers often will look through them when considering where to set rates. However, Fed officials fear that the longer the war drags on, the higher the likelihood that the spike will make its way through the broader economy and become embedded in consumer and business expectations.
Prices also have faced pressure from President Donald Trump 's tariffs as well as demand for goods associated with the artificial intelligence build-out.
In recent days, a number of key policymakers have expressed the belief that the Fed doesn't need to rush to implement another hike. However, most say they expect another increase this year. Market pricing implies the Fed could raise rates at least twice more in 2027.
Fed officials follow the CPI and a host of other metrics but use the Commerce Department's personal consumption expenditures price index as their primary forecast and policymaking metric. The PCE numbers for September won't be released until later this month.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI engineer arrested after recording device found at San Francisco office
articles.title_zh: OpenAI engineer arrested after recording device found at San Francisco office
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's head of international sales, Guillaume Princen, told Bloomberg TV that open-source alternatives to the company's artificial intelligence models could have more cybersecurity risks.
“We need to be really careful with open-source on safety,” Princen said at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Wednesday. “I can’t talk for open models. But by definition, there’s more risk with them.”
Anthropic has advocated for slowing down AI development until firms can reliably get a handle on rogue models and prevent further AI hacks.
The company also warned this week that some AI models will soon be able to self replicate and inhabit internet-connected devices. In a report Monday, Anthropic said these capabilities could be just "months away."
President Donald Trump's top science advisor, Michael Kratsios, said the United States is four to six months ahead of China in the artificial intelligence race .
During an appearance Wednesday morning on Fox Business's 'Big Money in the Morning,' Kratsios also addressed a recent warning by Anthropic that advanced AI models could soon infect internet-connected devices in people's homes.
"I think we always have to be vigilant and think very carefully about the cyber risk presented with new technologies, and I think that's one of the core cruxes of the superintelligence task force," Kratsios said. "We want to make sure that we're leading the world in SI, but at the same time making sure that we're on top of and monitoring these national security threats to the country."
Anthropic said Wednesday it will be opening an office in Singapore after it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the island nation.
The MOU sets out "areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors," according to Anthropic.
The Singapore office is Anthropic's fifth location in the Asia Pacific region. The company's other offices are located in Tokyo, Japan; Bengaluru, India; Seoul, South Korea; and Sydney, Australia.
Britain's media regulator Ofcom said on Wednesday that it had placed new restrictions on Grok, the chatbot created by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI, formerly xAI.
Users in Britain are no longer allowed to use Grok to view, generate or share pornographic content, Ofcom said.
Companion chatbots, include the anime-inspired "Ani," are also banned from engaging in sexually-explicit conversations with users.
Earlier this year, Ofcom began investigating reports of Grok being used to create sexual deepfakes of real individuals
Nvidia announced Tuesday that it will invest $10 billion in four artificial intelligence firms based in France .
The companies include Doctolib, Entalpic, Genesis AI and Pigment.
Doctolib develops AI agents for healthcare providers and patients; Entalpic uses AI to develop advanced materials for semiconductors and electronics; Genesis AI is building general-purpose robots; and Pigment offers AI-powered business planning and forecasting software.
An adversary can interrupt an artificial intelligence system without defeating its software. It need only strike the infrastructure that keeps the system running. Ukraine proved the point inside Russia this past week.
President Trump and his national security team should take note before an enemy tries the same thing here. On October 8, a Ukrainian drone attack forced Yandex, the technology company often called "Russia’s Google," to suspend operations at its Sasovo data center. The next day, another strike knocked out several modules at its Kaluga facility, which Yandex had called its most powerful data center in Russia . On October 11, the company announced that its Vladimir-region data center had shut down completely after a drone attack. Ukraine disrupted three major Yandex computing facilities in four days.
The Sasovo facility housed two of Yandex’s three supercomputers used to train its AI models, including YandexGPT. Yandex said it could not yet determine whether the equipment could be restored. Whatever the final damage assessment, Russia’s leading AI developer lost a major computing hub in a single night.
During my years as an Army officer and Pentagon strategist, I learned to judge a military capability by whether it would be there when needed. A weapon that dazzles on the test range becomes a liability when its supply line fails in combat.
That standard should govern our dependence on AI.
A Saudi national has been arrested and charged after allegedly planting a recording device inside an OpenAI office in San Francisco, authorities announced Tuesday.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was taken into custody last week. Security footage captured Alfozan near the executive conference room multiple times prior to the device’s discovery, despite having no authorization to access the space or attend meetings there, federal prosecutors said.
"FBI and partners arrested this individual after he allegedly concealed a recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence tech," FBI Director Kash Patel wrote on X. "Protecting American SI innovation is critically important and FBI views it as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities."
Alfozan had been employed by OpenAI since July 2025. Around Sept. 30, someone discovered a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside an OpenAI building in San Francisco , a federal complaint states.
The company later determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed two days before it was found, and that its contents were encrypted.
According to authorities, a chatbot account linked to Alfozan’s spouse — which shared key identifiers with Alfozan’s own account — submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 regarding the assembly and deployment of surveillance hardware. The queries sought information on building continuous audio recorders, customizing Wi-Fi connectivity, improving live listening capabilities, encrypting SD cards, and obfuscating remote-access devices. Prompts also included specific technical details, such as the device's custom header and unique MAC address.
In a statement, OpenAI said it discovered the "sophisticated" recording device and "used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier."
"We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest," the company said, adding that it will continue supporting the ongoing investigation. "We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors... and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
OpenAI noted there was no evidence that Alfozan accessed or exfiltrated model weights, source code or customer data.
Alfozan has since been terminated.
Covered by: James Cirrone , Louis Casiano and Lt. Col. Robert Maginnis, (ret.)

articles.title_orig: Cardinal Tagle reads Pope Leo’s homily to bishops: ‘The world has no future without strong families’
articles.title_zh: Cardinal Tagle reads Pope Leo’s homily to bishops: ‘The world has no future without strong families’
articles.content_orig:
VATICAN CITY (OSV News) — Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the newly elected dean of the College of Cardinals , presided over the closing Mass for the Vatican meeting of bishops on marriage and family on Oct. 14, reading aloud a homily that had been prepared by Pope Leo XIV prior to his lung cancer surgery, saying, “The world has no future without strong families.”
Pope Leo had been scheduled to preside over the closing Mass in St. Peter’s Square himself before he shocked the world on Sunday with the announcement that he would be having surgery. As a result, the morning Mass took place without the presence of the pope, just hours after the Vatican announced that late Oct. 13 that the surgery had confirmed a diagnosis of lung cancer for the 71-year-old pope.
Participants in the Oct. 7-14 gathering of the world’s bishops’ conference presidents and the heads of Eastern Catholic churches marking the 10th anniversary of Pope Francis’ document on the family, “Amoris Laetitia,” prayed for Pope Leo’s recovery in the Prayer of the Faithful during the Mass and listened to the words that the pope had prepared for them.
“The world has no future without strong families open to the gift of children and attentive to their education and growth,” Pope Leo wrote in his homily, which emphasized the important role of families in educating and forming the young in the virtues.
The pope highlighted, quoting Amoris in part, that “the importance of the virtues, among which a special place is given to  chastity, which is ‘invaluable for the genuine growth of love between persons,'” in preparing young people for true love in marriage.
“Marriage preparation programs conscientiously developed for this purpose in parishes and pastoral areas are commendable. Yet such courses alone are insufficient, for they must be preceded and supported by an education in love that accompanies a person’s growth from childhood,” he wrote.
Pope Leo highlighted Pope Francis’ post-synodal apostolic exhortation that followed the Synod on the Family, saying that “marriage preparation begins at birth.”
“In this way, love lived within the family — with its moments of struggle, mistakes and failures,  yet also with the marvel of its unpredictable, everyday life — becomes the first school of human affection, the first precious and irreplaceable apprenticeship in the ‘joy of love,'” Pope Leo said.
Pope Leo said that “the values of openness to life and respect for life, from conception to natural death, are also rooted in this charity, which is fundamental to our existence and to our life together as human beings.”
“The family is the foremost guardian of these values, a beacon for the good of humanity,” he added.
As Cardinal Tagle read aloud the pope’s prepared homily, the cardinal noted the presence of Patriarch Paul III Nona, the patriarch of Baghdad of the Chaldeans, whom Pope Leo granted ecclesiastical communion in April.
“I myself have the honor of presiding over this celebration by special mandate of His Holiness Pope Leo XIV, in order to manifest publicly the ecclesiastical communion he has granted to His Beatitude Paul III Nona, Patriarch of Baghdad of the Chaldeans, who is participating in this Eucharist,” the cardinal said.
“Your Beatitude, your presence helps us better understand our identity as the Church, which is  a communion in Christ the Lord of the Churches of various rites and traditions, in a unity that is  expressed tangibly with the Successor of Peter,” he added.
The Vatican did not provide an update on Pope Leo’s clinical condition in the morning following the announcement of his cancer diagnosis, other than that the pope’s first night in the hospital passed calmly.
Following the closing Mass, the bishops, families and experts taking part in the “Amoris Laetitia” meeting are scheduled to meet again in the late afternoon for the presentation of the meeting’s synthesis report at the closing session of the weeklong event.
Due to the personal request of Pope Leo prior to his surgery, the meeting’s final synthesis report will no longer be made public on Oct. 14. Jesuit Father Giacomo Costa, a consultant to the General Secretariat of the Synod, said that the pope requested to postpone the meeting’s final report , noting that Pope Leo “wanted to listen to it and be able to offer his own word on it himself.”
Courtney Mares is Vatican editor for OSV News. Follow her on X @catholicourtney .

articles.title_orig: World’s oldest shipwreck off Turkey: 4,700-year-old amphorae discovered
articles.title_zh: World’s oldest shipwreck off Turkey: 4,700-year-old amphorae discovered
articles.content_orig:
Underwater excavations carried out off the island of Kekova in Antalya have brought to light amphorae dating back around 4,400–4,700 years. The finds, which are said to belong to a wreck from the Early Bronze Age, are expected to shed light on Anatolia's maritime history and trade links in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Turkey's Minister of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, in a post on his social media account, underlined the importance of the ancient vases recovered during the excavations, saying: "In our 'Blue Homeland', we are bringing to light traces of the world's oldest shipwreck."
Clay analyses carried out on the amphorae, which are thought to have been used to transport olive oil or wine, indicate that the jars were probably produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley. The discovery of similar examples in Egypt, Troy and Crete reveals traces of trade and cultural interaction between different regions.
Ancient Roman shipwreck with hundreds of amphorae found off Sicily
Ersoy stated that they would continue to illuminate Anatolia's maritime history with new findings and to preserve the underwater cultural heritage for future generations. The minister also congratulated Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, who's leading the scientific excavations, and the team involved in the work.
Divers conduct research in the wreck area off Kekova. - Credit: Turkey Tourism Promotion and Development Agency
Amphora samples taken from the remains of a wreck identified off the island of Kekova during underwater surveys carried out in previous years by Akdeniz University showed that the ship may date back to the Early Bronze Age.
Acting on permits from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, excavations in the area began in 2026 under the leadership of the Antalya Museum Directorate.
The fact that similar vessels have been found near the pyramids of Giza, Saqqara and Abusir in Egypt, as well as in Troy and Crete, suggests that the cargo carried by the wreck may have been linked to an extensive trade network. Researchers believe that the ship set sail from a port on the Levantine coast and headed towards Troy or Crete.
Divers conduct research in the wreck area off Kekova. - Credit: Turkey Tourism Promotion and Development Agency
One of the amphorae found in the excavations stands out with two holes in its body and nine distinct marks on it. Initial examinations suggest that the jar may have been a churning amphora used in the production of cheese or butter.
This possibility raises the prospect that sailors of the period may have carried goats on long voyages, milked them on board and produced their own dairy products. The finds therefore contribute not only to research into the transport of commercial goods, but also to studies on the everyday conditions of sea journeys and eating habits.

articles.title_orig: Morgan Stanley’s Wealth Arm Brings in Record New Money From IPOs
articles.title_zh: Morgan Stanley’s Wealth Arm Brings in Record New Money From IPOs
articles.content_orig:
Morgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise.
Here's what the company reported:
The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Revenue climbed 12% to $20.34 billion.
The firm's equities trading division, long a marquee business for Morgan Stanley, posted a 41% increase in revenue to $5.8 billion, exceeding the StreetAccount estimate by about $909 million.
Morgan Stanley cited widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. The gains in that business helped offset disappointments elsewhere.
Fixed income trading revenue fell 7% to $2.01 billion, driven by declines in credit and commodities, which is roughly $260 million below expectations.
Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower IPOs and a decline in fixed income underwriting.
Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note.
Morgan Stanley shares declined about 2% in premarket trading.

articles.title_orig: Bulgaria says Russia was likely behind Black Sea drone strikes as rescue operations continue
articles.title_zh: Bulgaria says Russia was likely behind Black Sea drone strikes as rescue operations continue
articles.content_orig:
Eleven sailors are missing following a drone attack on a vessel off the coast of Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian officials, prompting the country’s government to summon the Russian ambassador.
Overnight there were two attacks on merchant vessels in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials said, with one Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship, the “HS Dignity,” being sunk 15 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian village of Krapets – leading to an urgent search and rescue operation.
The search for the missing crew members – believed to be Syrian and Egyptian nationals – is still ongoing as of Tuesday afternoon, the Bulgarian Interior Ministry told CNN. Five people in the 16-person crew had already been rescued by other merchant vessels, the ministry said.
Another cargo ship called the “Chelsea 3,” which sails under the Maltese flag but is Ukrainian-owned, was struck by three drones as it sailed off the coast of Byala, Bulgaria.
Bulgarian border police said they rescued the entire crew of that vessel, which included seven Ukrainian nationals and eight Azerbaijani nationals, some of whom were injured in the attack. All were safely transported to the port of Varna, where the injured crew members received medical assistance, authorities said.
The country’s president and prime minister both strongly condemned the attacks in the vicinity of Bulgarian waters, which they indicated were likely connected to Russia.
“Bulgaria continues to seek support for an investigation into the attacks to determine the country of origin of the drones,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in a social media post on Tuesday.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side. However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation,” Radev added. “I will therefore summon the Russian Ambassador for a meeting today.”
Russian authorities did not immediately comment on the incidents. CNN has reached out to the Russian Embassy in Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, for comment.
Radev added that he informed NATO allies and the European Union of the attacks, as Bulgaria seeks assistance to strengthen air and maritime surveillance and defense.
“I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast,” she said. “Those responsible should be held accountable.”
“The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable,” European Commission President Ursula von Der Leyen said in a statement, condemning the attack without explicitly mentioning Russia.
The latest attacks come after two ships were attacked by marine and aerial drones last week inside Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone. One of those vessels was damaged and the crew were all rescued, Bulgaria’s prime minister said at the time. A second vessel sank after being attacked and the search operation for the 10-person crew was eventually called off.
Attacks in the Black Sea have also heightened fears about global food security, as Ukraine is one of the world’s largest exports of grain.
Russia has repeatedly bombed Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, forcing the country to rely on shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO member states Bulgaria and Romania, as well as on Danube river ports. Meanwhile, Ukraine has also stepped up its attacks on Russian grain-exporting ships.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul condemned Tuesday’s strikes on merchant vessels near Bulgaria, calling them “an attack on international shipping & on global food security, depriving the most vulnerable of much-needed supplies” in a post on X.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that the alliance “will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea” and has “already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank.”
A CNN analysis of vessels near where the “HS Dignity” was sunk found that a NATO warship belonging to the Bulgarian Navy appears to be assisting in the search and rescue operations.
In a statement, the Syrian Seafarers’ Union expressed its “deep concern over the fate of the crew members who are still being searched for.”
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Eyad Kourdi and Thomas Gould contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: WCC commission reviews global initiatives in education, charts future priorities
articles.title_zh: WCC commission reviews global initiatives in education, charts future priorities
articles.content_orig:
The World Council of Churches (WCC) Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation (EEF) concluded its meeting at the WCC Ecumenical Institute at Bossey, reviewing ongoing initiatives and discerning priorities for the future of ecumenical education and formation.
The WCC EEF Commission met at the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey from 4 to 9 October.
Under the theme “ Ecumenical Formation as Ethos and as Programme,” commissioners engaged in theological reflection, strategic planning, and dialogue with WCC leadership, as well as the institute ’ s faculty and students. The meeting also coincided with celebrations marking the 80th anniversary of the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey.
Global and regional initiatives
Discussions focused on strengthening ecumenical formation across the WCC ’ s work, particularly through the Global Ecumenical Theological Institute (GETI) and Regional Ecumenical Theological Institutes (RETIs).
Dr Sara Gehlin, of the Church of Sweden and University College Stockholm, presented outcomes of the 2025 Ecumenical Summer Academy, RETI Europe, held in Sweden under the theme “ Ecumenical Peacebuilding in Times of War: The Legacy of Stockholm 1925.” The programme combined online teaching with seminars and activities during an Ecumenical Week marking the centenary of the 1925 Stockholm Conference.
“ Summer Academy students actively contributed to the jubilee programme as panel speakers. Moreover, students at University College Stockholm helped design, prepare, and implement the rich programme of the Ecumenical Summer Academy,” Gehlin said.
The commission also heard about the North American Regional Ecumenical Theological Institute (NATI–RETI), held in Detroit and Toronto in August 2026, and welcomed ongoing preparations for the Latin American RETI, planned for 2027 as a collaborative, continent-wide initiative bringing together churches, theological institutions, and ecumenical networks across the region.
Commissioners also received the GETI 2025 narrative and visual reports and final publication, which bring together the voices, theological reflections, and hopes of young ecumenists who gathered in Egypt alongside the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order.
Discussions about GETI ’ s future focused particularly on the WCC 12th Assembly in 2030.
“ We have an opportunity to reimagine what it means for GETI to take place alongside a major ecumenical gathering. Rather than remaining a parallel event, GETI should become an integral and active part of the assembly itself, where the theological reflections, lived experiences, questions and challenges of young ecumenists contribute directly to dialogue, discernment, and decision-making,” said Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi, WCC programme executive for Ecumenical Theological Education and GETI 2025 coordinator.
Prof. Dr Vassiliki Stathokosta.
Ecumenical networks take shape
Rev. Tamsyn Kereopa, an Indigenous Māori theologian and ordained minister of the Anglican Church in Aotearoa, New Zealand and Polynesia, updated the commission on the development of the WCC ’ s Global Ecumenical Indigenous Women ’ s Theological Network.
The initiative seeks to address isolation and limited access to mentoring, advanced studies, and international connections. Planned activities include online meetings, research, publications, scholarships, leadership development, storytelling, and intergenerational exchange. The network will be shaped by Indigenous women themselves, with links to GETI and RETIs under consideration and an in-person launch planned for 2028.
Prof. Dr Vassiliki Stathokosta, professor of Orthodox Theology and the Ecumenical Movement at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, presented the Orthodox Women Scholars Network, a global initiative developed by the WCC and the Finnish Evangelical Lutheran Mission.
The network aims to foster collaboration, academic exchange, joint publications, and ecumenical dialogue among women from Eastern and Oriental Orthodox traditions. Planned activities include scholarships, research initiatives, and participation in international theological programmes such as GETI and RETIs. The official launch of the network is planned for March 2027 at the Orthodox Academy of Crete, Greece.
The commission also welcomed the completion of Ecumenism 101, an online introductory course developed by one of its working groups as part of the EEF ’ s commitment to strengthening theological education.
Designed to make ecumenical learning accessible to a wider audience, the course introduces participants to the history, theological foundations, and contemporary challenges of the ecumenical movement. The course will be soon accessible through the WCC website.
The meeting celebrated Bossey ’ s longstanding contribution to theological education and intercultural and interconfessional formation, while considering how the institute can respond to churches ’ needs and prepare future leaders.
Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi and Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung.
Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung, moderator of the EEF Commission, shared joy about the meeting and the 80th anniversary of Bossey.
“ I felt real companionship from the commissioners on our journey as a working commission. There was an honest evaluation of what we have done so far,” she said.
“ Personally, I hope our Bossey students could have more contact with Swiss local churches beyond the French-speaking area. Additionally, Bossey could offer a platform with the theological faculties of European universities because it is geographically very close, and discourse on ecumenism is more important than ever.”
The commission ’ s work will help shape priorities towards 2028 and beyond, ensuring that ecumenical education remains rooted in the realities of churches and communities and equips new generations to advance Christian unity, justice, and reconciliation.

articles.title_orig: World Lung Day 2026 activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients
articles.title_zh: World Lung Day 2026 activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients
articles.content_orig:
Home » World Lung Day 2026 activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients
Catch up on World Lung Day activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients around the world.
From schools in Pakistan to communities in Ethiopia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine, organisations supported through Healthy Lungs for Life grants marked World Lung Day on 25 September with lung health awareness, screening and support activities.
World Lung Day is an annual global awareness day that highlights the importance of lung health and encourages people to take action to prevent lung conditions and protect their lungs.
The grants help organisations deliver projects tailored to local needs and many of this year’s activities focused on communities facing barriers to accessing health services because of geography, displacement or limited resources.
In southern Ethiopia, READIO Ethiopia worked with Community Health Workers and healthcare professionals to bring lung health checks (spirometry) and education directly to Chukare Kebele, a rural community with limited access to healthcare services.
The initiative reached 266 households and more than 1,300 people, including over 180 children under five. It also trained 27 Community Health Workers to recognise warning signs of lung disease, promote early care-seeking and support referrals. Education sessions covered topics including pneumonia, tuberculosis, clean air, smoke-free living, vaccination and recognising when to seek medical advice, helping build local knowledge that will benefit the community beyond World Lung Day.
In Sheffield, United Kingdom, SOAR Community hosted a “Breathe Better, Move More” event in Burngreave, one of Sheffield’s most diverse communities. The event brought together around 80 local residents to learn more about lung health and wellbeing.
Residents could access lung health checks (spirometry), smoking cessation advice, pulmonary rehabilitation information, breathing and singing exercises, and support from local charities and healthcare professionals. The event also brought together local health and community organisations, helping residents learn more about the support available in their area.
The Helping Hand Foundation in Multan, Pakistan, delivered 10 days of activities across schools, healthcare facilities and underserved communities.
More than 1,300 students took part in lung health checks (spirometry) and over 1,200 received structured lung health education. Community outreach activities focused on air pollution, tobacco exposure, vaccination and lung disease prevention, while people needing further assessment were referred for follow-up care. The project also encouraged young people to become ambassadors for lung health within their schools and communities.
In Ukraine, Dnipro State Medical University delivered educational activities and lung health checks (spirometry), despite the ongoing challenges facing the region.
The project also expanded support for internally displaced people living in university accommodation, including access to specialist lung health consultations for those whose healthcare had been disrupted by the conflict. The work demonstrated the determination and commitment of local teams to maintain access to care despite difficult circumstances.
Although each project responded to different local needs, all shared the same goal: helping more people understand their lung health and access the information and services they need.
The European Lung Foundation thanks all Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients, volunteers, healthcare professionals and community partners whose commitment and hard work helped make World Lung Day 2026 a success.
Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients featured in this article included:
Healthy Lungs for Life is the European Lung Foundation (ELF) and European Respiratory Society (ERS) campaign that raises awareness of lung health and encourages people to take action to protect their lungs. Each year, the campaign supports organisations around the world to deliver activities that respond to the needs of their communities, whether through education, screening, prevention or public awareness.
Earlier this year, the European Lung Foundation (ELF) awarded Healthy Lungs for Life grants to organisations across Europe, Africa and Asia. The grants support local activities that raise awareness of lung health, encourage prevention and help people access information and support where they live.
