Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Thanks for joining us today. We’ll close the blog there.
The Nationals brought pineapples to parliament to warn against “risky” imports at issue in negotiations over a trade deal with the European Union.
Labor’s trade minister, Don Farrell , said Coalition MPs walked out of a meeting on the proposed trade deal .
The Reserve Bank has warned staff their pay rise “will not proceed” as planned, if it is rejected in a vote that opens tomorrow.
The Liberal MP Angie Bell said she reached out to Anne Aly over her “poor choice of words” when suggesting she should be “shamed and stoned”.
Pauline Hanson said Bell’s comments were said “in the heat of the moment” and a Nationals MP defended the comments .
Australia and Jordan signed a joint statement on defence and security .
Angus Taylor claimed the prime minister repeatedly “humiliated” the treasurer .
Jim Chalmers introduced Labor’s trusts tax legislation to the House of Representatives.
A Coalition bid to send the bill to an inquiry failed but the Greens deputy leader called for an inquiry to close “loopholes” in the tax.
Anthony Albanese said his “thoughts and prayers” were with Pope Leo XIV following the pope’s cancer diagnosis .
Krishani Dhanji will be back with you tomorrow for the last sitting day of this week. See you then.
Husic rejects Wong’s criticism of Palestinian Authority delaying elections
Ed Husic has pushed back at Penny Wong’s criticism of the Palestinian Authority delaying its elections until 2027.
The foreign minister, with counterparts in Canada, France and the United Kingdom, has called the delay “deeply disappointing”.
double quotation mark Gaza has been levelled. There are Palestinians trying to hold on to their homes in the West Bank. Imagine trying to put a polling station in that circumstance.
The issue is, trying to make sure you have a election process that you can be confident in, that is held in a time that that can occur, and I don’t think it can be, not with those current circumstances …
And there are people who say, well, and the foreign minister I know has made this point, that our [Australia’s] recognition of the state of Palestine was predicated on the elections, and I absolutely agree. But there is a time and a place. And this is not the right time.
Husic says he understands ‘discomfort’ at PM’s office helping write a letter to itself
Ed Husic , the Labor backbencher, has backed independent David Pocock’s concern at the process by which the AI parliamentary committee wrote its letter to the prime minister.
Anthony Albanese’s office signed off on language in the bipartisan letter on the AI inquiry before it was sent to the prime minister. Husic told the ABC:
double quotation mark I think the time for inquiries is over … But having said that, if we are going to do an inquiry, the expectation is it’s done thoroughly. Normally the process would be if you want to do an interim report, you do a report, and the secretariat gets involved, and it puts it together, and the committee has a chance to go through it, and make sure that it’s a thorough response.
So, you know, I can understand why there would be some discomfort about, you know, a letter being put forward in the way that it was done. If you’re going to do it, do it right.
Greens deputy leader hopes to be in government in ‘not too distant future’
The Greens’ new deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May , says she wants the minor party to form government and hopefully soon.
Hodgins-May was on the ABC just now, discussing her objections to the government’s planned reform to its minimum 30% tax rate on discretionary trusts.
She said the Greens still wanted the reforms to happen “this year” but wanted an inquiry to find and close any loopholes in the proposed system:
double quotation mark We’re saying what the government’s dished up at present isn’t good enough. They’ve watered down something to the point where we’re uncomfortable with it. We think that it’s going to create further inequity in the taxation system and benefit the 1% …
Even if it’s not perfect, well, we’re going to fight for it to be better than it is.
Asked whether she accepted that the Greens could not make the laws “perfect,” Hodgins-May said:
double quotation mark Well, until the Greens are in government, which I do hope happens in the not too distant future – when we can put up legislation that we are incredibly proud of and that we think Australians would also get behind – yes, there’s a level of compromise. But let’s be clear, we are sending this to inquiry. We will interrogate it.
US is repeatedly warning Labor on algorithm reforms, says trade minister
Don Farrell has said the US representatives to Australia have repeatedly complained about Labor’s planned algorithm laws but made no direct threats.
The digital duty of care laws are expected to be introduced to parliament this week. Farrell told the ABC:
double quotation mark They’ve been raised with me every time I’ve met with the Americans. We obviously have a difference of opinion. We certainly don’t believe anything we are doing is contrary to our free trade agreement … I’ve tried to explain to the Americans that our objective is to protect our citizens, particularly young people. And so far, there hasn’t been a direct response.
He said the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer , has raised a range of social media issues but there had never been a threat of a consequence for the laws.
double quotation mark In a few minutes, I’m meeting the new American ambassador. He may or he may not [mention the laws]. I don’t know. But if he does, I will explain to him, as I’ve explained to Jamieson Greer, our job as an Australian government is to protect our citizens, and this is one of the ways we’re doing it.
The trade minister says Coalition representatives have walked out of meetings on the European Union trade deal but some of its members might still be interested in getting the deal done.
Don Farrell has told the ABC that Ted O’Brien had walked out on him while he was explaining the deal, along with the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, who protested the trade deal while holding a pineapple earlier today.
But Farrell told Patricia Karvelas the Coalition’s and Greens’ objections to the deal did not mean it could not proceed, adding:
double quotation mark I have to find nine sensible senators beyond the 30 that I’ve got. I’m discussing it with everybody. And don’t think for one moment, Patricia, that the opposition is united in their position against this agreement …
I’m hopeful, in fact, I’m perhaps even confident that there are enough senators in the Australian Senate right now who understand just how important this agreement is for Australia to get through.
The Reserve Bank of Australia has told its staff they will miss out on their pay rise if they don’t support a disputed wage deal.
RBA staff rejected a 9.5% increase over three years in July and have fought management for a better offer but the bank will put a roughly similar offer to a vote tomorrow.
Susan Woods , the RBA’s chief operating officer, told staff in an email today the 9.5% offer was competitive. She said:
double quotation mark We have genuinely negotiated to arrive at this position and are at the limit of what we can responsibly offer while meeting our obligations as a public institution and Australia’s central bank.
Staff have already missed six weeks of pay rise as their deal would have started in September. Woods told staff the RBA would not offer any back pay, adding:

articles.title_orig: How the pre-election search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home breaks Justice Dept. norms
articles.title_zh: How the pre-election search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home breaks Justice Dept. norms
articles.content_orig:
Vice President JD Vance told Fox News Digital the administration will find out if Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., committed a crime after Homeland Security Investigations raided her Washington, D.C., home.
EXCLUSIVE: TYLER, Texas — Vice President JD Vance told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that the Trump administration has no plans to "butt in" on a Department of Justice (DOJ) investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., after the raid on her Washington, D.C., home the day prior.
Vance, however, insisted that the law will be enforced if immigration fraud is uncovered.
"We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," the vice president said in an exclusive interview following a midterm campaign rally in the Lone Star State on Tuesday.
"We really want to let the law, the facts drive this," he continued. "And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to."
Omar's Washington, D.C., home was subject to a predawn raid on Monday conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the principal investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), as first reported by Fox News Digital.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’
Conservatives repeatedly accused then-President Joe Biden's DOJ of politically persecuting President Donald Trump and his allies after his first term in office ended.
Most notably for critics, Trump's Mar-a-Lago home was infamously raised by the FBI as part of an investigation into alleged mishandling of classified documents. That case was closed when Trump again won the presidency in 2024.
"In the Trump administration, unlike the previous administration, we let the facts and the law drive this stuff — so the president and I really don't butt ourselves in the DOJ investigations," Vance said. "We're not trying to micromanage this. We're not trying to tell [Attorney General] Todd Blanche to do one thing or another. We try to let the facts drive this thing."
"So we're gonna let the investigation unfold," he went on before warning: "If, of course, criminal wrongdoing is discovered or potentially fraudulent immigration is uncovered, then obviously there will be legal proceedings to follow that."
Rep. Ilhan Omar dismissed Vice President JD Vance’s claims that the Justice Department is investigating her for alleged immigration and fraud violations, referring to House Republicans' attention to the matter as politically motivated. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
While an investigation into potential immigration fraud related to a sitting member of Congress is unprecedented, Vance reiterated that authorities will go where the facts take them — no matter the circumstances of the case.
"I think we have to let the facts and the law drive this, right? So I don't think you can say because politics might be difficult or politics might be easy, you can't follow the law. You have to actually enforce the law as it exists," he said.
COULD TRUMP REVOKE ILHAN OMAR'S CITIZENSHIP FOR ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE? EX FEDERAL PROSECUTOR BREAKS IT DOWN
Additionally, the vice president slammed Omar for what he views as a negative attitude towards the United States despite it being the country where her family fled to escape civil war in Somalia in 1991.
"And to the question of it being unprecedented, I mean, what I'd say is that Ilhan Omar herself is a very unprecedented person," he said.
Rep. Ilham Omar, D-Minn., is seeking another term in Minnesota’s heavily Democratic 5th Congressional District. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call/Getty Images)
"We have very rarely had a person in Congress who seems to have such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life," Vance said. "Now, that's not a crime."
"But we're going to see whether she did commit a crime. And if she did, we're obviously going to follow the law," he reiterated.
Vance made the comments after rallying on behalf of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton at the Tyler Pounds Regional Airport in Tyler, Texas, a city about 100 miles east of Dallas.
Paxton is running in a neck-and-neck race with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico just three weeks before Election Day, as Republicans fight desperately to hold control of Congress.
ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME
Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Tyler Pounds Regional Airport on Oct. 13, 2026, in Tyler, Texas. Vance is in Texas to campaign for Republican candidates on the November midterm ballot. (Saul Loeb-Pool/Getty Images)
Omar responded to the raid on social media Monday afternoon, both from her personal and government X accounts.
"I’m ok," Omar wrote on her own X account hours after the search. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."
TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID
In a post from her official government X account from just after 1:30 p.m., Omar elaborated further.
"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," she said.
"Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Omar's office for comment, but did not hear back before publication.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Cornell cancels fraternity parties over sexual assault case
articles.title_zh: Cornell cancels fraternity parties over sexual assault case
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as it faces a backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago.
Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house.
In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the remainder of the university year.
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said.
"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.
Members of the university's Faculty Senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff, are due on Wednesday to debate whether they have confidence in the Cornell leadership to "effectively address the ongoing crisis".
The issue is expected to be put to a vote in due course, though a majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture.
Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.
In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".
"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.
Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.
The university also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate support systems as well.
Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, universities are required to provide measures of support to help survivors continue with their studies after assaults.
Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault. In an interview with the New York Times, published on Tuesday, Kotlikoff said he had only learned that Jane Doe had withdrawn from the university after she filed a legal case over the alleged assault last month.
In his written statement, which was addressed to the Cornell community, Kotlikoff  said the university would allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.
These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", the university president added.
Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.
Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.
State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.
Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".
He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

articles.title_orig: Prosecutor calls Russell Brand a ‘ruthless’ sexual predator at trial
articles.title_zh: Prosecutor calls Russell Brand a ‘ruthless’ sexual predator at trial
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Russell Brand behaved as a “ruthless” sexual predator when he assaulted six women over the course of a decade, a prosecutor said Wednesday as she opened the rape and sexual assault case against the actor-comedian.
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The charges involve six women and alleged offenses between 1999 and 2009.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors at Southwark Crown Court in London that the six women, who do not know each other, were assaulted in “a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at (Brand’s) home address.”
Russell Brand arrives at court for sexual assault trial
She said that at the time Brand had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact, and “women were simply a means to an end.”
“He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said.
Brand is on bail and arrived at court Wednesday to a crowd of photographers and video journalists. He said he felt “blessed.”
“I feel, of course, concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved,” Brand said. “That’s my prayer.”
Known for risque stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.”
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

articles.title_orig: Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
articles.title_zh: Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
articles.content_orig:
UK foreign secretary will call for World Bank and others to help governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt.
Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign.
“The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say.
“In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.”
Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs.
“We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say. “Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.”
The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.
He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill.
Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence.
Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education.
Miliband will argue that making the global financial system work better for emerging economies will also help to attract more private investment – a key aim of the World Bank under the current president, Ajay Banga.
The UK is due to take up the presidency of the G20 group of nations next year – a key global forum for discussing global financial issues, including sovereign debt, which includes emerging economies such as China, India, South Africa and Brazil.
The chancellor, John Healey , will set out his own G20 priorities in Bangkok later this week, including mobilising more resources from the balance sheets of the IMF and the World Bank.
after newsletter promotion
When the UK held the chair of the narrower G8 group in 2005, at the leaders’ summit at the Gleneagles hotel the UK secured agreements that eventually resulted in more than 30 countries receiving large-scale debt write-downs.
Miliband will say resources are now more constrained – but as well as debt refinancing for a large number of countries, he will demand an overhaul of the “common framework” for restructuring the debts of countries unable to pay.
The framework is widely criticised as too slow and cumbersome. Among other reforms, the UK wants to see changes to ensure private creditors cannot hold up negotiations – as has happened in recent cases including that of Ethiopia.
The foreign secretary will also call for overhauls to allow help to be made available more rapidly to countries in trouble. “We need finance teed up in advance of crises, so that governments get support in days, not months,” he will say.
Miliband will be speaking at the launch of a report by the Rockefeller Foundation that calls for a “surge” in affordable financing from the IMF and the World Bank to debt-burdened countries.
Tim Jones, the policy director of the campaign group Debt Justice, welcomed Miliband’s focus on the issue but said a litmus test of any plan would be whether private sector creditors bear some of the costs. “Action on debt relief is urgently needed. That must include private lenders sharing in the cost. Otherwise public money will just bail out private lenders rather than be used for investment.”

articles.title_orig: Fairphone’s latest repairable earbuds are smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting
articles.title_zh: Fairphone’s latest repairable earbuds are smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting
articles.content_orig:
The Fairbuds 2 are just as repairable as the first pair, and are launching in the US.﻿
The Fairbuds 2 are just as repairable as the first pair, and are launching in the US.﻿
Repairable, ethical phone brand Fairphone has released its second pair of earbuds. The Fairbuds 2 are just as repairable as the first generation , but deliver improved audio and almost twice the battery life. The Fairbuds 2 are out now in the UK and Europe from £99 / €119, and a US launch at $119 will follow on November 2nd.
The Fairbuds 2 have been redesigned from the ground up, moving to a stemmed design, available in black or green, and a case that’s 37 percent smaller than the first generation. Despite that shrinking hardware, Fairphone has almost doubled the buds’ battery life, which now totals 40 hours without active noise cancellation, with eight hours on the buds alone, dropping to six with ANC on. Charging is over USB-C, and takes a couple hours for a full top-up. Sadly Qi wireless charging isn’t supported — though it isn’t on Apple’s $129 AirPods 5 either.
I never used the original Fairbuds, but sound should be improved here thanks to new bio-cellulose dynamic drivers, though still at the same 11mm size, plus refined ANC and new support for the LDAC codec. Multipoint connectivity supports two devices at once, and a five-band EQ in the app lets you fine-tune audio.
I’ve been using the Fairbuds 2 for a couple of weeks, and while I wouldn’t say they’re the most polished or premium earbuds you’ll find for $120, I’ve got no real complaints either. They look great, the simple touch controls work well, and audio quality is good, if a little muddy at times, lacking the expansive sound stage of some other buds. The ANC has impressed me too, cancelling out most background noise I’ve wanted rid of.
Of course, the main reason to buy Fairbuds is the repairability, which remains relatively unique — though European legal changes will force other manufacturers to catch up soon. Here, Fairphone has concentrated on matching what it offered in the first Fairbuds, but that’s still impressive: the battery in each earbud can be removed in less than a minute without any tools, while a single T5 screw is all that’s between you and the cell in the case. Spare parts will be sold on Fairphone’s site, with a total of seven user-replaceable parts, including the eartips and sleeves. An IP54 rating guarantees some additional measure of protection against rain and sweat, though not complete waterproofing, and a three-year warranty should deliver a little extra peace of mind.
The other side of Fairphone’s promise is transparency about its production and materials. The company says that 49 percent of the materials in the Fairbuds 2 are “fair and recycled,” including recycled plastics and rare earth minerals, and cobalt, gold, and silver sourced with fair mining credits . It also says the buds themselves are assembled under fair working conditions.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title_orig: Oil price hikes, Saudi-Houthi strikes carry on amid Trump's midterm pause on Iran war
articles.title_zh: Oil price hikes, Saudi-Houthi strikes carry on amid Trump's midterm pause on Iran war
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Civil Defense issued an early warning Wednesday for Riyadh and Al-Kharj, alerting residents to potential danger, according to a local news outlet cited by a public Telegram board.
The alert came as Saudi Arabia faced renewed threats from the Iran-backed Houthis, who urged “international shipping companies,” civilians and workers to evacuate airports and oil facilities, which they declared legitimate military targets.
The Saudi-led coalition said earlier Wednesday that it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh, while several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.
Saudi authorities had also issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh before the warning was lifted.
The escalating conflict has threatened Saudi oil infrastructure, regional shipping lanes and the kingdom’s broader economy as the Iran war continues to spill across the Middle East.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Record-high oil tanker rates are squeezing Asian refiners that rely heavily on Middle Eastern crude, as the Iran war continues to drive up the cost of shipping fuel through the Strait of Hormuz , the International Energy Agency said Wednesday in a new report.
Asian oil refiners have faced the highest transportation costs because cargoes are being moved through the Strait of Hormuz to secondary tankers for onward delivery, the IEA reported.
The freight rate for a very large crude carrier from the Middle East Gulf to Asia rose to around $36 a barrel by early October, more than five times the cost before the Iran war, the agency said.
Refiners can partly offset the spike by buying U.S. crude , but those freight rates have also surged. Shipping costs from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China have topped $37 a barrel, according to the IEA.
The higher delivered crude costs pushed margins for Asian refiners processing medium sour crude into negative territory in September, adding another strain on global fuel markets as the war disrupts oil flows and shipping lanes.
Reuters contributed to this report.
The European Commission proposed delaying methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports by one year Wednesday, citing concerns over fuel supply as the Iran war continues to disrupt global energy markets.
The rules, originally set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027, would require foreign oil and gas suppliers to the European Union to monitor and report methane emissions.
Under the proposed change, the rules would begin in 2028, while importers would have until May 31, 2029, to prove their oil, gas and coal imports from the previous year complied with EU-equivalent reporting standards.
“This one-year postponement of the import-related provisions is designed to help avoid additional pressures on the security of supply of imported fossil fuels in the current geopolitical context,” the European Commission said.
The law was designed to clamp down on methane leaks from oil and gas infrastructure, but it has faced growing pressure after the Iran war disrupted global energy supplies and intensified concerns over fuel availability this winter.
The United States, Europe’s biggest liquefied natural gas supplier, warned the EU in June that the methane law could disrupt fuel deliveries, a position backed by companies including ExxonMobil.
French President Emmanuel Macron also pressed for a delay, warning the rules could create legal risks for Europe’s fuel importers.
Industry groups want an even longer three-year postponement, arguing suppliers are not ready to comply and could divert LNG cargoes away from Europe.
“Without a mechanism for further extensions, we risk finding ourselves in exactly the same situation 12 months from now,” a spokesperson for the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers said.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Iran might be getting a midterm reprieve on action from the U.S. military and President Donald Trump , but that might be running out in a few weeks, Trump warned Tuesday night.
He told his Alaska rally crowd the U.S. has "had it" with Iran.
“ We're going to do a number ,” Trump said. “They're just waiting. They're waiting.
" Wait until you see what we do to Iran ," he added. “Because we sort of had it, you know, we've had it, but, you know, it doesn't matter.
“The big thing is they were not going to have a nuclear weapon. And they want what's buried under thousands of tons of rock."
President Donald Trump told supporters at an Alaska rally that Iran is “the bully of the Middle East no longer,” while predicting the war will “end very soon” and arguing Tehran will not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
“They were the bully of the Middle East, but they’re the bully of the Middle East no longer ,” Trump said. “But it’s going to end very soon. Very soon. They have no Navy. They have no air force. They have no anti-aircraft.”
Trump said Iran was “two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon” before U.S. action, adding that “other presidents should have done what I did.”
“You’re not going to have a nuclear Iran,” Trump said. “Because if you did, if you want to see trouble, if you want to see trouble, let them have a nuclear weapon. You’ll see trouble. That’ll be real trouble.”
Trump also tied the war to oil prices, saying the U.S. had kept key waterways open.
“We opened the straits. The straits have been open,” Trump said. “We’ve been taking more oil out of the straits now than we did before the war started. Believe it or not, we control the straits . That’s why the oil stayed where it is.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he does not favor a preemptive strike against Iran before Israel’s Oct. 27 election, while warning Tehran and its proxies that Israel would respond forcefully if attacked.
“It is not convenient for us, it’s no good,” Netanyahu told Israel’s Army Radio when asked about a possible preemptive strike and claims from political rivals that he was seeking a military confrontation ahead of the election.
“Even if Iran fires missiles at us they will blame me,” Netanyahu said.
He declined to elaborate on whether Israel could strike Iran after the election or on his recent discussions with Washington about Tehran.
Israel and Iran have not traded fire since June, after months of direct conflict following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran and Tehran’s retaliation against Israel and Gulf states.
Asked whether Israel was helping Saudi Arabia respond to widening attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthis, Netanyahu said, “I don’t get into those matters. I can only tell you that many countries in the Middle East are turning to us following our massive success and tremendous achievements.”
Defense Minister Israel Katz separately warned Hezbollah against attacking Israel from Lebanon.
“Hezbollah will suffer a severe blow and lose additional territories in southern Lebanon within the Nabatieh and Litani regions, which will become part of Israel’s permanent security zone. The IDF (Israel Defence Forces) is prepared to carry out the manuever,” Katz said.
Reuters contributed to this report.
U.S. consumer prices accelerated in September as gasoline costs surged, adding fresh economic pressure on President Donald Trump and Republicans weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.6% in September after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said Wednesday.
Over the 12 months through September, CPI advanced 3.7%, up from 3.4% in August.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected CPI to rise 0.6% on the month and 3.6% from a year earlier.
Gasoline prices soared 7.1% in September, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data, as the Iran war and threats to Middle East oil flows continued to roil energy markets.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Roller coaster rider’s death puts spotlight on the safety of ever more thrilling rides
articles.title_zh: Roller coaster rider’s death puts spotlight on the safety of ever more thrilling rides
articles.content_orig:
On a warm Columbus Day afternoon, with many area schools closed for Fall Break, the winding midways of Six Flags Over Georgia must have made a wooded stretch about 10 miles west of downtown Atlanta feel both electric and nostalgic.
Carousel music mixed with the thunderous roar of roller coaster carts exploding through dizzying loops and heart-stopping drops. The piercing screams and cheers of thrill seekers clashed with blaring music and barkers calling crowds to their games. The sweet, woody scent of Georgia pines blended with the wafting aroma of sizzling hot dogs and hamburgers.
Under a skyline of soaring steel structures, the Goliath roller coaster stands as one of the Southeast’s most popular attractions. The 210-second ride reaches a top speed of 70 miles an hour and an elevation of 200 feet along 4,480 feet of track, featuring “razor-sharp turns” and “colossal hills,” according to the park . The “hypercoaster,” as Six Flags describes it, celebrated “ 20 years of airtime ” last June and “challenges even the bravest of the brave.”
On Monday, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old Atlanta resident and “cherished member” of Wesley International Academy, an Atlanta public charter school, died after falling from the coaster , according to police. Several other park-goers were injured.
Kariem was Wesley International Academy’s IT manager, a technology teacher and robotics coach, the school said.
A fun-filled, early autumn holiday turned into successive moments of unforgettable horror. Park-goers watched as Kariem was ejected from the ride, striking other patrons as he plunged onto the roof of a haunted house attraction, one witness told CNN affiliate WXIA.
It was shortly before 4 p.m.
“Someone has fallen off of the Goliath ride,” a 911 dispatcher is heard saying, according to WSB Radio. “Come to the park.”
Part of the horrifying incident, as Kariem struck the cart, was recorded on the coaster camera that captures images for riders, another witness told the station. The images have been taken down.
Kariem struck the cart three times, a couple who were on the ride told CNN affiliate WXIA.
“We were having a great time and to just screaming ‘Oh my God, what is happening?’ ” the woman said. Before the ride, she said, workers checked the safety harnesses.
Another witness described Kariem, at one point, landing on a girl two rows in front of her.
CiCi Nelson was in line to ride the Goliath coaster when a cart pulled up. One seat was empty. Other riders were in hysterics. She recalled one man “freaking out, saying someone fell off.” He urged park staff to call for help.
The safety bar over the empty seat appeared loose, Nelson said. A girl on the cart, covered in blood, appeared to be injured, she added.
“My stomach just dropped and I was terrified,” Nelson told CNN.
What caused him to fall remains unclear. Investigators were examining the circumstances surrounding the incident, according to the Cobb County Police Department’s Major Crimes Unit.
Emergency personnel rushed to the loading station as Nelson and others were asked to leave the area.
Moving away, Nelson said, she could see riders in another cart stuck on the steel track high above the park. If not for an issue calling up a ride pass on her phone, she recalled, she would have been on the cart with the now empty seat.
“If it wasn’t for that one extra minute my group had to wait for my flash app to show the ride attendant my QR code, we would’ve been on there,” Nelson said.
One of those trapped on Goliath’s 200-foot incline was Ben Edwards, who was visiting from Canada. Above Atlanta’s suburbs, Edwards and others were stuck for at least an hour.
“Obviously, where the chaos was, that was the priority, and evacuating everybody else,” he told WANF TV.
Below, Edwards could see park staff and paramedics swarming the ride’s entrance.
“We realized that there was something bad that happened,” he said. “Very tragic. The first thing you think about is the people you’re on the ride with.”
Rahim Hakmati, a Six Flags Over Georgia season ticket holder, arrived at the park as large groups of people were leaving. A person had fallen off Goliath, he heard someone say. As he approached the ride, security directed people away.
The night before, Hakmati told CNN, he rode Goliath and “didn’t notice anything unusual or experience any problems.” Now he and others were being asked to leave the park.
On the coaster’s steep incline, the stranded riders were guided down a stairway along tracks by park staff around 5 p.m., aerial video from WXIA showed.
Kariem was found unresponsive and not breathing when police arrived.
His “presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched,” the school district said. “Atlanta Public Schools extends its deepest condolences to the family, friends, and loved ones of Mr. Kariem.”
He was with the district for over 12 years, a spokesperson said.
“Our thoughts are with everyone mourning his loss during this difficult time,” the statement said.
At least 10 roller coasters across six other Six Flags in the US and Canada have been temporarily closed “out of an abundance of caution,” a Six Flags spokesperson said.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” Six Flags Over Georgia said in a statement. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones.”
The manufacturer of the roller coaster, Bolliger & Mabillard, described Monday’s incident as “tragic” and said the company is “actively investigating” it. The company declined further comment until it has “a better understanding of what transpired.”
Monday’s tragedy occurred nearly two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in California announced it would permanently close its world-famous ride X2, following a CNN investigation that documented reports of serious injuries and deaths associated with the ride.
“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” Cobb County Board of Commissioners Chairwoman Lisa Cupid said.
“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories.”
Caleb Sedam and Brandon Casper, Indianapolis residents who were visiting Atlanta, spent Monday at the park with friends. They told WXIA the fatal accident occurred one cart ahead of them. They were stuck on the coaster for about an hour.
“When you go to a park, you have this natural presumption that you’re there for a good time and that you’re going to be safe,” Sedam said Tuesday.
At the entrance to the coaster, a woman cried. She later told them she witnessed the fatal fall.
“It could have been anybody. It could have been us,” Casper said.
CNN’s Isabel Rosales, Meredith Edwards, Julianna Bragg, Avni Trivedi, Elise Hammond, Karina Tsui, Rebekah Riess, Sara Smart, Catherine Nicholls, Mark Morales and Chenelle Woody contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Cousins make mark in art world
articles.title_zh: Cousins make mark in art world
articles.content_orig:
Cousins and artists Shelley Elser, left, and Kevin Davenport, right, live on one of the more recognizable properties along South Park Loop Road, adorned with their own art and collected works from artists across the world.
Artistic duo Shelley Elser and Kevin Davenport share an art compound — a well-known landmark for South Park Loop travelers. The cousins are part creators, part archivists, and 100% community members.
As doves move from tree to tree, Davenport and Elser hold space not just for traditional trades and craft work but for the evolution of art. The property is unmistakeable, outlined by gigantic metal daisies and dotted with work by John Simms, a former neighbor and mentor.
Davenport was nominated to complete Terry Chambers’ unfinished golden bear sculpture, which stands on its hind legs outside the two-floor studio on the property. The studio itself is clearly highly functional — blacksmith shop on the bottom floor, countless creative materials and other tools on the top. And yet, being filled with everything from partially constructed, unfinished pieces to photography, glass and Elsner’s foraged items and vignettes, the space feels a bit like a Victorian-era curiosity cabinet on steroids.
“Did you know mourning doves mate for life and everyone hangs out together, all the generations?” Davenport said while walking between his fence made of vertical mufflers and a shed adorned with beehive patterns.
The cousins are eight years apart; Elsner was born in 1966, and Davenport in ’74, and are avid bird fans, monitoring the nesting pair of osprey on the property, known to them as “ShelleyStone Park.” The “park” is filled with birds and art in every direction.
The duo is behind many creative projects in Jackson, including clubhouse fireplaces and staircase railings. Elsner has a background in jewelry making; she worked with former husband and business partner Dan Harrison at Dan Shelley Jewelers, once located in Gaslight Alley. Elsner moved to Jackson in the mid-1970s, and her family members soon joined. She and Harrison built their business of Teton- and totem-infused designs and men’s rings, among their silversmithing.
Davenport unapologetically said his cousin told him to move here to make art, so he did. Fover 25 years, he has curated an atelier spanning glasswork and bronze casting to metalwork, welding and milling. He’s created fireplace doors, railings, gates, lighting, signs and sculpture (with details like a Hardy fishing rod and reel, cutthroat trout and the Tetons etched in fireplace tools).
Davenport’s shop pays homage to those who have passed through. A garage door doubles as a white wall for sentiments and signatures. Along another wall hangs American sculptor David Smith’s entire collection of tools. Smith was known for abstract and Impressionist designs.
“Right now,” Davenport said, “I am working on a bespoke metal sheetwork that’s flat and 20-gauge thin (to) make it three-dimensional form. And so I’m making queen bees that walk across there and then the idea is that they’ll be freestanding.”
A member of the California Blacksmith Association, Davenport said he travels around the world about every two years to teach with other members.
Both artists love bones and history, but repairing an elk mount and making it a bronze took nearly a year and a half. Davenport had to find a mold maker in Cody and worked with a foundry in Oregon to find the right patinas.
Elser suggested doing mounts of grizzlies. While grizzly skulls are illegal in Wyoming, the Alaska Department of Game and Fish worked with Davenport to obtain a Kodiak bear skull — one that he’s been able to cast into new line of sculpture.
Some sculpture, on the other hand, has ancient origins. Before leaving his shop, Davenport pulls out a 75-million-year-old ammolite gemstone for which he’s designing a stand.
Elser has been running support for her younger cousin and has lately been spending more time prioritizing self-care, including taking classes at the Senior Center.
“We’re not married,” she said. “Being relatives is so much easier.”
Visit Davenport’s website at MetalByKevin.com .
Contact Tibby Plasse via valley@jhnewsandguide.com .

articles.title_orig: The Geerlings Gaze Into Their Crystal Ball for Radio
articles.title_zh: The Geerlings Gaze Into Their Crystal Ball for Radio
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › News Makers
During Radio World’s late-summer conversation with Joe and Jeff Geerling, the dynamic father-and-son duo who combine broadcast engineering and software development expertise, a funny thing happened: An impromptu podcast broke out.
As we discussed with the Geerlings the convergence of traditional RF tools and IT management, we asked them about two topics on the minds of station managers and engineers this fall: cybersecurity and AI.
Finally, in such a competitive landscape, Joe and Jeff offer one simple piece of advice to radio station operators: Stay small.
And a reminder to check out our September story on what makes the Geerlings tick .
Joe’s grandfather was born in 1900. When he was 82, Joe recalled, he made a remark about the velocity of changes he saw over his lifetime following the industrial revolution.
“When he was born, there were really no cars. He saw streets pop up, buildings, airplanes, rockets, air conditioning. In his mind, how could anyone see as much change as he did?
“Well, I’ve seen a whole lot change too in my lifetime, and with the tools we have, I don’t think it’s going to slow down,” Joe said.
An engineering veteran, Joe has spent decades protecting physical transmitter buildings. He sees network security as a natural extension of the job.
“Every time you connect something to the internet, you should be thinking about security,” Joe said. “I think the majority of engineers always had that mindset, protecting the plant. So this requirement is welcome. You have to do something.”
But recent FCC mandates regulating IT and security in the audio chain have opened a window of concern for smaller stations.
“You’re never going to get high-end Cisco gear at a small tower site,” Joe explained. “By protecting the EAS first, everybody is going to make sure they have a router with a complicated password and that’s probably going to solve 95% of the problem.”
Jeff, meanwhile, grew up in the dawn of the internet age. It would be a delight to shop with him at a certain computer retail outlet.
Taking advantage of the conveniences that running audio over IP offers requires configuration ahead of time. Network security has become a fundamental part of most businesses.
Jeff pointed out that the engineers who built the legacy systems still running today were RF experts, not IT professionals. Thinking about digital security requires a different mindset.
“There is still gear running from the early 1990s that doesn’t use encryption,” Jeff warned. “If they get physical access or into your network remotely, it’s game over.”
Even today’s broadcast software carries baggage. Joe observed how some on-air automation systems still demand administrative privileges to run simply because that is how they were coded 20 years ago.
Then there is the elephant in today’s tech room. AI.
Both Geerlings view the AI boom through a nuanced lens. For Joe, it brings back memories of broadcasters relying entirely on the AP teletype wire.
“When I first started, it wasn’t unusual for stations to ‘rip and read’ off the AP teletype,” he recalled. “They would tear off the story and read it on air without thinking about relating it to their audience.
“For me, AI is the same thing. You need to make sure you are using it and that it isn’t using you.”
Joe sees potential for AI as an internal tech support knowledge base. But he draws a hard line at replacing on-air talent.
Jeff uses AI as a sounding board for his software development but he is wary of large-language models that slurp up creator content and summarize it without attribution.
He’s seen fluctuations in visits to his blog and realizes the proliferation of AI slop plays a part.
“And worse, these AI tools take the things I write, summarize them and just give people the little nugget they want,” Jeff said.
Still, he admits the tech is impossible to ignore. He describes it with a clever analogy.
“I think of it like a drill,” Jeff said. “I have a manual hand drill where you crank the chuck. Now, you have battery drills you only have to charge once every six months. AI is similar for me.”
Jeff does not perform as much software development as he used to. He looks at AI from a content creator perspective. But he knows other developers who will burn as many as two million AI tokens a minute — tokenmaxxing as it is known in some circles — spending around $500 a day.
“I think it goes back to what my dad said,” Jeff explained, “you work with it and check, rather than saying, ‘give me this thing’ and immediately shipping it. It’s like the news. Grabbing a summary and pasting it directly only on your website is much different from helping to identify themes within an article.”
Our chat could have gone on for much longer. The pair offered well-spoken, articulate takes on all the topics we covered. Nothing was off limits. Midterm general election predictions, anyone?
But with their uniquely different perspectives looking at radio, it felt like the most opportune time to ask the Geerlings to gaze into their crystal ball: What is over-the-air radio’s path to stay relevant?
A desire for genuine human connection tied directly into Joe’s primary advice for smaller broadcasters.
“Stay small. Small is cool,” Joe advised. “Nobody was going to sit there and say, ‘I’m going to play the same thing as St. Louis’s big rock station, won’t that be cool?’ Listeners could already hear the big stations. Small stations had to be local and if they stopped, they would die.”
As we’ve heard previously, operating a small-town radio station might offer the chance to run a “boutique” style business . Despite his busy schedule with video creation, Jeff has those feelings. He even told us that running a small station would be a dream gig.
But the barrier to entry, he said, ends up a detriment.
“When I look at the licensing fees and the companies that you’d compete with just to get a tiny slice of the pie, it’s just discouraging,” Jeff said.
But despite the red tape and the uncertain future of the AM band, the Geerlings are optimistic about the underlying technology and the medium itself.
“I think that there’s always room for broadcasting with RF just like in TV,” Jeff concluded. “The only way it can die is if the industry kills it, not if people stop listening. People stop caring if the industry doesn’t care.”
If the father-and-son duo in St. Louis are still infatuated with the medium, that feels like the best vote of confidence we could have.

articles.title_orig: Namibia takes step towards nuclear power
articles.title_zh: Namibia takes step towards nuclear power
articles.content_orig:
In an announcement from the Office of the Prime Minister, John Titus, a Director in the Department of Energy in the Ministry of Industries, Mines and Energy, has been named as Namibia's Nuclear Commissioner. As well as coordinating the technical programme of the Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation (NEPIO) and heading its Secretariat, Titus's appointment establishes a central focal point for coordinating the country's nuclear energy preparatory work.
"The decision to support a long-term nuclear power programme is a decision to invest in the institutional, technical and human capacity required to prepare Namibia for its future energy needs," Prime Minister Tjitunga Elijah Ngurare said.
Ngurare has also constituted the NEPIO Management Committee to provide "high-level policy coordination and strategic oversight". Made up of executive directors from the Office of the Prime Minister, the Ministry of Industries, Mines and Energy, the Ministry of International Relations and Trade, the Ministry of Health and Social Services, and the National Planning Commission, and guided by the International Atomic Energy Agency, the NEPIO Management Committee will assess issues ranging from nuclear safety and security to financing, radioactive waste management, environmental protection, human resource capacity, nuclear power and public engagement.
Namibia holds about 7% of the world's uranium reserves, and has a long history of uranium mining: the Rössing uranium mine has marked 50 years of production this year. The country's 2024 uranium production of 7333 tU made it the world's third largest producer behind Kazakhstan and Canada.
Namibia's domestic electricity production is currently dominated by hydro, and the country relies heavily on imports of electricity, mainly from South Africa.
The Namibian government approved its first Nuclear Industry Strategy in October 2025, and earlier this year a draft nuclear bill - replacing the 2005 Atomic Energy and Radiation Protection Act and establishing a nuclear commission, a nuclear institute and an independent regulatory authority - underwent nationwide public consultation.
"Namibia's substantial uranium resources have strengthened the case for exploring nuclear energy as part of efforts to secure the country's long-term energy needs, promote local mineral beneficiation and value addition, and unlock greater economic value from its natural resources," according to the Office of the Prime Minister.

Why we built our Center for Energy and the Environment
The world needs more energy. That energy will help power factories, deploy AI, electrify the economy, and expand energy access. Meeting that demand while balancing affordability, security, reliability, and sustainability, what we call the "Four Forces,” is one of the defining economic opportunities of our era.
In 2021, JPMorganChase set ambitious targets to help us seize that opportunity: our portfolio-level carbon intensity targets and our $2.5 trillion Sustainable Development Target. We are helping increase supply by facilitating nearly $100 billion each year to add new energy from all sources. We are also helping decarbonize: our tax-oriented investing team alone has helped finance one in four gigawatts of U.S. renewables and storage. For more than 125 years, we have banked companies that help build and power the global economy, and we intend to bank companies that help power the world for the next one hundred and twenty five.
We are proud to have helped shape the banking industry’s approach to climate, including as the first U.S. bank to publish detailed financed-emissions targets and an Energy Supply Financing Ratio. Since we set targets, we said that our approach would evolve as conditions changed and better information became available, so we continue to test our approach against experience and evolve as appropriate. We believe that is part of disciplined management.
Based on that belief, we also continue to evolve how we approach energy and environmental issues more broadly. This includes the launch of the JPMorganChase Center for Energy and the Environment (CE&E). CE&E is JPMorganChase's hub for expertise on the Four Forces shaping energy and environmental outcomes. One of the things my team is focused on is our environmental targets, which we have evolved to better reflect how we support low-carbon energy and to reflect updated decarbonization pathways.
Meeting energy demand while balancing affordability, security, reliability, and sustainability, what we call the 'Four Forces,' is one of the defining economic opportunities of our era.
Head of Center for Energy and the Environment and Global Head of Sustainability
The changes to our environmental targets are rooted in the lessons we have learned during the prior five years. And we believe these evolutions sharpen our strategy: helping to mobilize more capital, address the energy system as a whole, and use our platform to help address barriers that financing alone cannot solve.
Here are a few of the lessons we have learned:
Based on these lessons and our belief in the opportunities ahead, we have developed the following principles to guide our approach.
These principles are already changing how we organize, engage, and measure progress.
These principles reflect how we intend to lead: with pragmatism, candor about the trade-offs, and clear focus on helping our clients succeed in a complex and rapidly evolving world. The opportunity in front of us is enormous. Let’s get to work.

articles.title_orig: New data reveals Japan is world’s top international public financier of fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: New data reveals Japan is world’s top international public financier of fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
New analysis reveals that Japan is the world’s largest provider of international public finance for fossil fuels, providing USD 4.1 billion annually for overseas gas, oil, and coal projects between 2023 and 2025 – more than any other G20 country.
The updated data is available at energyfinance.org , alongside a first-ever publicly available carbon capture and storage (CCS) and hydrogen subsidies database.
A factsheet based on the data, Tipping the Scales: G20 & MDB clean energy finance overtakes fossil fuel finance , by Oil Change International and Friends of the Earth United States, highlights that a handful of bad actors are blocking a just transition to renewable energy with outsized support for fossil fuels.
This finding is a stark contrast to overall G20 and Multilateral Development Bank (MDB) international finance for clean energy surpassing fossil fuel finance for the first time.
Public finance for fossil fuels from G20 countries’ development finance institutions (DFIs) and export credit agencies (ECAs) and multilateral development banks (MDBs) averaged at least USD 36.3 billion a year between 2023 and 2025, compared to USD 52.7 billion for clean energy during the same time period. Still, clean energy finance is nowhere near the scale needed to deliver a globally just transition that keeps temperatures rising as close as possible to below 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming, nor is it flowing to where it is most needed, with just 2% flowing to low-income countries.
Makiko Arima, Senior Finance Campaigner at Oil Change International, said:
Japan stands out as the world’s top international public financier of fossil fuels. Japan is driving fossil fuel expansion at a time when the dangers of relying on volatile fossil fuels are all too clear. Japan must end its financing for fossil fuels and shift support to renewable energy to help countries achieve lasting energy security and avoid the worst impacts of the climate crisis.

articles.title_orig: The Iran war's unexpected impact on US defenses against China threat downplayed by top Army leader
articles.title_zh: The Iran war's unexpected impact on US defenses against China threat downplayed by top Army leader
articles.content_orig:
Gatestone Institute senior fellow Gordon Chang warns that Beijing's military buildup and cyberattacks on Taiwan are designed for intimidation. Chang explains that leadership vacancies within the Chinese Communist Party's Central Military Commission leave the military unready for a full-scale invasion of the main island. These aggressive actions from China are stiffening Taiwanese opposition rather than forcing submission.
Amid growing concerns that the Iran war is drawing away critical U.S. defenses from China's doorstep, the Army's top commander in the Pacific says the forces are using this unexpected opportunity to modernize.
Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, provided his assessment that diverting Patriot missile defenses to the Iran war has not increased risk to forces in the Indo-Pacific despite concerns about deployments impacting America's readiness for potential conflict with China.
"Actually, it's given us an opportunity to modernize our systems here," Clark told Fox News Digital during a small-group interview at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday.
Patriot systems have been redeployed from the Indo-Pacific to support operations in the Middle East, while U.S. forces in South Korea have also sent Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors to the region.
U.S. Army Gen. Ronald Clark, commanding general of U.S. Army Pacific, speaks with NSS guests during National Security Seminar Week at the U.S. Army War College in Carlisle, Pa., June 4, 2026. (Elizabeth Bukowski/US Army War College)
An October Congressional Research Service report cited estimates that U.S. forces had expended roughly 1,700 Patriot and 200 THAAD interceptors during the conflict, while the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the military had used between half and two-thirds of certain interceptor inventories. The Pentagon's inspector general has cited strategic inventory shortfalls and manufacturing bottlenecks stemming from the conflict, raising questions about how quickly the U.S. could replenish its defenses in the event of another major confrontation.
Clark said the deployments are giving Patriot crews firsthand experience defending against enemy attacks, while equipment upgrades are expanding what individual batteries can accomplish.
He said an upgraded Patriot battery can now provide coverage that previously required an entire battalion, though he did not specify whether he was referring to geographic coverage or the number of threats the system can engage.
Asked whether recent diplomatic progress between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had changed his assessment of the threat from China, Clark said he believes the People's Liberation Army (PLA) is continuing its build-up.
"Well, I believe they're continuing to prepare," Clark said.
XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT
U.S. President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on October 30, 2025 in Busan, South Korea. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The assessment comes weeks after Trump welcomed Xi to Washington for a high-profile state visit that produced new trade agreements and commitments to improve military communications. But the diplomatic progress has not resolved tensions over Taiwan and China's growing military reach across the Indo-Pacific, where American commanders continue preparing for a potential conflict.
Clark did not say whether China's military preparations had accelerated or whether diplomatic outreach had changed Beijing's intentions. He emphasized that the U.S. military's responsibility is to remain ready for a potential conflict while working to prevent one.
TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD
"Hopefully my legacy in this job is that when we walk away from command of USARPAC, that the deterrent posture of our command is such that we have not just prevented war, but we're preventing war in the future," Clark said.
Clark said Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, recently discussed reviving disaster-management exchanges between the U.S. Army and China's PLA during talks with his Chinese counterpart.
The exchanges would provide an opportunity for American and Chinese military personnel to work together on disaster response, restoring a channel of direct engagement that Clark said he hoped to see revived.
"If you're able to have a conversation with your adversaries, you're able to share information with them in a way that makes them not want to fight," Clark said.
A Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel, labeled DA-BFAR MMOV 3015, navigates in close proximity to another ship during a maritime encounter. (Chinese Coast Guard)
He said U.S. Army Pacific would be responsible for coordinating the exchanges with its Chinese counterparts if the effort moves forward. He did not announce a date or say that Beijing had formally agreed to resume the program.
The U.S. and Chinese militaries have periodically conducted disaster-management exchanges in the past, including an event hosted by the Army at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state in 2017.
"The cost of going to war is just so high that it's our duty to, one, be absolutely prepared for that eventuality, but two, to prevent that from happening," Clark said.
The diplomatic outreach comes amid continued confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces in the South China Sea. As Fox News Digital previously reported, the Philippines tracked 101 Chinese navy and coast guard vessels around disputed waters in September, nearly double the number recorded in August. More recently, Philippine authorities accused Chinese forces of obstructing maritime operations and carrying out dangerous maneuvers near Philippine aircraft.
CHINESE MILITARY ACTIVITY NEARLY DOUBLES AROUND KEY US ALLY IN DISPUTED WATERS
Meanwhile, the Army has been expanding its capabilities across the Indo-Pacific, positioning additional forces and equipment closer to potential flashpoints as part of its effort to deter Chinese aggression.
China launched rockets near Taiwan during massive live-fire drills, surrounding the island with warships, aircraft and military pressure as tensions rise. (PLA Eastern Theater Command via Reuters)
Clark said the Army now has more resources committed to the region than at any previous point in his career, including additional divisions, a corps headquarters and specialized formations designed to conduct long-range strikes and operations across multiple domains.
"The Army is now better resourced in the Pacific than I've ever seen it," he said.
He pointed to the Army's growing ability to support naval and air operations, including land-based weapons capable of striking targets at sea.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Clark said recent military war games have demonstrated the importance of those capabilities, including one maritime scenario in which the addition of Army forces changed an unfavorable outcome.
"It's really tied to existing capabilities we have," Clark said, citing the Army's ability to detect targets, conduct strikes, protect military assets and sustain operations from land.

articles.title_orig: The genetic technique that finds (almost) every infection
articles.title_zh: The genetic technique that finds (almost) every infection
articles.content_orig:
It identified Covid-19. Now this genetic technique is helping doctors to make life-or-death decisions.
In late December 2019, a team of virologists from three major Chinese cities began analysing swabs taken from patients hospitalised with mysterious cases of severe pneumonia.
All had been present at the Huanan Seafood Market, Wuhan, before rapidly falling unwell. But when the virologists ran the samples, they drew a blank: the genetic material did not match any previously discovered pathogen.
The doctors turned to a new screening method known as metagenomic testing. Instead of checking for known microbes, the test could reveal all the microorganisms present in the samples – previously identified or not.
It enabled them to see that the pathogen in the patients' samples bore a close resemblance to the coronavirus family, a group that included viruses which had previously caused outbreaks of severe pneumonia in humans, such as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (Mers). The scientists had just discovered Covid-19.
"It was a gamechanger compared with previous pandemics," says Niranjan Nagarajan, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore. Knowing what the pathogen was made it possible to rapidly develop Covid diagnostics to try to curb the spread, and kickstarted the frantic search for treatments and vaccines around the globe .
This remains the best-known use of metagenomics to date. But the test is now increasingly being used in hospitals. And from quickly diagnosing sepsis to identifying the causes of unexplained ailments, it's already saving lives.
Whenever a patient arrives in a neurological ward displaying signs of confusion and drowsiness, and complaining of fever, headache and weakness, doctors are acutely aware that it could be a life-or-death emergency.
How metagenomic testing works
Metagenomics, the study of all the DNA and RNA found in a particular environment, is seen as an increasingly important clinical approach . Metagenomic testing involves extracting genetic material from a sample, then using advanced sequencing methods to identify the genetic codes of everything that's there. These results can be analysed by computers with reference to large databases, allowing doctors to pinpoint the exact organisms present, such as bacteria or viruses.
This constellation of symptoms can indicate meningitis or encephalitis – deadly conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord. Yet doctors often face a critical dilemma. The most suitable treatment would depend on whether the patient's condition was due to a virus or bacteria, or an overreaction from the brain's immune system. With limited tests and time, however, doctors are often forced to hedge their bets.
"You need to make a decision immediately," says Charles Chiu, a professor and infectious diseases expert at the University of California San Francisco Department of Medicine in the US, who has been carrying out new studies into the use of metagenomic tests. "Currently, with patients who are critically ill, doctors treat them for infection and for autoimmune disease."
In some ways, this is contradictory, because it involves suppressing the patient's immune system even though they might have an infection. "But there's often no other choice," says Chiu.
Metagenomics is now helping to inform these decisions. Chiu and his colleagues have developed a pioneering metagenomics test for identifying pathogens within cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid that bathes the brain and spinal cord. The test has already flagged cases where, unbeknownst to doctors, a pathogen was driving a patient's symptoms.
For example, Chiu encountered a patient who had been diagnosed with meningitis and liver failure, and was scheduled to receive a liver transplant. But the metagenomics test on her spinal fluid revealed that she was actually infected with the hepatitis E virus. While hepatitis E is a known and treatable cause of liver disease, it is not commonly tested for in high-income countries such as the US.
"We gave her an antiviral medication, she got better, and we spared her from undergoing the transplant," says Chiu.
Until recently, the use of metagenomics has been limited by the length of time required for the analysis. Separating human and microbial DNA, and identifying the signs of a potentially worrisome pathogen, requires highly specialist skills. "Doing the sequencing and the analysis can take several days to a week," says Nagarajan. "The patient might die before you're able to get a result."
Now, though, machines can sequence DNA within as little as one to two hours, and AI tools can ingest vast datasets to decipher patterns within them. And it's finally making metagenomics more widely accessible.
For people with poorly functioning immune systems, any infection can swiftly turn into a potentially deadly threat. Transplant recipients, cancer patients undergoing immune-suppressing treatment and those living with autoimmune diseases must be on constant high alert.
Studies have suggested that immunosuppressed patients who develop sepsis or blood poisoning due to an infection are at a 23% higher risk of dying in hospital. However, making a quick diagnosis in these cases is not always easy.
"Conditions such as pneumonia or sepsis can be caused by hundreds of potential pathogens which results in a very long diagnostic odyssey where we have to send test after test," says Chiu. "It can be a race against time."
In Singapore, Nagarajan is leading a project to see whether AI-enhanced metagenomic screening can lead to faster, more targeted treatment for immunocompromised individuals.
A typical dataset, says Chiu, is littered with spurious information. This includes the seemingly harmless viruses carried by most people and microbes from the lab that have accidentally contaminated the sample . AI can help with this by decluttering metagenomic datasets, making it quicker and easier for doctors to get an idea of what's going on.
A patient might also be carrying multiple co-infections, only one of which is making them ill, or damage might be related to an autoimmune response and not linked to a pathogen at all.
AI can help to pick out which pathogens are causing the damage by analysing how the person's genes are being expressed, such as which proteins they are making. This can be used to ascertain whether it’s likely that a patient's immune system is fighting a virus or happily co-existing alongside it.
"[This] gives us the ability to do precision medicine… that will enable us to customise or tailor the optimal treatment," says Chiu.
As data rolls in on just how effective metagenomics can be, it could play an ever-increasing role in hospitals. Last year, for example, a pilot study carried out in two London hospitals looked at whether metagenomics could provide additional information on patients hospitalised with respiratory infections. It found that the tests could identify pathogens which aren't routinely detected 30% of the time.
In one case, the test saved a patient from having to undergo invasive surgery. The individual had tuberculosis rather than what had been assumed to be lung cancer.
The test also identified two cases of the respiratory virus parvovirus B19. It found them months before UK and European agencies issued public health alerts about its increasing prevalence, suggesting a role for metagenomics in providing a heads up to authorities on emerging epidemics.
Indeed, Nagarajan says that several labs in Singapore are now running metagenomics tests on sewage and air samples. The data is then passed through AI models trained to look for signs of new viruses, as part of their efforts to prevent the next pandemic.
Proactive monitoring could have similarly given an early warning about Covid-19. In Italy, an analysis of sewage has found that traces of Covid-19 showed up in wastewater months before the country's first confirmed cases.
