Sandra Guzmán is director at the Climate Finance Group for Latin America and the Caribbean (GFLAC), and Raju Pandit Chhetri is lead climate finance negotiator for the least-developed countries at the UNFCCC.
Recent catastrophic floods in Nepal starkly remind us that the climate crisis demands urgent action. The initial estimate that the country will need to spend $5 billion on recovery will likely remain a major concern. However, that is only one part of the story. No financial metric can capture the value of lives lost in crises like this.
And this is not a standalone event; from the mountains of Nepal to the coastlines of Latin America and the Caribbean, developing countries are increasingly facing severe climate impacts. The average annual loss from climate disasters in the Latin American and Caribbean region is estimated at $58 billion. Human suffering remains immeasurable in all these instances.
Climate finance has been a key demand from our regions and from all developing countries to meet the needs of their citizens. At the recently concluded pre-COP31 in the Pacific, several developing-country governments strongly warned leaders about the dangers of failing to act on both climate and climate finance.
Pacific leaders rail at climate finance failures after pre-COP trip to Tuvalu
Yet, two years after the Baku climate summit, where all governments agreed on the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) on climate finance - with multilateral development banks (MDBs) playing a key role in delivery - that discussion risks being sidelined at this week’s annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, Thailand.
The MDBs have a critical role in mobilising a share of the $300-billion-per-year goal for public climate finance adopted at COP29 and are key to scaling broader financing to $1.3 trillion per year by 2035. They entered the NCQG dialogues promising capacity to mobilise these resources and agreeing to be part of the solution.
This June, even as the World Bank announced the renewal of its Climate Change Action Plan, it dropped its 45% climate finance target under pressure from the US administration. That commitment was key to ensuring the bank continues to deliver on its promise to mobilise enough climate finance to meet the NCQG target.
This announcement was a setback at a moment when developing countries are looking to MDBs to step up and fill gaps left by cuts in official development assistance (ODA) by donor governments.
World Bank’s climate work can endure without finance target, experts say
MDBs have long said they can convert $1 provided by donors into $2-$4 for client countries and have promised to deliver impact. Official data does paint an encouraging picture overall. The MDBs have delivered an increase in climate finance almost every year so far.
While financing needs far exceed what has been provided, MDBs mobilised an average of around $75bn per year in climate finance for low- and middle-income countries over the last five years, showing they are still on track to deliver the $120 billion per year they committed to.
However, climate finance cannot be measured by quantity alone. As MDBs increase their focus on private-sector mobilisation to diversify their funding, tracking the quality of the financing they mobilise becomes even more critical.  Beyond scale, this is where the system currently lags most.
Between 70-90% of the financing provided by MDBs is in the form of loans, exacerbating the debt burdens that the World Bank and IMF have long warned about. This strains countries' economies at a time when developing countries face severe climate impacts, inflationary pressures, and global economic uncertainty. Adding further debt that climate-vulnerable countries must repay with interest does not necessarily translate into effective climate finance flows.
It is also essential to address barriers to accessing finance in low- and middle-income countries, particularly by prioritising transparency around how much climate finance goes to the most climate-vulnerable countries and communities.
Additionally, there needs to be clarity on how much climate finance is being mobilised to build resilience and address increasingly frequent climate disasters, as well as for renewable energy projects that would help developing countries achieve a just transition.
As climate-induced disasters become more frequent, countries are compelled to shift resources away from vital sectors such as health, education, food security and infrastructure that underpins development. For nations already grappling with limited fiscal budgets and mounting debt, climate change is becoming an even heavier burden, pushing them to borrow more.
These are also development issues at their very core - countering debt challenges, investing in resilient infrastructure, protecting schools and hospitals from climate disasters, and increasing crop yields to reduce the cost of food. So, when the World Bank talks about a smart development framework, it warrants a check on how much climate finance is provided and its quality.
Editor’s Desk: Nepal’s disaster has laid bare the world’s adaptation accountability gap
MDBs must now lead the charge by publishing a clear plan to deliver on the scaled-up climate finance goal as a first step, and make financing accessible and affordable, including grant-based instruments. The plan must also define clear accountability metrics to track delivery, access, affordability and reach and commit to at least triple adaptation finance.
MDB shareholder countries also have a role in backing the institutions to deliver on these promises. When World Bank and IMF management meets with finance ministers this week in a region battered by the worst climate impacts, they must not leave climate finance off the agenda.
They must give the World Bank and IMF the mandate, the capital and the political backing to make real scale-up possible. The true test of this financial system will not be found in conference rooms in Bangkok, but in the lives saved in Nepal.

articles.title_orig: Christina Koch Retiring From Flight Status
articles.title_zh: Christina Koch Retiring From Flight Status
articles.content_orig:
Christina Koch, who flew Orion around the Moon after launching from Kennedy Space Center in April, is trading her flight status for a leadership post at NASA headquarters. The agency announced she will become acting deputy chief engineer on November 1st.
Koch succeeds Katherine Van Hooser, who retires Oct. 21 after more than 35 years with NASA. The move makes Koch a management astronaut, which means she will not be assigned to future spaceflights. With that transition, all four astronauts who flew on Artemis II are now retired from flight status.
As an astronaut, Koch has spent roughly 337 days and 15.5 hours in space. She currently holds the record (with her Artemis II crewmates) for distance traveled away from Earth, and as part of that record, she is the highest-flying woman in history. She spent 328 days, 13 hours, and 58 minutes aboard the ISS, which at the time set a spaceflight duration record for women, and has traveled about 140 million miles in space during her flight career.
As deputy chief engineer, Koch will help direct the agency’s engineering workforce. The job covers technical oversight and mission readiness across NASA’s programs and projects.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman pointed to Koch’s experience on both ends of the hardware. He said she has helped build complex systems on the ground and then relied on them to stay alive in space. Isaacman tied the appointment to the agency’s near-term agenda, including landing astronauts back on the lunar surface, building a Moon base, advancing nuclear power in space and preparing for Mars.
Amit Kshatriya, NASA’s associate administrator and chief engineer, credited Van Hooser with steering the agency’s engineering community through critical milestones and transitions. He said he was “confident Christina will continue the tradition of technical excellence” at NASA.
Koch’s appointment comes six months after Artemis II, the first crewed flight around the Moon in more than half a century. She flew as a mission specialist on the flight, which drew crowds across the Space Coast for its April launch.
NASA kid from Cocoa Beach, FL, born of Project Apollo parents and family. I’m a writer and photographer sharing the story of spaceflight from the Eastern Range here in Florida.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX launch creates ‘space jellyfish’ over Grand Isle, Southeast
articles.title_zh: SpaceX launch creates ‘space jellyfish’ over Grand Isle, Southeast
articles.content_orig:
GRAND ISLE, La. (WAFB) - Talk about a grand view!
A resupply mission to the International Space Station gave Grand Isle a front-row seat to a glowing “space jellyfish” early Tuesday, part of a sky show seen across the Southeast.
Landon Braud, a high school teacher and coach from Ascension Parish, captured photos over Grand Isle just after 5:30 a.m. Tuesday.
SpaceX launched the Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The Dragon spacecraft, carrying more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and scientific equipment, is scheduled to reach the space station Thursday.
The pre-dawn liftoff created a signature “jellyfish cloud” also seen over the Tennessee River in Knoxville, Tenn., and elsewhere across the southeastern and eastern United States.
The striking effect happens when a rocket’s exhaust plume expands rapidly in the thin upper atmosphere during a launch near dawn or dusk. At very high altitudes, vapor exhaust freezes into ice crystals. Because the sun is still below the horizon for observers on the ground, its light hits the high-altitude plume, illuminating the crystallized gases into a glowing, translucent bulb with wispy, tentacle-like trails against the dark sky.
The Associated Press contributed heavily to this report.

articles.title_orig: Scientists discover 'D-rex', a giant fungus from Chinese forests whose unique lineage dates back 65 million years
articles.title_zh: Scientists discover 'D-rex', a giant fungus from Chinese forests whose unique lineage dates back 65 million years
articles.content_orig:
Deep in the forests of southwest China, scientists have discovered a ‘fungal giant’ that challenges our understanding of how large fungi can become.
The newly described species, Dianjunus rex , or “King of Dian,” named for an ancient Chinese kingdom, produces vertical fruiting bodies up to 20 inches high and weighing up to 5 pounds.
Scientists in China, Thailand, and Mexico made the discovery, which constituted not only its own new genus, but whole new family of fungi within the Phylum of Ascomycota .
Analysis of its genome suggests that the new family arose approximately 65 million years ago, strikingly soon after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction which killed off the dinosaurs, when new niches for wood-decomposing fungi, a niche which “ D. rex ” inhabits still to this day, may have opened up.
“This remarkable species represents a new fungal family, Dianjunaceae , and provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms,” said Dr. Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species of the Kunming Institute of Botany in China and corresponding author of the new study, published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology.
“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests.”
During fieldwork in a mix of temperate coniferous forests and tropical rainforest in the province of Yunnan, scientists from the Kunming Institute found large, whitish, fruiting bodies (called stromata) clearly belonging to an unknown ascomycete fungus growing on the woody roots of Chinese cork oak.
With more than 64,000 species, Ascomycota is the largest group of fungi. They don’t grow true mushrooms but instead release spores from tiny, sack-like structures inside or on the surface of such fruiting bodies.
Though a reader might not know any Ascomycetes by name, they’re one of the most influential group of organisms on the Earth next to humans. Among those 64,000 species one finds various molds and yeasts that create bread, beer, wine, penicillin, Stilton, Roquefort, Brie, Zola, and Camembert cheese, soy sauce, sake wine, and the organ-rejection inhibitor ciclosporin. They also include the prized morels, truffles, cordyceps, and dead-man’s fingers.
If one were to make a “cons” list of similar gravity, it could include species that cause Dutch elm disease, chestnut blight, apple blight, powdery mildew, histoplasmosis, ergot, the most common lung infection in humans ( Aspergillus fumigatus ), vaginal yeast infections, and valley fever.
And out all these and so much more, D. rex is the biggest of them all, a true king among fungi.
Collecting the fruiting bodies they found, the team of scientists grew spores on media to study the morphology of the fungus, and also sequenced its genome.
Genetic results confirmed by a detailed study of its morphology revealed that Dianjunaceae could be set within the order Xylariales . The closest known relative to D. rex is Graphostroma platystoma , which grows on dead hardwood across the Northern Hemisphere and by itself forms the family Graphostromataceae .
From a ‘molecular clock’ analysis of the new species’ DNA, while comparing it to the genome of hundreds of fungi with known evolutionary age, the authors were able to estimate that the Dianjunaceae arose around 65 million years ago. Strikingly, this is only one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction event—famous for wiping out the dinosaurs besides countless other animals and plants.
“This timing raises an intriguing possibility. After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material,” said Senanayake. “For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities.”
FUNGAL NEWS FEEDS: Scientists Map Underground Fungal Networks and Find They Cover 62 Quadrillion Miles
Yet those days are long gone, and D. rex still grows so uncommonly big; why? Until now, the record-holders among ascomycete fruiting bodies measured 20 to 30 centimeters tall, around half the size of D. rex.
“A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests. However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs,” hypothesized Senanayake.
Though sharks, sea turtles, and crocodilians are famous for having remained relatively unchanged from an evolutionary standpoint for hundreds of millions of years, there are some plants—static though they may be—which have shaded both dinosaurs and humans; most notably the ginkgo biloba, but also the so-called “ dinosaur evergreen ” of Australia.
BIGGEST MUSHROOMS IN THE LAND: Giant Puffball Mushroom Feeds Her Family for a Week
The researchers predicted that more discoveries of fungi from subtropical China lie in store.
“This region combines exceptional habitat heterogeneity, climatic stability, and complex biotic interactions that promote fungal diversification,” said said Senanayake.
“Historically, however, fungal diversity in these ecosystems has been underestimated due to logistical difficulties in field sampling, the seasonal and cryptic nature of fungal fruiting, and a historical emphasis on economically important fungi.”

articles.title_orig: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
articles.title_zh: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Equity investors are skeptical of Chinese companies' rapid expansion overseas, according to Goldman Sachs.
The "market wants to look for profitable expansions," Trina Chen, co-head of Greater China equity research at Goldman Sachs Research, said on a podcast that the investment bank published Tuesday.
Sluggish consumer demand in China has pushed many companies, such as electric car brands, to accelerate plans for entering other countries. Automaker Geely is one of the latest Chinese companies to push further abroad, announcing Friday it plans to enter Canada next year .
Chinese companies' overseas market share will likely reach 31% by 2035, up from around 18%, Chen and her team predicted in a Sept. 14 report. Their analysis covered more than 10 sectors, including express delivery, industrial robots and so-called white goods such as air conditioners.
Chinese businesses often find higher profit margins abroad than they would at home, enabling the companies to charge lower prices than local competitors.
Investors need to be convinced the global expansion "does not end up with something similar to involution, where the price actually gets killed because of competition," Chen said Tuesday, adding that geopolitics and market access restrictions also weighs on stock performance.
Involution refers to race-to-the-bottom competition in China, which regulators have attempted to address in recent years.
That uncertainty means Chinese companies have very little of their global expansion opportunity priced into their stocks, Chen said.
But on the flip side, she noted that investors are "ruthless" when incumbent companies lose their market share: A 10% to 15% loss could shrink market capitalization by 50% to 80%.
The Chinese players are not just looking at the U.S. and Europe. Goldman Sachs noted some of the most rapid growth is in emerging markets, as the businesses also pursue areas underserved by competitors.
"Chinese brands are no longer simply market challengers," Euromonitor said in a report last month. "Brands are becoming long-term, embedded competitors capable of reshaping market dynamics across Latin America.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV's brother Louis Prevost also battling cancer, wife tells CBS News
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV's brother Louis Prevost also battling cancer, wife tells CBS News
articles.content_orig:
Louis Prevost , Pope Leo XIV's older brother who lives in Florida, has multiple myeloma, his wife told CBS News on Tuesday. The news comes amid the Vatican's earlier announcement that the pope has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung.
Deborah Prevost did not share what stage Louis' cancer is in but said he's currently in a clinical trial at a local hospital where he's being treated.
Multiple myeloma is a type of cancer that affects plasma cells, according to the Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation .
Deborah Prevost said Louis was first diagnosed in 2017 but was able to maintain it at a "very low level" after undergoing treatment in 2019 that included stem cell treatment and a clinical trial. He "fell out of remission" three months ago, she said.
She could not comment on the specifics of Pope Leo's condition but said her husband and his brother spoke last week before Louis went in for his clinical trial.
"He called to let us know what would be happening," Deborah said. "We keep praying, keeping spirits up for both of them."
Pope Leo underwent surgery Tuesday that confirmed he has lung cancer, the Vatican said earlier in the day. The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican didn't disclose what stage the cancer was in or whether the cancer may have spread. It also did not detail what further procedures or treatment the pope may have to undergo.
Deborah Prevost told CBS News the family was "going through a lot," but she was hopeful that Leo's cancer was in the very early stages. She said she hadn't heard about any potential radiation or chemotherapy treatment.
In an interview with CBS News in May 2025, after then- Cardinal Robert Prevost was chosen as the new pope , Louis Prevost said the family knew "from a very young age, there was something special about Rob."
Pope Leo is the first U.S.-born leader of the Catholic Church. He grew up alongside his two older siblings, Louis and John, in the Chicago area.
"While I was out playing boy games, you know, whether it was baseball, cops and robbers, tag, flashlight, whatever kid games, Rob used to like to play priest," Louis Prevost told CBS News at the time. "Since way back then, he's had that calling."
"He will always be Rob," Louis added. "If we do get over there and do get to meet him, I'm still going to treat him like my little brother. Give him a hug, say 'Rob, you idiot, what have you done?' Take his hat off and give him a nuggie."
Faris  Tanyos , Kierra  Frazier and The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: American Amplifier Technologies Acquires ERI
articles.title_zh: American Amplifier Technologies Acquires ERI
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Headlines
Electronics Research Inc. has a new owner.
American Amplifier Technologies LLC, which in recent years has purchased several familiar broadcast companies including Shively Labs and Kathrein-Scala, now has acquired majority ownership of ERI from Tom Silliman.
The terms were not disclosed.
Silliman, its president/CEO since 1977, is retiring.
ERI designs, manufactures and installs broadcast antennas, towers, transmission line, filters and combiners.
AAT owner Steve Wilde told Radio World that he will continue its products and operations, including its facility in Chandler, Ind. ERI customers, he said, should expect continuity in service, support and business relationships, and can continue communicating with their contacts through existing channels.
“The acquisition is intended to strengthen ERI by providing additional resources, expanded capabilities and continued investment in the company’s long-term success,” he said.
He highlighted ERI’s significant market share in broadcast antennas and said its other offerings compliment AAT’s business. He noted the companies’ combined engineering, manufacturing, RF laboratory analysis, field-service and installation capabilities.
“We see tremendous opportunity in ERI. It has a long-standing reputation for producing proven, high-quality products and has earned the loyalty and trust of its customers.”
ERI, he continued, has “an exceptional facility, a highly capable structural steel division and extensive engineering expertise. What truly sets ERI apart is its unique combination of manufacturing capabilities and an installation division. Few companies in the industry can offer this level of expertise and capability.”
AAT makes and carries a diverse line of RF products. Wilde founded the company in 2008, along with sister firm SWE Services.
Over the past seven years he has been active at seeking acquisition opportunities.
In 2019 AAT acquired Mauna Towers, which operates tower facilities in Hawaii and Arizona. In 2023, it purchased antenna and filter manufacturer Shively Labs and also started a partnership with System Engineering Solutions . Then in late 2025, AAT acquired Kathrein Broadcast USA , also known as Kathrein-Scala.
AAT is based in Citrus Heights near Sacramento, Calif. Kathrein-Scala continues to run out of White City near Medford, Ore. [Read a history of AAT .]
“ERI, Shively and Kathrein-Scala are names that generations of broadcast engineers know and trust,” Wilde said.
“We recognize the responsibility that comes with bringing companies with those histories together. We intend to protect what makes each of these companies special while giving the personnel and technologies new opportunities to grow.”
Electronics Research Inc. was founded during World War II, making antennas for military aircraft. Later moving into broadcasting, its innovations have included the Rototiller antenna line, the Lambda optimized FM mounting system and Cogwheel master FM antennas.
In 2003 ERI acquired Andrew Corp.’s Broadcast Products business, including its television antenna products, rigid transmission-line products and related broadcast RF components.
Wilde called ERI “an exceptional company with a remarkable history.”
ERI’s headquarters and main manufacturing facility include over 100,000 square feet of manufacturing, design and office space. The facility also houses a 70,000-cubic-foot anechoic chamber, which according to ERI’s website is the largest of its kind in North America. [Read a history of ERI .]
The Silliman name has long been associated with ERI. Robert Silliman was involved with the company from its earliest years, eventually becoming one of its owners. Tom joined the company in 1969 and became president/CEO in 1977. Robert received the NAB Engineering Achievement Award in 1993, and Tom received it in 2008. Robert Silliman died in 2001.
“One of our primary goals is to honor Tom Silliman’s legacy by continuing his commitment to quality, engineering excellence and innovation, while expanding our capabilities to better serve the broadcast community,” Wilde said in the announcement.
Tom Silliman was quoted: “I am proud of what the people of ERI have built over the years, and I believe AAT is well positioned to carry that work forward. We share a commitment to engineering, quality, customer service and the broadcast industry.” [Read our 2001 profile of Tom Silliman .]

articles.title_orig: Police confiscate robot that groped 16-year-old girl, probe whether young men were at the controls
articles.title_zh: Police confiscate robot that groped 16-year-old girl, probe whether young men were at the controls
articles.content_orig:
German police have launched an investigation into two teenagers accused of controlling a robot that allegedly groped a 16-year-old girl.
Police in Cologne have confiscated the red and gold robot that allegedly grabbed the girl's buttocks and made thrusting motions against her before she screamed and moved away.
North Rhine Westphalia Police said the robot's 16-year-old owner and his companion, 19, are believed to have streamed the incident live on social media and commented on it.
According to a police statement on Facebook, the 120cm (3.9ft) tall device approached the girl from behind while she was with her friends close to midnight local time (23:00 BST) on Saturday.
The girl was in front of a fast-food outlet near the city centre when the incident took place, police said.
Emergency services were alerted, and the teenage boy and the man now under investigation with him were found a block away a short time later. The robot was discovered in the back of a car, where the boy had placed it, police said.
A photo released by police showed the robot wearing a black moustache, a gold-coloured chain and white vest.
Along with the robot, police seized two mobile phones belonging to the suspects. They are trying to determine whether someone was deliberately controlling the robot's movements at the time of the incident.
In a follow-up post on Facebook, police warned some social media comments on the case "can be a crossing of the line and in the worst case, a criminal offense".

articles.title_orig: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street
articles.title_zh: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street on Wednesday, as the UK announces it will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.
Burnham is also expected to set out how his government will draw up further sanctions against Russia.
Speaking ahead of the meeting, Burnham said the UK was with Ukraine "for as long as it takes", adding: "Russian aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent."
The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
This will be Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. His first was in late July, days after Burnham entered No 10, when the pair met troops and led a news conference at a naval base in Portsmouth.
Burnham said: "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.
"My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.
"It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do."
Among the measures being announced is the quicker delivery of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), with the UK having already committed to send more than 5,000 worth £1.6bn over the next four years.
The UK will also reaffirm its plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG exports.
The meeting between Zelensky and Burnham follows what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described as a "very difficult few days" for UK-US relations due to President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
Zelensky criticised the US deal with Russia, calling it a "gift" to President Vladimir Putin. Trump, in response, called for new leadership in Ukraine and criticised Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries.
Meanwhile, Healey will ask partners at the IMF to step up support for Kyiv and ensure Russia heeds the US' call for a full energy ceasefire.
Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire - but hours later, Zelensky said Russian attacks on energy facilities had continued.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine did not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

articles.title_orig: Trump debates calling off livestream of firing squad execution after learning Fort Hood shooter was paralyzed
articles.title_zh: Trump debates calling off livestream of firing squad execution after learning Fort Hood shooter was paralyzed
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump and his advisers are debating whether to call off plans to livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter, with Trump having remarked privately that he did not initially know that Nidal Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down, two sources familiar with the discussions told CNN.
The president was not aware that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was announcing last week that the administration planned to let the public watch the execution, the sources said, and was not sure what to make of it at first. Trump was, however, firmly behind the decision to execute Hasan via firing squad , multiple officials told CNN, and he’s often defended it in public.
And even after Hegseth posted on X on Thursday confirming that the Pentagon planned to livestream the execution, Trump polled several of his advisers and allies about how to proceed.
It was during the those conversations that Trump learned Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down — he was shot in the back by law enforcement during the 2009 shooting at Ford Hood — and that he now uses a wheelchair, the sources said, which made showing the execution publicly less palatable to the president.
One of the sources familiar with the discussions pointed to Trump’s deep understanding of imagery as a key reason why he may decide to ditch plans for the livestream. The president has also listened to the argument that a public execution by firing squad could serve as propaganda for foreign adversaries and terrorists to try to paint Hasan as a martyr, a Trump adviser told CNN.
The White House on Tuesday referred CNN to the president’s comments on Saturday in which he acknowledged “two thoughts” about what to do and said he’d make the ultimate decision.
“He was vicious. He was violent,” Trump told reporters about Hasan over the weekend. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So, I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
The Pentagon is also reevaluating plans to fully livestream the execution, according to a source familiar with the discussions. Even if there is a broadcast of the event, the source said, it will likely be cut before shots are fired, in part, due to concerns that the moment could offer a propaganda opportunity for terrorist groups.
Hegseth’s office has not responded to additional requests for comment about whether plans to livestream the execution have changed.
The plan to livestream the execution has faced bipartisan backlash, and people across the Pentagon and the Army were caught off guard, CNN has previously reported .
Trump told reporters on Friday that he was not involved but said, “I understand the decision,” adding that some people “want to set an example” by livestreaming the execution.
Hegseth had initially recommended death by firing squad for Hasan — who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding dozens of others — and Trump approved it.
The execution, which is scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the US Army’s first such execution of a soldier since World War II and its first imposition of any death penalty on an armed service member in 65 years.
A US-born citizen of Palestinian descent, Hasan said he was targeting soldiers he was set to deploy with to Afghanistan and wanted to protect the Taliban and its leaders from the US military.
CNN’s Zachary Cohen contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: One UI 9 Release Date: Update Lands On Galaxy S24, A57 Today
articles.title_zh: One UI 9 Release Date: Update Lands On Galaxy S24, A57 Today
articles.content_orig:
Published: October 14th, 2026 at 03:00 UTC+02:00
SamMobile has affiliate and sponsored partnerships, we may earn a commission .
One UI 9 brings plenty of the same improvements to the Galaxy S25 and S26 series, but there are some differences.
Daniel Scuteri / SamMobile
One UI 9 on the Galaxy S25 Ultra and S26 Ultra
Samsung’s One UI 9 update brings plenty of the same improvements to the Galaxy S25 and Galaxy S26 series . Owners of both lineups get new Galaxy AI tools, more ways to customize their phones, and changes to some of Samsung’s apps and settings.
The S26 series launched with One UI 8.5, and some of its camera features were already available before the latest update. One UI 9 brings more of that functionality to the S25 series, though Samsung’s newer flagships still offer a few additional options.
Both lineups get the Galaxy AI features My FanCam, Call Brief, and custom cards for Now Brief.
My FanCam can take an existing recording of a group of people and create a cropped version that follows one person . You can choose who to follow after recording, so you can try it with videos already sitting in your Gallery.
Call Brief can show relevant information during calls , such as a shared calendar event or the local time when you call an international number. It won’t show a card during every call, but it may save you from opening another app to look something up.
Custom Now Brief cards give you more say over your daily briefing. You can choose weather, health, or video information and schedule when the card should appear. For example, you could have a weather card ready in the morning before leaving home.
The home screen changes are similar, too. You can add a dedicated Finder bar to the home screen so you can search for apps, settings, files, and other content on your phone without first opening the app drawer.
Asif Iqbal Shaik / SamMobile
Finder and Google Search bars on home screen
Bixby widgets give you a convenient way to type or speak to Bixby while keeping Gemini assigned to the power button. You can use the widget whenever you want Bixby’s help without changing how you launch Gemini.
Both lineups also get more Quick Panel customization, easier desktop management in DeX, and the Warranty and care menu for warranty information and support.
One UI 9 brings Super steady with Horizontal Lock to the Galaxy S25 series . The S26 series already offered this with One UI 8.5. With Horizontal Lock enabled, your video stays level even when you tilt or rotate the phone.
Both lineups also get a new vertical split layout for dual recording in Video mode. On One UI 8.5, you had picture-in-picture and horizontal layout options, so you now have more choice over how the final video looks.
Daniel Scuteri / SamMobile
Vertical layout dual recording on One UI 9.0
The Galaxy S26 series gets exclusive rights on some camera features. For example, it provides a wider selection of frame rates in Pro video mode.
At Full HD and UHD resolutions, the S26 series can record at 120, 60, 48, 30, 24, 100, 50, and 25 fps. The S25 series is limited to 120, 60, 30, and 24 fps. At 8K resolution, the S26 series get a 25 fps option in addition to 30 and 24 fps.
If you generally record at 30 or 60 fps, those extra choices may not mean much to you. But anyone who wants to use one of the additional frame rates has more flexibility on the S26 lineup.
There’s also a difference for still photos. The S26 lineup lets you enable the 24MP resolution in the standard Photo mode through Samsung's Camera Assistant app, which remains missing on the Galaxy S25 series after the One UI 9 update.
It's all about convenience here: you can select 24MP while using the regular camera on a Galaxy S26-series phone. S25 owners can shoot at that resolution as well, but they have to open a separate app — Expert RAW — to do it.
The Galaxy S25 FE misses out on Call Brief, so that’s one Galaxy AI feature you won’t find after updating. The Galaxy S26 FE doesn’t support it either, even though it launched with One UI 9.
But One UI 9 does bring a useful sharing feature to the S25 FE: Quick Share support for Apple devices . You can now share photos, videos, and other files with iPhones, iPads, and Macs.
First Samsung device: SGH-D500

In addition to phones and mobile devices, his interests include gaming on both PC and console, PC hardware, and spending countless hours on YouTube watching videos on tech, movies, games, politics, and internet dramas.

articles.title_orig: Real-World, First-Line IO-Based Combos Are Associated With Improved OS vs TKI Monotherapy in Advanced RCC
articles.title_zh: Real-World, First-Line IO-Based Combos Are Associated With Improved OS vs TKI Monotherapy in Advanced RCC
articles.content_orig:
First-line IO-based combination regimens were increasingly used and associated with longer observed survival in advanced renal cell carcinoma.
First-line immuno-oncology (IO)–based combination regimens, particularly IO plus a TKI, were associated with improved overall survival (OS) compared with TKI monotherapy in a real-world cohort of patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma (RCC), according to findings from a retrospective real-world study presented at the 2026 Kidney Cancer Research Summit . 1,2
Findings showed that at a median follow-up of 13.9 months, the median OS in the overall population (n = 2123) was 34.7 months. 1 Notably, the median OS was 44.1 months among patients who received an IO-TKI combination (n = 987) compared with 32.8 months for those given an IO-IO combination (n = 746) and 29.8 months for patients given TKI monotherapy (n = 390).
Notably, from 2019 to 2024, the proportion of patients receiving an IO-TKI combination increased from 33.8% to 48.6%, whereas IO-IO decreased from 40.5% to 34.5% and TKI monotherapy decreased from 25.7% to 16.9%.
“The advanced RCC treatment landscape continues to evolve toward IO-based combinations in [the] first line and continued TKI monotherapy in later lines,” lead study author Neil J. Shah, MBBS, and colleagues wrote in the poster. “While health care resource utilization [HCRU] and costs remain substantial, these results underscore both the clinical progress achieved and the ongoing opportunity to optimize resource use in advanced RCC care.”
Shah is an assistant attending physician and genitourinary medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, New York.
Investigators conducted a retrospective cohort study using Optum’s deidentified Clinformatics Data Mart Database, with the database period extended from January 1, 2017, through December 31, 2024, and included commercially insured and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.
Eligible adults had at least 2 claims with an RCC diagnosis, evidence of secondary metastasis, and initiation of a National Comprehensive Cancer Network–recommended first-line systemic regimen on or after April 19, 2019. Patients were categorized according to whether they received IO-TKI, IO-IO, or TKI monotherapy.
Investigators evaluated outcomes included treatment patterns, treatment sequencing, OS, all-cause and advanced RCC–related HCRU, and costs. OS was estimated using an unadjusted Kaplan-Meier analysis, and HCRU and costs were calculated on a per-patient-per-month (PPPM) basis.
The mean age of the overall population was 68.1 years (standard deviation [SD], 9.6), and the median age was 69.0 years (interquartile range [IQR], 63.0-75.0). The respective mean ages were 67.4, 68.2, and 69.5 years in the IO-TKI, IO-IO, and TKI monotherapy groups. Men comprised 70.9% of the overall population, including 71.6%, 72.8%, and 65.6% of the respective treatment cohorts.
Overall, 50.2% of patients were non-Hispanic White, 7.3% were non-Hispanic Black, 13.6% were Hispanic, and 2.2% were Asian; race or ethnicity was unknown for 26.7% of patients. Most patients lived in the South (45.1%), followed by the Midwest (25.1%), West (19.5%), and Northeast (10.3%).
Medicare Advantage covered 71.1% of the study population, and 28.9% had commercial insurance. The proportion covered by Medicare Advantage was highest in the TKI-monotherapy group at 78.7%, compared with 71.0% in the IO-IO group and 68.1% in the IO-TKI group.
Additional data showed that 32.3% of patients remained on their initial treatment, 29.0% advanced to second-line therapy, and 18.7% died. Another 20.0% discontinued treatment without a recorded death or subsequent therapy.
TKI monotherapy was the most frequently used treatment class in both the second- and third-line settings. Among patients who received second-line therapy, 47.2% received TKI monotherapy compared with 23.1% who received IO-TKI, 9.3% who received IO monotherapy, 7.6% who received a TKI plus an mTOR inhibitor, 7.0% who received IO-IO, and 5.8% who received another regimen.
In the third-line setting, 42.1% of patients received TKI monotherapy, 18.8% received IO-TKI, and 14.2% received a TKI plus an mTOR inhibitor; other treatments were administered to 15.2% of patients.
Overall, 61.3% of patients had at least 1 inpatient admission, including 57.6% treated with first-line IO-TKI, 66.6% treated with IO-IO, and 60.5% treated with TKI monotherapy. The median PPPM inpatient admissions was 0.1 overall. Median lengths of stay were 1.0 day with IO-TKI, 1.1 days with IO-IO, and 1.3 days with TKI monotherapy.
At least 1 emergency department visit was reported for 64.1% of patients, whereas 99.8% had at least 1 outpatient visit. The median number of outpatient visits PPPM was 5.4 overall, including 5.5 with IO-TKI, 5.6 with IO-IO, and 4.3 with TKI monotherapy.
Median total health care costs PPPM were $32,829 overall, $38,408 with IO-TKI, $30,484 with IO-IO, and $24,098 with TKI monotherapy.
Median medical costs PPPM were highest with IO-IO at $26,589, compared with $21,800 for IO-TKI and $7462 for TKI monotherapy. Conversely, median pharmacy costs were $15,871 with IO-TKI, $15,103 with TKI monotherapy, and $415 with IO-IO. Investigators noted that the oral administration of TKIs may have contributed to higher pharmacy costs, whereas intravenously administered IO agents may have contributed to higher medical costs.

Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.
China rattled the memory trade on Tuesday. But by the close, investors had made up their minds about who actually has a problem. It's the DRAM makers.
ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's biggest memory chipmaker, said over the weekend it had made real progress on a new chip design that crams more data into less space, CNBC reports. Asia took it badly: SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in Seoul and Samsung fell over 7%.
U.S. memory stocks opened in the same hole, with nearly every name down 5% to 8%. Then the buyers showed up.
Seagate, Western Digital and SanDisk clawed back almost all of it and closed down less than 2%. Micron didn't get the same rescue. It finished down 3.6%, its second straight loss. SK Hynix's U.S. shares fell 3.2%. The S&P 500 ended flat.
One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.
The split makes sense. CXMT makes DRAM, the same chips Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung sell. A Chinese rival closing the gap is a direct shot at their pricing. Hard drives and flash storage are a different business.
Some analysts think the market overreacted. Rayliant's Phillip Wool told CNBC that CXMT still hasn't shown it can produce at scale, and it isn't a threat yet in the high-bandwidth memory chips that power AI. He said the selloff showed "how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment."
Still, the CXMT news looks more like an excuse than a cause. Memory stocks were already well off their highs before the weekend, with Micron down about a quarter from its peak and Western Digital down by half. Investors have been hunting for a reason to take profits on the AI trade's biggest winners. China handed them one, and they used it on the stocks with the most to lose.

articles.title_orig: David Cromer Will Direct Peter Friedman in Hanukkah Spectacular World Premiere
articles.title_zh: David Cromer Will Direct Peter Friedman in Hanukkah Spectacular World Premiere
articles.content_orig:
Max Posner's comedy will begin at the Woolly Mammoth Theatre in November.
October 13, 2026 By Andrew Gans
Washington , D.C.'s Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company will present the world premiere of Hanukkah Spectacular , a new comedy by Lucille Lortel Award nominee Max Posner, beginning November 14.
Directed by Tony winner David Cromer ( The Band's Visit , Dead Outlaw , The Sound Inside ), performances will continue through December 13.
Stage and screen star and Tony nominee Peter Friedman ( Succession, Ragtime , JOB ) will lead a cast that also includes Laura Heisler , Ben Edelman , Ben Beckley , and Ethan J. Miller.
Set over a long weekend at a Midtown talent agency, Hanukkah Spectacular follows a group of Jewish artists brought together to create a commercially viable holiday hit about Hanukkah.
“The first time I saw a reading of Hanukkah Spectacular three years ago, I knew I had just experienced something unforgettable, and I’m so lucky to get to share its world premiere with D.C. this holiday season,” says Woolly Mammoth Artistic Director Reggie D. White in a statement. “Seeing Max [Posner] and [David] Cromer collaborate feels like once-in-generation chemistry. Watching them amplify, interrogate, and deepen each other’s work is like you’re witnessing two brilliant artists write the book on collaboration in front of your very eyes. Max’s play is a hilarious and deeply recognizable story about a group of people trying to make something honest while figuring out what they actually believe. This production promises to be exactly the kind of work we come to the theatre to see: disarming, surprising, and so true that that it sends you back into the world thinking about your own life a little differently.”
Posner's play The Treasurer , also directed by Cromer, premiered at Playwrights Horizons and received a Lucille Lortel Award nomination for Best Play. He is a Sundance Institute Fellow, a recipient of the Helen Merrill Award and three MacDowell Fellowships, and was the 2024–25 Sun Valley Playwright-in-Residence at the Hemingway House.

articles.title_orig: How you can prepare for 6% bond yields
articles.title_zh: How you can prepare for 6% bond yields
articles.content_orig:
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell on Thursday as traders digested comments from a top Federal Reserve official along with another long-dated bond auction.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was down more than 4 basis points at 5.229% after reaching its highest level since 2002 this week. The 30-year Treasury bond yield dropped more than 5 basis points to 5.602% after trading around a 24-year high recently.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that more hikes are needed to bring inflation down after around 5-and-a-half years above the central bank's 2% target, but suggested rates did not need to rise immediately.
"The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings," Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul. "But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
His comments initially sent yields higher on the day. However, rates gave back those advances after President Donald Trump said the U.S. won't attack Iran until after the November midterm election . Yields also pulled back after a solid 30-year Treasury bond auction.
The department sold $22 billion in 30-year paper, with indirect bidders — which include central banks — scooping up 72.3% of the sale. That's above a 10-auction average of 68%. Direct bidders, including institutional investors, took 20.9% of the auction, just below an average of 22%. The yield at auction ease 5.618%.
That marks the final auction of the week. The department sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday and another $39 billion in 10-year notes.
Thursday's sale "was decent but nowhere close to as good as the 10 yr auction yesterday," wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of One Point BFG Wealth Partners.
— CNBC's Brianna Bernath contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Peru governor touts Chinese interest in deep-water port pitched as Chancay alternative
articles.title_zh: Peru governor touts Chinese interest in deep-water port pitched as Chancay alternative
articles.content_orig:
Scaled back to US$844 million from a US$7 billion plan, Corio terminal in Arequipa has yet to secure an investor or operator
A planned US$844 million port in southern Peru has drawn interest from several foreign investors, including Chinese companies, a regional governor said on Monday, as the government began promoting the project abroad.
“Several companies have approached us. We have investors from the US, China and India who are very interested,” Rohel Sanchez, the governor of Arequipa, told reporters after signing an agreement with the state investment agency Proinversion.
He said firms from Turkey and the Netherlands had also been in touch, as had South Korean investors interested in technology for a logistics park to be built alongside the terminal.
Proinversion president Luis del Carpio said Corio would likely handle general cargo and containers but could also be used to export copper from the region to Asia.

articles.title_orig: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
articles.title_zh: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
articles.content_orig:
President Trump stops to speak to members of the media as he departs the White House on Oct. 13, 2026. Win McNamee/Getty Images hide caption
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."
Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.
His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.
Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham , who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.
"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.
"The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9 th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.
Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."
They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."
When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.
"Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."
The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

articles.title_orig: World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update
articles.title_zh: World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Fewer people from West Africa are reaching Europe by sea, but the journey has not become safer, the UN migration agency (IOM) said on Tuesday .
Arrivals from Mali, Senegal, Guinea and The Gambia fell by 59 per cent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, to 4,566 people.
But the drivers of migration persist. West Africans made up a growing share of arrivals on the Mediterranean routes, accounting for 21.9 per cent on the Western route, up from 15.6 per cent, pointing to a shifting landscape.
On the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands, arrivals fell 62 per cent between 2024 and 2025, yet recorded deaths and disappearances barely changed – 1,172 compared with 1,215.
Tighter controls in Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal are pushing departures south, adding up to 750 kilometres to crossings of around 2,200 km.
“No single country can solve this alone,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope. “We need to protect migrants wherever they are.”
Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) to order the United Kingdom to halt an offshore oil project near the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), the Hamburg-based court said on Tuesday .
Buenos Aires wants the Sea Lion development in the North Malvinas Basin stopped while an arbitration case launched by Argentina on 28 September is under way.
It also wants London to refrain from steps that could aggravate the dispute, such as granting new permits.
A hearing date will be announced shortly.
The UN lists the Falkland Islands (Malvinas) as a non-self-governing territory and has long urged both sides to negotiate.
Britain has administered them since 1833; Argentina claims sovereignty and the two countries went to war over the islands in 1982. Buenos Aires seeks to resume bilateral negotiations over the islands.
London says the islanders have the right to determine their own future and no discussion over sovereignty can occur without their consent.
Tensions have risen in recent weeks, after President Javier Milei gave London a two-week ultimatum over the project, announcing tougher measures against any companies involved in oil and gas exploration around the islands.
Farmers in Gaza are facing increasing risks as they try to return to their fields.
In an update on Tuesday, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization ( FAO ), warned that the so-called Yellow Line of demarcation controlled by the Israeli military continues to expand into western Gaza.
This has increasingly limited access to agricultural land and prevented farmers from planting new crops.
FAO highlighted the case of 39-year-old grower Maryam, who described her small vegetable farm as a “lifeline” for her family of eight in southern Gaza.
Maryam is one of 1,700 farmers supported by FAO to purchase seeds, water and the other inputs they need to grow crops. The agency also helps herders and fishing families in Gaza
In her first season, Maryam harvested approximately three tonnes of okra.
“Farming is my life and my family’s life. It is the income source I depend on. Being able to farm again means that I am alive and that I can live with dignity with my family,” she told FAO.
There’s a new call from the UN World Health Organization ( WHO ) to reform mental health services by developing community-based models .
According to WHO, about half of all those living in psychiatric hospitals and other institutions around the world had no choice when they were admitted.
This is despite the fact that people living with mental health conditions “can flourish in their communities when given the right support”, the agency insisted.
Mark van Ommeren, Head of WHO’s Mental Health and Substance Use Unit, said large numbers in need of services “are forced to live beyond closed doors. About half were brought in against their will, stripped of basic daily choices like what to wear, when to eat and cut off from the outside world.”
Who said on Tuesday that many countries still rely heavily on psychiatric institutions and that across the world, nearly half of all public mental health funding is spent on maintaining them.
This leaves millions of people unable to get the care they need in general hospitals or in the community.
The WHO applauded Sri Lanka for replacing its isolated mental health institutions with community-based services.
Today, the country delivers care through inpatient and outpatient units in hospitals, clinics and rehabilitation units.
“When care is characterized by coercion, rigid control, or social isolation, it risks becoming a form of confinement rather than care,” WHO stressed.

articles.title_orig: Sizing up Meta’s push into the crowded world of enterprise AI
articles.title_zh: Sizing up Meta’s push into the crowded world of enterprise AI
articles.content_orig:
Meta’s plushy new homunculus wants to pull up a chair in your office.
As the Muse personal agent/cartoon mascot gains traction among consumers, Meta is also making a play for the crowded enterprise agent market.
Meta has hired former MongoDB CEO Chirantan “CJ” Desai to build out a new enterprise platform, as the company looks to provide services beyond advertising tools. It also announced a new Muse for Small Business tool that will integrate the agent into tools like Box, Figma, and Shopify, among many others. Details are vague right now on what an enterprise platform will look like, but Muse Code and Meta Business Agent will be among the already-existing offerings.
Business leaders and marketers we talked with said Muse shows computer use capabilities beyond those of other agents on the market, and could be more accessible to small and medium-sized businesses that already number among Meta’s advertising customers. But a wider enterprise play also comes with security concerns and wariness about Meta pulling in ever more data.
Meta is certainly not the first company to try to parlay consumer AI momentum into an enterprise product.
It might not be an obvious enterprise tech vendor in the same way as Big Tech rivals that boast cloud arms and office software suites. But Forrester principal analyst Kate Winick said the social platform company is already seen as a growth partner by the millions of businesses that use Meta Ads Manager. On that platform, Meta has been rolling out plenty of AI meant to speed or enhance the creative and audience targeting processes, to some mixed reactions from advertisers.
“The question of whether or not you personally trust Meta with your data is a different question than whether or not your company runs business through Meta,” Winick told us. “For most businesses, the answer is already yes. And so this allows [Meta] to sort of bring together the frontier model that they’ve built with the enterprise relationships they already have.”
But Meta Ads Manager is not without frustrations for some advertisers and agencies that use it regularly. For Jeremy Schulkin, SVP of services at marketing agency Hawke Media, there’s the problem of Meta “grading its own work.” Would Muse ever tell business users that their marketing money might be better spent on TikTok, for instance?
“We have fought hard to not hand over the keys to Meta,” he told us in an email. “Connecting QuickBooks, Stripe, your customer list, and your email gives Meta a full view of your business.”
Diego Lomanto, CMO at AI enterprise startup Writer (which would compete with Meta’s new platform), said Meta needs to demonstrate some form of “separation between church and state” between its consumer data-driven ads business and its enterprise platform in order to convince companies to trust it with their data.
Some companies that have experience with Meta’s agentic offerings have found them compelling, if sometimes limited.
Jack Johnston, VP of social innovation and growth at marketing firm Tinuiti, said the agency has piloted Meta’s model context protocol (MCP) server, which connects AI agents to advertising tools. He said the new agentic campaign manager in Muse for Small Business leans heavily on the MCP and is good for small businesses that might be unfamiliar with Meta ads.

“Comparing it to enterprise or SMB advertisers that already operate in Ads Manager, it can be a useful guide, but it lacks some of the sophistication that may be required,” he told us via email, adding that he expects Meta to add more sophistication as it moves beyond small businesses.
Kevin Gosschalk, founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm Arkose Labs, which also advertises on Meta platforms, said he’s found Muse to be far and away the best enterprise agent that he’s used, in terms of its computer use capabilities. That prowess is also evident in Arkose’s web data, he said, which shows more traffic on the web driven by Muse since it started to take off with consumers.
Arkose is currently having its security team review Muse for enterprise use, evaluating whether it would comply with the strict data requirements of client companies like financial institutions. He’s hoping that Meta eventually creates a version of Muse that it can host locally, like Meta’s latest models.
“Muse currently is a cloud-based service. So anything you give it goes into Meta’s data centers. That, we’re not able to do generally in a workforce environment,” Gosschalk said. “But Meta itself has a lot of businesses that use their platform—small businesses and things like that—where they don’t have those security requirements I’m describing. There’s a big divide between those kinds of businesses and a company like us that works with banks and stuff.”
Meta spokesperson Kamran Mumtaz pointed us to a blog post in which the company said it designed Muse to have “multiple layers of privacy and security protections.”
This new enterprise push isn’t Meta’s first attempt to sell workplace products beyond its core ads business. Since 2016, Meta had offered a communication platform called Workplace that was shuttered in May of this year.
“It was groups, it was internal messaging, and frankly, internal comms is a much lower priority for most businesses than growth and revenue,” Winick said. “This is targeted at a much more critical part of the business and working on much bigger problems than Workplace was ever intended to address.”
Still, it remains to be seen whether Meta can make a compelling case to businesses in a crowded space where its competitors have already spent years entrenching their own enterprise AI, Winick said.
“They’re going to have to make a strong case for why people need to switch or why the ad partner is the right person to build the overall business infrastructure,” she said. “They have relationships and they have a way in, but it’s not going to guarantee them the sale.”

articles.title_orig: Comments to the FCC on on Recommendations Approved by the World Radiocommunication Conference Advisor Committee - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.title_zh: Comments to the FCC on on Recommendations Approved by the World Radiocommunication Conference Advisor Committee - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.content_orig:
The Information Technology & Innovation Foundation (ITIF) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the World Radiocommunication Conference Advisory Committee’s draft recommendations regarding Article 22 equivalent power flux density (EPFD) limits under Agenda Item 9.2 at the 2027 World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC-27), with an eye toward fuller adoption of the FCC’s standards at WRC-31. [1] For purposes of Agenda Item 9.2, View A is the better step toward more productive use of satellite spectrum and would avoid unnecessary regulatory restraints that would limit the consumer benefits from non-geostationary orbit (NGSO) systems without significant benefit to geostationary (GSO) systems.
The rise of NGSO systems has been a major benefit to consumers as they now provide higher bandwidth and lower latency than GSO systems. While GSO operations still have important applications, regulations designed for a pre-NGSO world will artificially constrain the parallel benefits from NGSOs. The FCC has already taken the lead in updating domestic spectrum-sharing rules between NGSO and GSO systems, which will expand NGSO capacity, enhance consumer speeds, and provide more broadband to more people in more remote areas. [2] And the new rules do all this while allowing GSO operations to continue without significant degradation. These rules are a success story of updating regulations that would otherwise have held back the benefits of new technologies to those who can benefit from them most.
Thus, as the United States makes the case for this framework around the world, it should not go backwards by adopting a 100-percent-of-the-time EPFD limit, as proposed by View B, which would recreate unreasonable restrictions on NGSOs. The fundamental advance of the FCC’s updated sharing rules is to not guarantee certainty. View A’s unavailability criterion already limits the impact of interference events on GSO systems. An additional limit is unlikely to have an appreciable marginal benefit while the marginal cost could be large. View B would create a new limit not based on accepted technical anchors, which would not only substantially limit the consumer benefits of NGSO systems but would invite other countries to negotiate it to become even more restrictive.
Moreover, View A would adopt stringent protection criteria that protect GSO transmissions while removing unreasonably conservative EPFD limits that prevent NGSO operation even when doing so does not appreciably degrade GSO service. View B argues that View A insufficiently protects GSOs by, for example, lacking a 3-degree avoidance angle. View A, however, would still result in NGSO’s avoiding in-line geometry in practice. An NGSO system that cannot meet View A’s substantive protection of GSOs without avoidance angles will implement them. An NGSO system that can protect GSOs without avoidance angles would provide no additional benefit by bearing the cost of implementing them.
The benefits of NGSO systems are likely even greater in other countries than they are in the United States. For parts of the world without developed communications infrastructure, NGSO satellites promise high-speed, low-latency connectivity for the first time. The United States should, therefore, lead the way to maximize the benefits of NGSOs around the world and bring other countries along with it. It should not hamstring American satellite companies while also limiting consumer benefits of connectivity around the world. The United States should, therefore, support View A on Agenda Item 9.2 and reject View B.
Thank you for your consideration.
Joe Kane Director, Broadband and Spectrum Policy

articles.title_orig: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
articles.title_zh: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
articles.content_orig:
Fraternities on Cornell's campus will not be allowed to host parties or events for the rest of the academic year. Jeongyoon Han for NPR hide caption
Cornell University has banned parties and social events at fraternities for the rest of the school year and will bring sexual assault investigators into its police unit, in response to a former student's allegation of gang rape in 2024.
The changes came on Tuesday as the university said it is committed to addressing a "deeply disturbing" culture of drug and alcohol abuse, and a rise in sexual violence on campus following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student, Jane Doe, which set off national outrage and a crisis at Cornell.
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," Michael I. Kotlikoff, who is Cornell's president, wrote in a letter addressed to the campus on Tuesday. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action."
The lawsuit, which Doe filed nearly one month ago, alleges that Doe was plied with ketamine and was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity during a party in October of 2024. The details of the allegations, which disclosed how fraternity members used a Snapchat group chat to discuss the woman and events at the party with openly crude language, sparked fury across the nation.
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told news outlets that Doe has been sent death threats and police swarmed her family's home since she filed the lawsuit.
The administration's changes come after student groups organized protests last week on campus.
"The administration is clearly feeling the heat and needed to make a move," says John Hartnett, a sophomore at Cornell who has helped organize protests. He called the changes a "half measure," and said that banning frats was not a long term solution to systematic issues at the university.
The faculty senate is considering a vote of no confidence in the university administration at a meeting scheduled for Wednesday. It's a rare move that demonstrates the deep seated frustration and distrust stemming from the 2024 case.
"Trust is still eroded on campus — that hasn't changed," says Julia Chang, an associate professor of Hispanic studies in the Department of Romance Studies. "The fact that these changes are coming about now — two years later — is a testament to the power of the student movement and the global conversation it has sparked; not the integrity of the administration."
The moratorium on events at fraternities is expected to have a reverberating effect on campus, where about one-third of all students participate in fraternities and sororities. The university's ties to Greek life, Kotlikoff said, has in part created a toxic culture on campus that requires serious course correction.
"While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship," Kotlikoff wrote.
Ray Epstein, who works with a consent education company, and is one of the organizers of a rally planned just steps away from Cornell's campus on Tuesday, said that while the measures from Cornell are "overall a win," they also serve as an "effort to save face."
"What I think they should be doing, is operating first instead of as a business, the way that they are now, as institutions that are meant to educate and keep their students safe," Epstein said.
Kotlikoff said that in addition to enhancing bystander training programming, the university will also improve its services to survivors of sexual assault by increasing staffing in its civil rights office, which would help individuals navigate the reporting process for incidents.
Additionally, the university will work with the New York State Police's criminal investigators on campus sexual assault investigations. The move allows the investigators, who are independent from the university, to take on cases in which survivors pursue criminal charges.
The university plans to bring in faculty who are experts in sexual assault and rape culture to help reform the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault through listening events with the Cornell community.
Kotlikoff's letter did not explain why these events are only being issued now — two years after administrators at Cornell learned about the allegations in 2024.
Although the district attorney did not prosecute the case in 2024, Cornell's Title IX office conducted an investigation in 2025. In March 2025, a panel of staff and faculty at Cornell moved to expel or suspend some of the men. The panel required the remaining men to write "essays" in addition to other sanctions.
Cornell also barred the Chi Phi fraternity chapter, which was closed in 2024.

articles.title_orig: One of the World’s Largest Chinstrap Penguin Colonies Is Shrinking Fast
articles.title_zh: One of the World’s Largest Chinstrap Penguin Colonies Is Shrinking Fast
articles.content_orig:
Scientists are sounding the alarm after discovering that one of the world’s largest chinstrap penguin populations has collapsed.
Zavodovski Island, a remote, uninhabited volcanic island between South America and Antarctica, lost 63 percent of its chinstrap penguins between 2011 and 2025, according to a new study published October 7 in the journal Current Biology .
Researchers attribute the losses—which amount to half a million breeding individuals—to climate change, which they say is disrupting the birds’ food supply.
“Imagine losing 60 percent of a country’s entire population in that timeframe,” Lucas Krüger García , an ecologist with the Chilean Antarctic Institute who was not involved with the research, tells National Geographic ’s Avery Schuyler Nunn. “It’s really concerning. The fact that this single colony represented 30 percent of the global chinstrap population makes it even more concerning.”
Zavodovski Island, part of the South Sandwich Islands , was once home to the largest penguin colony on the planet, a combination of chinstrap and macaroni penguins. But, since 2011, as chinstrap numbers have plummeted, the island has lost more than a quarter of its total penguin population. Because of the declines, scientists say the island has now lost its world’s largest penguin colony title to the Adélie penguins living at Cape Adare in Antarctica’s Ross Sea.
Chinstrap penguins have been declining across the Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding islands since the 1980s. But, for years, the birds living on Zavodovski Island, located some 1,240 miles from the nearest permanent human settlement, appeared to be holding their own.
In December 2023, scientists decided to check in on the Zavodovski chinstraps. They were in for a shock: Their analysis—conducted using a combination of drone surveys, aerial photography and satellite tracking data from individual birds—revealed that the island now has the highest rate of chinstrap population decline in the world.
In 2011, scientists counted nearly 543,000 breeding pairs of chinstrap penguins on the island. By 2025, that number had plummeted to roughly 201,000 breeding pairs, according to the paper.
The team ruled out a variety of explanations for the birds’ demise. The island has plenty of breeding habitat, so the chinstraps likely weren’t competing with their macaroni neighbors for space. Krill harvesting is banned in the waters surrounding the island, which eliminated local overfishing as a culprit. The March 2016 eruption of the island's Mount Curry might have killed some of the birds, but it doesn’t explain the chinstrap population’s steady decline since 2011.
Instead, the evidence points to climate-driven changes to the Southern Ocean that are affecting krill , the tiny crustaceans that make up the bulk of the chinstrap penguins’ diet. As the ocean warms and sea ice shrinks, krill are becoming increasingly scarce around Zavodovski—and chinstrap penguins are paying the price.
Tracking data shows the birds prefer to forage in the cooler waters northwest of the island, where they would normally find abundant krill. However, as ocean temperatures rise, the krill are increasingly moving south into the Weddell Sea .
Since chinstrap penguins rely so heavily on krill, even small changes in its availability can have significant consequences for their survival. The chinstrap penguin is “quite a specialist species that’s got a very limited global range, and that range is getting squeezed,” lead author Norman Ratcliffe , an ecologist with the British Antarctic Survey, tells CNN ’s Laura Paddison.
Did you know? Emperor penguins are also in trouble
Earlier this year, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) listed emperor penguins as “endangered.” Projections suggest the birds’ population could shrink by as much as half by the 2080s.
Meanwhile, the island’s macaroni penguins are holding steady. The birds’ numbers increased by 28 percent between 2011 and 2016, and have remained stable at roughly 217,000 breeding pairs since then. Zavodovski Island now has a combined chinstrap and macaroni penguin population of roughly 419,000 pairs, per the paper.
Scientists think macaroni penguins are faring better than chinstraps because their diet is broader and more flexible. They also like to eat krill, but can supplement with or switch to other food sources, such as fish and crustaceans, when necessary. Tracking data suggests they’re doing just that, heading to the warmer waters northeast of the island to forage for alternate prey.
Overall, it’s good news that Zavodovski’s macaroni penguins are flourishing. But researchers worry that the decline of chinstrap penguins could have broader ripple effects.
“Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely,” Ratcliffe tells the Guardian ’s Jonathan Watts.
Sarah Kuta is a writer and editor based in Longmont, Colorado. She covers history, science, travel, food and beverage, sustainability, economics and other topics.
