articles.title_orig: Why advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: Why advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Pope Leo XIV diagnosed with common form of lung cancer
Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.
But in recent days it has appeared helpless in the face of b arrages of missiles and drones fired by the Houthi rebel group from neighboring Yemen. The attacks have struck Saudi airports , killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors and work from home.
The Iran-backed Houthis , once seen as little more than a ragtag militia, have grown into a formidable fighting force. They have inflicted damage on the region’s top oil producer , threatened critical supply routes in the Red Sea and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands.
The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defenses failed to stop the Houthis’ attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict:
Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12% of all U.S. arms exports from 2021-2025.
Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defense systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers.
Saudi Arabia’s annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles.
The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia’s large size.
Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country’s sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles through rugged desert areas.
“Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday.
At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help.
Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support.
President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision.
Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting.
The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defenses.
The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023 . While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year.
Andreas Krieg, a professor at King’s College London, said this experience in challenging Israel’s cutting-edge air defenses has given the Houthis confidence and expertise as they now strike Saudi Arabia.
“They’ve learned how to over-saturate the radars,” he said.
The Houthis, working with allied militias in Iraq, have also targeted Saudi oil installations, including a vital pipeline used to export oil through the Red Sea while movement through the Strait of Hormuz is limited. The Houthis have also seized territory in Yemen near the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea waterway, putting additional pressure on Saudi oil exports.
Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, says the kingdom assumed the Houthis wouldn’t strike civilian targets like airports. Doing so marked “a paradigm shift,” he said.
Ratney, now an adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Saudis now find themselves in a position where they have to respond while also trying to prevent the fighting from spinning out of control.
“They can’t not strike back — they were attacked in a very brutal way by their archenemies,” he said. “They need to exert military pressure on the Houthis and then find a way to kind of deescalate.”
Rather than sending troops into Yemen, the Saudis will likely launch airstrikes against the Houthis and ramp up support of nationalist forces, several analysts said.
“It will be surrogate warfare,” Krieg said.
While the Houthis don’t have the firepower of Saudi Arabia, they have grown into a fearsome force controlling roughly one-third of Yemen thanks to help from Iran.
The United Nations estimates that the Houthis by 2024 had recruited up to 350,000 fighters. That’s up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in the internationally recognized Yemeni government’s civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade.
Ratney says the Houthis now have a “symbiotic relationship” with Iran and should not be seen as an Iranian puppet.
The strikes on Saudi airports and economic assets symbolize a sharing of lessons in asymmetric warfare between the Houthis and the Iranians: how to not just puncture expensive air defenses, but also damage vulnerable energy installations and threaten global maritime routes.
“Over the course of the past few years, the Iranians have been innovating and sharing that with the Houthis and it’s gone both ways. The Houthis have been innovating, and sharing it with the Iranians,” Ratney said. “It’s no coincidence that they’ve ended up with a similar approach.”
Their recent military successes have made the Houthis feel “untouchable,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a fellow at Chatham House focused on Yemen.
“It’s very hard to convince a man he’s going on the wrong side if he just moved forward and he has a gun in his hand,” he said. But the Houthis are now likely to suffer a brutal Saudi counterattack, he said.

articles.title_orig: French supermarkets face millions in losses after cyberattack hits refrigerators nationwide
articles.title_zh: French supermarkets face millions in losses after cyberattack hits refrigerators nationwide
articles.content_orig:
A sophisticated cyberattack targets hundreds of French supermarkets by hacking refrigerators to heat up to 122°F. Ashley Webster reports how the temperature spike spoiled massive amounts of food and sparked fires across Europe.
A cyberattack in France forced multiple grocery stores to discard large amounts of temperature-sensitive product after hackers turned the heat up on food refrigerators in hundreds of stores across at least five chain brands.
The hack, according to Reuters and European officials, affected chains such as Carrefour, Monoprix, Les Mousquetaires, E. Leclerc and Coopérative U.
The CEO of Coopérative U, a retail group structured as a cooperative of independently owned businesses, confirmed the cyberattack in a Monday post on X.
"I confirm that a cyberattack has been affecting, since last night, the cold production facilities of several stores in our network Coopérative U," he wrote in the post.
FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS
View of the closed frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, October 12, 2026. (REUTERS/Stephane Mahe)
"Our teams are fully mobilized, in coordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible. An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack. Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he concluded.
IF HACKERS CRIPPLE AMERICA'S WATER, THE CONSEQUENCES COULD BE CATASTROPHIC
The Paris prosecutor's office also confirmed the cyberattack, characterizing it as a "large-scale" attack that affected "connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France."
Carrefour said roughly 80 of its stores were affected while Monoprix, which operates 490 stores in France according to Reuters, said 5% of its stores were affected.
View of the closed frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, October 12, 2026. (REUTERS/Stephane Mahe)
IRAN-LINKED HACKERS SUSPECTED IN UK POWER-PLANT SHUTDOWN AFTER ALLEGED MINNESOTA WATER ATTACK
Les Mousquetaires said fridges at approximately 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for six hours. A company spokesperson also said all affected food had been discarded, according to Reuters.
While the incident's financial toll on the supermarket has yet to be officially tabulated, experts estimated the losses to be upwards of 10 million euros, equivalent to roughly $11.2 million.
INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT
The attack likely resulted in the loss of "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day," Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard said during a televised interview in France, according to Reuters.
A source with knowledge of the refrigerator systems reportedly told AFP that the hackers targeted refrigerator controls systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES
Danfoss, in turn, told AFP that most of the affected equipment were "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates." The company also added that some of the systems affected were using "outdated firmware" which it had long-counseled its purchasers to update.
Danfoss did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu arrives to deliver a statement at the Hotel Matignon in Paris, Monday, Oct. 6, 2025. (Ludovic Marin, Pool)
TRUMP PLAN TAPS US FIRMS TO FIGHT FOREIGN CYBERCRIME
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France's National Cyber security Agency (ANSSI) to conduct an investigation. ANSSI has already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor," a source close to Lecornu reportedly told AFP.
Christophe Hansen, the European Union's Commissioner for Agriculture and Food, denounced the attack as an affront on European food safety .
IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW
"I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at Intermarche, Cooperative U, Leclerc. Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality," he said in a Monday post on X.

Fox News Digital contacted the Paris Prosecutor's Office, Carrefour, Monoprix, E. Leclerc, Les Mousquetaires and Coopérative U for confirmation and additional comment.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Democrats are ready to 'shock the world' in Florida, says DNC chair
articles.title_zh: Democrats are ready to 'shock the world' in Florida, says DNC chair
articles.content_orig:
The chairman of the Democratic National Committee said things are looking up for Democrats in Florida as the approval rating for President Trump hits an all-time low weeks before election.
Ken Martin told WLRN he sees hope from the top of the Florida ticket down to the bottom, and he expects that this cycle Florida Democrats will potentially benefit from the legislature’s aggressive redistricting efforts earlier this year.
“ This is how stupid the Republicans were on this, if I'm being really honest with you. In an attempt to draw these districts, both in Texas, Florida, and other parts of the country, they're actually thinning out some of what were typically very safe, reliably red districts,” said Martin. “It's making some of those traditionally really red — ruby red — districts much more competitive.”
READ MORE: Polls are a snapshot, and other helpful things to remember during the midterm elections
Martin said the party is confident of Democrat Eliott Rodriguez’ chances against Republican incumbent Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar in Miami. Also in the party’s crosshairs is Florida's 13th in Clearwater, where he said Democrat Leela Grey is surging against incumbent Republican congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna.
Democratic nominee Pia Dandiya is running a strong campaign against Republican Casey Askar in Florida's 22nd, he said. The district was newly created through redistricting, sprawling from western Palm Beach and Broward across rural communities on the shores of Lake Okeechobee and the Everglades, down to Marco Island and Naples. On paper, the district gives an advantage to Republicans, based on 2024 results.
The party even sees a chance to flip Florida’s 7th that includes much of Seminole and Volusia counties. Democrat Bale Dolton is running against Republican Ryan Elijah. The scandal-ridden incumbent Cory Mills was bested by Elijah in the Republican primary. Mills won the district with 56% of the vote in 2024, as did President Trump.
Martin said Democrats are in a position to make real gains in rural areas where they have struggled to compete in for decades.
“ Many parts of these rural communities supported Donald Trump, and his policies have disproportionately impacted the people that supported him the most,” said Martin.
He listed things like the federal government cuts made to rural programs under the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, DOGE, as well as slashes to Medicaid funding that disproportionately threaten the existence of rural hospitals. Tariffs have deeply impacted access to export markets for U.S. farmers. Aggressive immigration enforcement has created labor shortages for the agricultural sector, leading some Florida farmers to slash production targets . The US-Israel war with Iran has driven up fertilizer costs as well as the price of diesel fuel, impacting rural families the most.
“If it was just one or two of those things, it would be one thing. But all of these pieces month after month, now over the last 21 months, are devastating rural economies and rural communities, and frankly, people who live in those communities,” said Martin.
The optimism is tempered by the hard reality that Florida Democrats are facing the worst voter registration gap they have ever faced : There are over 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats in Florida. The Republican Party of Florida has held the governor’s office and both branches of the legislature since 1999.
Martin said the Democrats at the top of the ticket — David Jolly, the moderate gubernatorial nominee — and Angie Nixon — the progressive Black nominee for a U.S. Senate seat — are vital to overcoming the mathematical and historical problems.
“Both are running highly energetic campaigns, bringing in different sorts of parts of the constituency that haven't necessarily always supported Democratic candidates in the past,” he said. “ Nothing is permanent in politics, and this is what I wanna remind folks. There's no such thing as a permanent red state or a permanent blue state.”
Martin also expressed optimism on what he said a strong showing for Democrats could mean downballot, in the makeup of the Florida legislature. Republicans have held a supermajority in both the House and Senate since 2022.
“While we won't likely win majorities this cycle, we will start to pick up seats,” said Martin. “Then over time, as we continue that momentum, that's what eventually turns a state like Florida blue.  It's not gonna happen overnight, but certainly the strength of the candidates at the top, and then also our congressional candidates will help there in Florida this cycle.”
He said the Democrats feel the wind at their backs. The DNC has added several congressional districts to its Red-to-Blue program, bringing in extra money and resources for those races.
“ We've got a lot of momentum for sure, but momentum doesn't knock on doors, momentum doesn't register voters, and it certainly doesn't turn out voters,” he said. “So we've gotta do that work here with three weeks left, and if we do, I think we're going to shock the world there in Florida.”

articles.title_orig: 1926-2026: The 100th World Mission Sunday – ‘One in Christ, United in Mission’
articles.title_zh: 1926-2026: The 100th World Mission Sunday – ‘One in Christ, United in Mission’
articles.content_orig:
Dear brothers and sisters, For World Mission Day 2026, which marks the centenary of a celebration established by Pius XI that is very dear to the Church, I have chosen the theme “One in Christ, united in mission.” Following the Jubilee Year, I wish to encourage the whole Church to continue its missionary journey with joy and zeal in the Holy Spirit. This requires hearts united in Christ, reconciled communities and, in everyone, a willingness to cooperate with generosity and trust…
In his message for the 100th World Mission Day 2026 (quoted above), his Holiness Pope Leo XIV “encourages the whole Church to continue its missionary journey with joy and zeal in the Holy Spirit” and invites us to “reflect on being one in Christ and united in mission,” the theme that the Holy Father chose for this 100th celebration of World Mission Sunday.
In that message, which I encourage all readers to prayerfully read, Pope Leo goes on to reflect on three aspects of his chosen theme:
Towards the end of the message, Pope Leo refers to a video message that he gave for World Mission Sunday last year (2025), during the Jubilee of Hope, in which he spoke very personally about his own experience as an Augustinian Missionary in Peru and how he and his ministry were supported by The Pontifical Mission Societies (TPMS).
Briefly, if you’ve never heard of The Pontifical Mission Societies, it was founded by two women, a bishop, and a priest: Blessed Pauline Jaricot, Jeanne Bigard, Bishop Charles de Forbin-Janson, and Blessed Father Paolo Manna. TPMS cares for Churches in the world that are too poor, too persecuted, or too young to be self-sustaining so that the message of Christ reaches the ends of the earth: “Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19)
Also interesting to note is that the Catholic Church in the United States was mission territory until 1908, and many Catholic churches across the U.S. were built thanks to the generosity of TPMS supporters worldwide. Your generosity is now “paying it forward” to keep not only the work of evangelization, formation, and education alive but also to give critical aid for shelters and health centers in shunned and forgotten locations. Find out more here .
In a (3-minute) video for the 100th anniversary of World Mission Sunday, Pope Leo again speaks very personally, as he introduces the message with these words:
“As we mark World Mission Sunday, we give thanks to God for the abundant fruits he has bestowed upon the Church since my predecessor, Pope Pius XI , established this annual celebration 100 years ago. He desired that it would foster, in every Diocese and parish, a deeper understanding of the greatness of the missionary task, fervent prayer for the work of evangelization, encouragement for the missionary vocation, and support for the work of the Pontifical Mission Societies .”
Throughout the history of our Diocese of Paterson and up to the present moment, thanks especially to our pastors and parishes, there has been consistent and generous support for the missionary work of the Church, for The Pontifical Mission Society, and for visiting missionaries.
Mila Burdeos has done a wonderful job, leading the efforts of our Diocesan Mission Office as coordinator for more than 20 years and now serving as director for more than eight years, succeeding the late Msgr. John J. Demkovich. Over the course of the past six months, Mila has been dealing with some personal health challenges. We keep her in our prayers as she is now on the road to recovery. I wish to thank Msgr. Mark Condon, our Vicar General, and Sister Theresa Lee, F.M.A., our diocesan chancellor and delegate for Religious, for their efforts in continuing the work of the Mission Office.
Sister Theresa has been working with Father Henry Pinto, pastor, and parish leaders of St. Paul’s Church, in Prospect Park to prepare our Diocesan Mass for World Mission Sunday at noon on Sunday, Oct. 18. Many missionaries currently serving in our diocese and beyond who are directly helped by our Mission Office and The Pontifical Mission Societies will be present for our World Mission Sunday Mass at St. Paul’s. I know that many of our pastors and parish leaders are making plans to celebrate World Mission Sunday at Mass on Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 17 and 18, in their own parishes. World Mission Sunday Resources and information can be found on our diocesan website .
I hope that many readers are aware that one of the “best known” supporters of World Mission Sunday, creator of the World Mission Rosary (each decade a different color representing a continent), and the missionary work of the Church throughout the world served as the National Director of The Pontifical Mission Societies (TPMS) in the United States from 1950-1966. He is the recently beatified (on Sept. 26, 2026) Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen. Many would say that it is “more than a coincidence” that Archbishop Sheen’s beatification took place in the same year, only a few weeks before the 100th World Mission Sunday. For more information on Blessed Archbishop Sheen’s life, ministry, support and promotion of the missions, you can go to the website of TPMS: A Life Dedicated to Evangelization and Mission and The Microphone Was Never the Mission .
It is important for us to remember that, before he was elected as our Holy Father on May 8, 2025, Pope Leo spent many years as a pastor and as a missionary bishop. He is very aware that both prayers and financial contributions are important to support missionaries and the Church’s mission (evangelization). At the conclusion of his World Mission Sunday message, before closing with a prayer and blessing, he writes the following:
“… Inspired by these testimonies, let us all commit to contributing to the great mission of evangelization — which is always a work of love —according to our own vocation and the gifts we have received. Your prayers and practical support, particularly on World Mission Day, will be a great help in bringing the Gospel of God’s love to everyone, especially the poorest and those most in need. Every gift, no matter how small, becomes a meaningful act of missionary communion.”
Please know of my deepest gratitude to all those who, by your prayers and financial support, by generously sharing your “time, talent, and treasure,” support the missionary work of the Church, both here, at home in our diocese, and by supporting the missionaries and missionary work of the Church throughout the world.

articles.title_orig: World's largest in-water sailboat show returns to City Dock in Annapolis
articles.title_zh: World's largest in-water sailboat show returns to City Dock in Annapolis
articles.content_orig:
The Annapolis Sailboat Show -- the largest in the world of its kind -- is returning to City Dock for four days beginning on Thursday.
Visitors attending the show can step aboard more than 150 sailboats and connect with more than 500 vendors showcasing marine electronics, rigging, safety equipment, apparel, accessories and services, a news release announced . Attendees can also compare boats and layouts, meet manufacturers and dealers and find resources for every stage of the sailing journey.
Show hours run Thursday through Saturday from 10 a.m. until 6:30 p.m. On Sunday, the hours are from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Organizers say the event is the largest in-water sailboat show in the world.
General admission tickets for adults are $32 (military discount $22 on Sunday). Children 7-15 years of age pay $10, while kids 6 and under get in for free. Military personnel and first responders in uniform will be admitted for free.
The boat show brings together sailing enthusiasts, prospective buyers and industry professionals to celebrate life on the water and explore the latest in sailing, the news release said.
"This is the moment when Annapolis becomes a boating town in the truest sense," said Sheila Jones, Annapolis Boat Show's General Manager. "The docks are full, the boats are ready, and there is something happening everywhere you turn. Come shop for your next boat, get out on the water, learn something new, or simply enjoy a great fall weekend in Annapolis!"
Also happening at this year's show will be courses part of the Cruisers University program, an educational resource visitors will be able to take part in. Cruisers University offers seminars and hands-on courses that aim to build confidence and improve sailing skills, the release said. Classes offered include coastal cruising and offshore sailing.
Because of onogoing construction work along City Dock for the City Dock Resiliency Project, the show will feature an updated layout. This will include tents for visitors to participate in family-friendly activities, while still maintaining the in-water display.
Attendees are urged to order tickets in advance from annapolisboatshows.com and plan for additional travel time due to traffic and construction restrictions in Downtown Annapolis.

articles.title_orig: Cyberattack Hits Hundreds of Supermarket Refrigeration Systems in France
articles.title_zh: Cyberattack Hits Hundreds of Supermarket Refrigeration Systems in France
articles.content_orig:
Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires.
Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported Monday.
Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores."
"Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post .
CNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back.
Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article.
"I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday.
"Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality."
Les Mousquetaires said it was expecting the damages, which affected around 180 stores, to reach "several million euros in losses," in an email to CNBC.
It said some fresh and frozen food displays have been out of service after the cyberattack affected one of its service providers responsible for managing refrigeration systems inside some stores.
"Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove and dispose of any affected products as quickly as possible, to ensure consumer safety," the Les Mousquetaires spokesperson said. "In some stores, the overheating of equipment resulted in smoke, but no fires have been reported."
They're now awaiting findings from a court-appointed bailiff and insurance experts to get more precise figures on damages.
Stop & Shop parent Ahold Delhaize , which owns popular Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said that it was experiencing a "security issue within its network," and that systems had been taken offline. It said its stores are still open.
This comes amid a broader wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes, which experts are warning are being enhanced by artificial intelligence. British online fashion retailer Asos experienced a cybersecurity breach last week which revealed some customers' personal information.
Meanwhile, a small power plant in the U.K. was shut down for four days in July after a cyberattack which was suspected to be linked to Iran.
Interpol's global chief information security officer, Bjorn R. Watne, recently told CNBC that AI can be used to target multiple victims at once, and is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks. "It's an evolution and not a revolution."
Correction: Bjorn R. Watne is global chief information security officer at Interpol. An earlier version misspelled his name.

articles.title_orig: They Pushed an Anti-Abortion Pill Law. Now, They’re Being Sued Under It.
articles.title_zh: They Pushed an Anti-Abortion Pill Law. Now, They’re Being Sued Under It.
articles.content_orig:
Kristan Hawkins was sued for an abortion pills stunt in Texas Ross D. Franklin/AP
In March, two Mother Jones videographers and I stood outside the Space Center Houston and watched Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life, order abortion pills online.
We were shadowing Hawkins through Texas for a profile , documentary , and radio story about her role overseeing one of the anti-abortion movement’s most influential organizations, which now claims 1,700 chapters nationwide.
On that spring day, we watched as Hawkins and a Students for Life spokesperson, Lydia Taylor Davis, attempted to show just how easy it was to obtain abortion pills in Texas, despite its stringent laws, in the hopes that state and federal officials would do more to stop the pills.
Now, Hawkins has been sued over the stunt, under a 2025 state law she and her team publicly lobbied for that was meant to target abortion providers and advocates.
On Tuesday, a 26-year-old Texas woman who says she was forced to carry two pregnancies to term because of the state’s abortion bans sued Hawkins, Davis, and two other Students for Life staffers in state court. The woman, who uses the pseudonym Maria Puerto, claims that the stunt Hawkins staged in the Houston parking lot not only broke the law, but “mocks” Texans like her who have suffered life-altering harms from the state’s draconian laws, which ban abortion under virtually all circumstances. The lawsuit cites Mother Jones ’ reporting, along with Students for Life’s social media posts about the stunt.
“Since Roe v. Wade was overturned, women have not experienced a free Texas. We have no ability to decide about our own bodies, our own families, our own lives.”
“Our client came to us because she has had a very difficult few years since Roe was overturned,” Molly Duane, litigation director of Amplify Legal , the litigation arm of Abortion in America, which represents Puerto, said in an interview Tuesday. “On the one hand, she loves being a mother, she has two beautiful children that she loves very much. On the other hand, she was forced to become a parent long before she was ready.”
The suit details how two unplanned pregnancies disrupted Puerto’s life. When she became pregnant the first time, in 2022, she was attending college on a scholarship, but she was forced to quit school when her financial aid was revoked because she missed class due to severe morning sickness. She was also fired from her job at a convenience store.“I lost everything, my job, my career. Everything,” the lawsuit quotes Puerto as saying.
With her second pregnancy, in 2024, Puerto became depressed, especially when she discovered she was having a girl. “Since Roe v. Wade was overturned, women have not experienced a free Texas,” she says in the complaint. “We have no ability to decide about our own bodies, our own families, our own lives.”
According to the lawsuit, Puerto and her two kids share a bed in a small room in her mother’s home, and she has been unable to find a job that would allow her to cover childcare costs.
“Where is universal childcare? Where is paid family leave? Where is food and housing support for people that struggle to make ends meet?” Duane said in the interview. “Texas has helped her with none of that.”
With “nowhere else to turn for assistance,” the lawsuit says, Puerto’s lawyers decided to sue Hawkins and members of her Students for Life team who participated in the pill-ordering stunt, though the organization itself is not named as a defendant. Puerto is seeking $459,782—the average cost of raising two children from birth to age 18 in the state of Texas, the lawsuit says.
In a statement , Students for Life deemed the lawsuit “misplaced” but called the allegation that their legislative work is stopping abortions a “backhanded compliment.”
“I feel so badly for this child who will forever have it in writing” that Puerto “wished them dead,” Hawkins wrote on X. “It’s child abuse. Texas CPS should be called on this mother asap.”
Duane said the attacks by Hawkins are “disappointing” though “not surprising,” and defended Puerto’s treatment of her children. “I’ve never met a better mother, actually, who’s kinder to her kids,” Duane said.
The 2025 law at the heart of the case, HB 7 , allows private citizens to sue anyone who mails, transports, delivers, prescribes or provides abortion pills to any person in Texas, or intends to do so. People who order the pills for themselves and use them to have an abortion cannot be sued, although Duane noted it’s unlikely Hawkins and her team would qualify for that exemption.
“Where is universal childcare? Where is paid family leave? Where is food and housing support for people that struggle to make ends meet?”
“The one thing that we can be sure of is that people who are categorically opposed to abortion didn’t take the pills themselves,” Duane said.
HB 7 was strongly supported by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, now running for US Senate, and his anti-abortion allies around the country, who have been irate that telemedicine providers have been able to circumvent red-state abortion bans despite the end of Roe in 2022.
Duane, formerly of the Center for Reproductive Rights, has been involved in several high-profile cases challenging Texas abortion laws, including a lawsuit aimed at forcing the state to clarify its “medical emergency” exception. Last month Amplify and Duane sued Paxton, as well several doctors, on behalf of the family of Tierra Walker , a Black woman who died from preeclampsia in 2024 after being denied emergency abortion care.
“Obviously, I have represented many clients with obstetrical complications during pregnancy,” Duane said. “Those are common, sure, but that is not the vast majority of people who are seeking abortion and can’t get it.”
“The vast majority,” she said, “look like Maria Puerto.”
Reported by Amy Littlefield , Video by Anna Yeo and Rachel de Leon

People gather at a local hopital after a boat capsized in the Ganga river, with several people feared drowned, in Bihar's Vaishali district on October 13, 2026.
                                          | Photo Credit: PTI
At least 13 children died after a boat capsized in the Ganga River in Vaishali district of Bihar, under Raghopur police station area on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) night.
The boat was ferrying villagers to another village, where they were to attend a feast. According to locals, the feast had been organised at the home of a person named Singheshwar Rai, near the Mata Maharani Sthan in Bhagtan Tola (Rampur Shyamchand Panchayat), and around 20 people were travelling on a small boat.
VIDEO | Vaishali, Bihar: Boat carrying 15–20 people capsizes in Ganga near Raghopur; Several feared dead. More details awaited.

(Source: Third Party)

#Bihar https://t.co/ZMVLjjT9yV
According to Vaishali District Magistrate Varsha Singh, seven people have been rescued and referred to Nalanda Medical College and Hospital (NMCH). She added that all the children on the boat were aged 15 or younger.
“The rescue operation will continue throughout the night. The SDRF team and local divers are also on site. So far, 13 dead bodies have been recovered,” she said.
Some of the rescued have been referred for better treatment to Patna.
When Varsha Singh reached the local hospital to check on the situation, she was met by angry locals, who shouted slogans against the district administration.
Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary expressed grief over the incident in a post on X. He also announced ex-gratia for the family members of the deceased.
“The news of the innocent lives lost in the boat accident in Raghopur, Vaishali, is extremely heartbreaking and soul-wrenching. In this difficult time, my deepest condolences are with the bereaved families. May God grant peace to the departed souls and provide the families with the strength to bear this immense sorrow,” Mr. Choudhary wrote.
He further wrote, “From the State government, an assistance of ₹4-lakh each [ex gratia amount] will be provided to the families of the deceased. Instructions have been given to the administration to swiftly complete relief and rescue operations and ensure better treatment for the injured.”
Separately, Prime Minister Narendra Modi also announced an ex-gratia of ₹2 lakh from the PMNRF to be given to the next of kin of each of those who lost their lives. The injured would be given ₹50,000
“The loss of lives in the boat capsizing incident in Vaishali, Bihar, is deeply painful. My thoughts are with the bereaved families in this difficult time. I pray for the speedy recovery of all those injured. The local administration is assisting those affected,” the Prime Minister said in a post on X.
Raghopur MLA and Leader of Opposition in Bihar Legislative Assembly Tejashwi Yadav also expressed deep grief over the incident by posting a video message on X. “I am deeply shocked by the heart-wrenching incident of the boat capsizing in Raghopur. May God grant peace to the departed souls and strength to the grieving families to bear this sorrow. At present, I am in Delhi to take part in the INDIA bloc meeting and tomorrow, as soon as I reach Patna, I will go to my constituency to meet the aggrieved family members,” Mr. Yadav said.

articles.content_orig:
MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum has said there was Russian interference in the the Brexit referendum, but warned against overstating its impact on the result.
It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham provoked a backlash from some Brexit campaigners by saying it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow in the 2016 vote.
Sir Ken said it was "a matter of public record" that there was interference in the referendum by online trolls and bots.
However, he suggested Russian trolls would be "delighted" to be front page news again, "despite the comparative unimpressiveness" of their efforts.
He added: "There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed.
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall."
Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart branded Sir Ken's comments "an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister".
In an interview released on Monday, Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."
He did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities during the interview, and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive.
The PM denied claims from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch that he was implying the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference.
He said it was a "matter of record" that Russia sought to interfere in the 2019 general election , adding: "We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time".
A No 10 spokesperson also clarified that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful.
The Conservatives accused Burnham of making an "embarrassing retreat" after "being caught out trying question the legitimacy of the referendum result".
Answering questions after his annual speech at MI5's London headquarters earlier, Sir Ken said: "It is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.
"And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth."
He added that he agreed "strongly" with the PM that there was a hack and leak during the 2019 general election campaign.
However, he raised concerns about the impact of the debate on Russian interference.
"It is kind of up to us how far we allow our various adversaries to divide us," Sir Ken said.
"And I'm a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, that Russian trolls who didn't appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they'll be delighted because they are front page news again despite the comparative unimpressiveness of what they do at all points along the journey."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has accused Burnham of lying, saying there was "no Russian interference" in the referendum.
Meanwhile, former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary, the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".
He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told."
In 2020, a parliamentary report did not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian "troll" accounts on social media.

articles.title_orig: 90-Year-Old Nevada man aims for world record after reaching the Summit of Mount Kilimanjaro
articles.title_zh: 90-Year-Old Nevada man aims for world record after reaching the Summit of Mount Kilimanjaro
articles.content_orig:
RENO, Nev. (KOLO) - A 90-year-old Nevada man is challenging assumptions about aging after climbing Africa’s highest mountain and seeking a Guinness World Record for the feat.
Jim Scott reached the 19,341-foot summit of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania at dawn on Aug. 28, 2026, nearly 45 years after first climbing the peak at age 45. He’s now submitting documentation to Guinness World Records to be certified as the oldest person to stand on the summit.
“To be on top of Kilimanjaro after all those years ... getting there at dawn, seeing the sunrise and seeing all of Africa spread out in front of you ... the thrill is never gone,” Scott said.
The climb capped months of training built on a lifetime of outdoor adventure. Scott has climbed hundreds of peaks, completed marathons and, at age 71, earned his Ph.D. from the University of Nevada, Reno.
He says his Kilimanjaro ascent was anything but a solo effort.
“It’s not an individual thing at all. It’s something depending on teamwork, planning and execution,” he said.
Scott insists the trip wasn’t about ego or bragging rights, but about finding joy in life and continuing to test his limits as he grows older. He says he’ll be the first to congratulate whoever eventually breaks his record.
“You don’t stop just because you got old,” Scott said. “I think that this, if anything, should convince people that you should just go out there and find out what your potential is. You can’t do that by staying well within some comfort limit.”
Scott turns 91 in February and is still waiting to hear whether Guinness will approve his record. He hasn’t decided what his next adventure will be, but says that as long as his health allows, he plans to keep seeking new challenges.

articles.title_orig: Trump backs diesel deal with Russia, says 'world market suffered with high prices'
articles.title_zh: Trump backs diesel deal with Russia, says 'world market suffered with high prices'
articles.content_orig:
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns Russia will use oil revenue to finance attacks while buying time at the negotiating table.
President Donald Trump's efforts to reach a diesel agreement with Russia could provide Russian President Vladimir Putin with fresh revenue to fund his war against Ukraine while allowing Moscow to buy time through negotiations it has little intention of honoring, a former NATO commander warned Sunday.
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove , former NATO supreme allied commander Europe and head of U.S. European Command, told Fox News Digital that Washington also risks undermining Ukraine's war effort by striking a deal with what he called "the enemy."
"And so we are cutting a deal with the enemy," Breedlove said, warning that "all of this money will go into fueling Mr. Putin's continued attacks in Ukraine."
The Russian government said Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports with immediate effect, following the new agreement between Putin and Trump for Russia to supply the U.S. and global markets, Reuters reported.
As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Trump's package calls for the release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace," followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another 1 million tonnes afterward.
KATIE ZACHARIA HITS GROUND RUNNING, PROMISES TRUMP DIESEL DEAL DELIVERS CHEAPER GAS FOR AMERICANS
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a briefing in Kyiv, Ukraine, Thursday, April 17, 2025. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)
The diesel agreement preceded Trump's announcement Sunday of what he called an " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine, with the president saying both sides had agreed to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social .
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , however, indicated that Ukraine had not been informed of a finalized ceasefire agreement but expressed willingness to halt attacks on Russian energy facilities if Moscow reciprocated. He also accused Putin of repeatedly rejecting peace proposals and continuing strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them – 'nyet,'" Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"We do hope that he will finally say something to America, Ukraine, and the entire world that will lead to a real and dignified peace," he added.
Zelenskyy also said Russian forces had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity generation and transmission facilities over the past week, along with 17 strikes targeting gas and oil infrastructure.
He said the attacks had killed more than 150 people and wounded more than 700 over the past week.
Trump's "energy ceasefire" announcement followed tension between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, a component of Ukraine's strategy to weaken Moscow's ability to finance its military campaign.
UKRAINE TARGETS RUSSIA WITH OVER 1,000 DRONES, KILLING 2 AS MOSCOW HOLDS LAST DAY OF ELECTIONS
A view of Russian President Vladimir Putin in front of the Kremlin. (Reuters/Tom Szlukovenyi | Photo by Contributor/Getty Images | Fox News Digital)
Breedlove argued that Russia and Ukraine are pursuing different objectives, accusing Moscow of targeting Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure while describing Kyiv's attacks on Russian energy facilities as an effort to disrupt the revenue sustaining Putin's war.
"Russia is carrying on a campaign of what we call counter value. In other words, Russia is attacking the Ukrainian people and trying to force their society to separate themselves from their president, President Zelenskyy," Breedlove said.
Breedlove also predicted Washington would pressure Zelenskyy to suspend attacks on Russia's oil industry despite their strategic importance.
"What I expect will happen is the United States will force or try to force Zelenskyy to stop bombing the petrochemical business in Russia," he said.
TRUMP'S DIESEL IDEA COULD HAVE UNLEASHED A PROBLEM AMERICANS NEVER SAW COMING
Overnight, Russia launched its largest aerial assault on Ukraine since the war started as fires burned in Kyiv on May 25, 2025. (Reuters/Gleb Garanich)
Trump has vehemently criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, arguing that they are disrupting global diesel supplies and driving up costs for American farmers and ranchers.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the administration's efforts to increase diesel supplies.
"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have," Bessent said Sunday on Fox News. "This is good for the American people, bringing these diesel prices down," he said of the new deal.
Separately, appearing on ABC News' "This Week," Zelenskyy offered to organize Ukrainian elections if Putin agreed to a reciprocal 60-day ceasefire, although holding a vote would face legal and logistical obstacles under Ukraine's martial law.
Breedlove also expressed deep skepticism that Putin would honor any such ceasefire, citing what he described as a pattern of Russian attacks following negotiations with Trump. "Russia has never kept a promise to this president in this war," Breedlove said.
UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. The two leaders are meeting for peace talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine. (Getty Images/ Andrew Harnik)
"He's never changed his expectations, and he's never delivered on his promises. Three out of four of the big cases, the very next day or that same night after the president and Mr. Putin talked, Mr. Putin launched huge attacks in Ukraine," Breedlove continued.
Breedlove also called for a tougher U.S. response.
"We now need an administration that leads from power. We say all the time, 'strength through power,' but when it comes to Russia, our demonstrated position is continued conflict through weakness," Breedlove warned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"He started this war. This war is to benefit Russia, and this war is to keep Mr. Putin in power. And our administration needs to tell him to stop."
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow falls 170 points despite strong Goldman Sachs earnings; chip selloff deepens
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow falls 170 points despite strong Goldman Sachs earnings; chip selloff deepens
articles.content_orig:
Chip stocks fell on Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition.
Memory chip giant Micron slipped about 5% while other memory-related names such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital also sank. SanDisk fell 5% while Seagate and Western Digital both dropped 6%.
The slide, which followed declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT .
Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space.
CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics . Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders.
"Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling.
"In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email.
CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai.
Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected.
But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share.
"More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said.
He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape.
"I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power.
The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks.
Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something.
"When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday.
European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open.
Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.4% — both hitting their lowest levels since August. SK Hynix's U.S.-listed stock was down around 5% in premarket trading.
In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares.
Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%.

articles.title_orig: Sarasota Memorial Surgeon Performs World’s First Heart Procedure Combining Two Emerging Technologies - Florida Hospital News and Healthcare Report
articles.title_zh: Sarasota Memorial Surgeon Performs World’s First Heart Procedure Combining Two Emerging Technologies - Florida Hospital News and Healthcare Report
articles.source: Florida Hospital News and Healthcare Report
articles.content_orig:
Posted by cfelixcpa | Oct 13, 2026 | SF STAT! | 0 |
Oct. 13, 2026 – Sarasota Memorial Hospital heart surgeon Jonathan Hoffberger, DO, has performed the world’s first heart procedure combining two new cardiac implants from Edwards Lifesciences to replace a failing tricuspid valve and reduce stroke risk associated with atrial fibrillation (Afib).
According to Edwards Lifesciences, the milestone procedure marks the first time its TRIFORMIS RESILIA tricuspid valve and ECLIPTIS left atrial appendage (LAA) exclusion system have been implanted together in the same patient anywhere in the world.
triformis valve medical illustration
“Patients who need heart valve surgery often have other cardiovascular conditions that increase their risk of complications,” said Dr. Hoffberger, chief of cardiovascular surgery at SMH. “By combining these two devices in a single operation, we were able to replace a diseased heart valve while also addressing a significant source of stroke risk, without requiring separate surgeries.”
The two new devices address separate but potentially serious heart conditions. The TRIFORMIS RESILIA, approved by the FDA in May 2026, is the first and only surgical implant designed specifically for replacing native or prosthetic heart valves. Surgeons previously used mitral valves for tricuspid valve replacement because there were no surgical replacement tricuspid valves approved for use. Unlike the other valves, the TRIFORMIS RESILIA is engineered to accommodate the unique anatomy of the tricuspid valve. It also incorporates advanced tissue technology designed to resist calcium buildup, a major contributor to deterioration of replacement heart valves.
The other new device, the ECLIPTIS system is designed to close the left atrial appendage, a small pouch in the upper left chamber of the heart. In patients with AFib, an irregular heart rhythm that affects millions of Americans, blood can collect in this pouch and form clots that may travel to the brain and cause a stroke. Cleared by the FDA in June 2026, the ECLIPTIS device is one of several new and evolving LAA closure systems that are increasingly becoming part of cardiac procedures.
Dr. Hoffberger is one of three cardiothoracic surgeons Sarasota Memorial’s First Physicians Group (FPG) who introduced the latest cardiac devices at Sarasota Memorial Hospital this month. On the same day as Dr. Hoffberger’s milestone procedure, fellow FPG heart surgeons Jeffrey Sell, MD, and Kristen Walker, MD, also performed combined cardiac procedures, implanting Edwards’ new stroke-prevention device in two additional patients undergoing heart surgery.
The milestone reflects Sarasota Memorial’s continued investment in advanced cardiac care and multidisciplinary approach to treating patients with complex cardiovascular conditions. The health system’s comprehensive cardiac program brings together cardiac surgeons, interventional cardiologists, electrophysiologists and other cardiovascular specialists to provide a wide range of treatments, from traditional, robotic and minimally invasive heart surgery to advanced valve replacement and repairs, and other advanced interventions and therapies for complex heart conditions.
About Sarasota Memorial Health Care System (smh.com)
Sarasota Memorial Health Care System is a regional medical center offering Southwest Florida’s greatest breadth and depth of care, with about 2,500 physicians and advanced practice providers, 11,000 employees and 2 million patient visits a year across its network of care. Sarasota County’s largest employer, the community-owned health system includes two full-service hospitals in Sarasota and Venice (and third under construction in North Port), freestanding ERs in North Port and Lakewood Ranch, a rehabilitation hospital, skilled nursing facility and comprehensive network of outpatient centers, urgent care clinics and SMH First Physicians Group primary and specialty care practices. Founded in 1925, SMH’s flagship Sarasota campus also is home to the Brian D. Jellison Cancer Institute, Cornell Behavioral Health Pavilion and Kolschowsky Research and Education Institute. Both Sarasota Memorial Hospital-Sarasota and Sarasota Memorial Hospital-Venice have earned the highest 5-Star quality ratings from the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). SMH-Sarasota is the only Florida hospital – and one of just 11 in the nation – to earn a perfect 5-Star rating from CMS every year since the federal rating program began in 2016.

articles.title_orig: Bank earnings takeaways: Here's how JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo and Citi performed in Q3
articles.title_zh: Bank earnings takeaways: Here's how JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo and Citi performed in Q3
articles.content_orig:
Four of the largest U.S. banks reported third-quarter results on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase , Wells Fargo , Goldman Sachs and Citigroup .
Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will post earnings on Wednesday.
The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs.
The banks that reported Tuesday put up mixed results . JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets and the largest in the world by market capitalization, posted a rare miss. Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, blew past estimates for revenue and earnings per share, led by strong equities trading.
Analyst calls for all four banks touched on the opportunities and risks associated with AI, citing robust financing demand and operational advantages, but also the threat of rogue agents.
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon also addressed recent reports of a CEO transition plan, and Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo joined CNBC to discuss the firm's growth and the state of the consumer.
Here's what you need to know:
Citi's analyst call is over, which means bank earnings reports for Tuesday are wrapped. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report on Wednesday to round out third-quarter results for the major U.S. firms.
Wells Fargo's Santomassimo told CNBC that both consumers and businesses are doing "really well."
"I think despite higher gas prices, both sides of the equation have been able to really work through that," he said. "We're just not seeing any sort of cracks around delinquency trends that would lead you to believe you're going to see any near-term stress that come through, at least at least for now."
Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the company's underlying results are "really good" and that the bank is seeing "continued momentum" across all of its businesses.
"As you look at the net interest margin, what that really shows is sort of this good stabilization of the underlying trends," he said. "You see the higher rate environment starting to come through in terms of helping it as you look forward, and so for us, the opportunity we have ahead of us is just as big as it was last quarter."
Citi's Fraser said on the call with analysts that macro environment conditions softened during the third quarter and that the "global economy has held up remarkably well."
"In the U.S., while much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much of the growth," she said. "The labor market is stable, and companies remain active. Our near-term economic outlook remains positive."
She added that the bank's clients have remained "engaged" and "healthy."
Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said on a call with analysts on Tuesday that the company is focused on reducing systemic risk while deploying AI firmwide.
"Our cyberdefense strategy is about being on the front foot, about moving fast and retaining trust," Fraser said. "We don't wait for risks to happen. We're constantly preparing and improving our defenses. We're in the business of managing risk everyday, and this is no different."
Investment banking fees at all four firms reporting on Tuesday largely held up during the third quarter, with most firms either matching or surpassing prior guidance. Still, the reports revealed declines on a quarter-over-quarter basis.
At JPMorgan, investment banking revenue was up 14% year over year but down 8% quarter over quarter. JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said the pipeline remains "very, very strong."
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon echoed that sentiment on his company's analyst call, while declining to say whether capital markets activity has peaked. That bank reported fees that were 21% higher from the prior year, but 5% lower than the second quarter.
"IPOs that came in September were really the result of conversations in May and June around valuation expectations. Things got a little bit softer in September," Solomon said. "The IPO market was wide open. It's just if you expected a valuation and you got something 10 %to 15% less, you might choose not to go forward, you might choose to wait."
Solomon added all the tech innovation and the AI infrastructure activity is a "real good ballast" for capital markets activity on a go-forward basis, noting that doesn't mean there won't be bumps.
Citi posted the largest quarter-over-quarter decline in the fees, at 13% down. Wells Fargo reported investment banking revenue that was down 5% from the prior quarter.
Solomon warned that the AI infrastructure boom could face a painful reset if higher borrowing costs or overbuilding undermine the economics of some data center projects.
"There is going to be a lot of financing to do, and we're going to be in the middle of that," Solomon said during the bank's third-quarter call.
"It may be that over time as the financing needs grow, that there's pressure on rates and that will affect the returns and the viability of certain projects," he said. "Not every project is going to be received as well."
For now, demand for computing power remains strong and supply has yet to catch up, Solomon said, meaning more infrastructure will be built and more financing from Goldman and others will be needed. It's impossible to predict when a reset might happen or how the technology would evolve and be deployed, he said, calling the dynamic "an unknown we have to live with."
"There will be a point in time when this recalibration resets, for sure," Solomon said. "When that does happen, of course there'll be some bumps."
Citigroup, the final bank of the morning, is beginning its conference call with executives and analysts to discuss its third-quarter earnings results.
Goldman Sachs CEO Solomon pushed back against reports of an impending transition to executive chairman, saying Tuesday that no succession process or timeline is underway at the investment bank.
Last month, news outlets cited anonymous sources that said Solomon would be replaced as CEO by Goldman President John Waldron as early as next year. The process would involve a vote by the bank's board that could happen in a matter of months, according to The Wall Street Journal.
"I just want to be clear, there is no succession transition or timeline underway at Goldman Sachs," Solomon said during the bank's earnings call.
"The board and I are singularly focused on our strategy to grow the firm and continue to serve our clients," he said.
The CEO also pointed to the firm's future growth prospects, saying his leadership team was focused on expanding the franchise and accelerating its earnings growth in the coming years.
"I have to say, at the point right now where we see the benefits of the effort that the broad team has made, I'm really enjoying the job," Solomon said.
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the AI investment cycle has become "a complicated macroeconomic force in its own right."
"Demand for semiconductors, networking equipment, power generation, data center infrastructure, cooling systems, storage, cybersecurity and advanced manufacturing equipment continue to surge," Scharf said.
"The scale of investment here increasingly resembles prior infrastructure booms, creating both significant opportunities but also risks given the significant leverage used to finance the build-out and the upward pressure on prices in selected industries and supply chains," he added.
Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company's customer base is "still strong."
"Our underwriting criteria recognize that at some point consumer credit conditions will weaken," Scharf said. "To be clear, we do not see signs of this yet, but we know that cycles are inevitable."
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company is "devoting significant management time and resources" to building out its AI capabilities.

articles.title_orig: US Treasury yield peak still ahead as Fed likely to tighten again, PIMCO's Ivascyn says
articles.title_zh: US Treasury yield peak still ahead as Fed likely to tighten again, PIMCO's Ivascyn says
articles.content_orig:
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell on Thursday as traders digested comments from a top Federal Reserve official along with another long-dated bond auction.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was down more than 4 basis points at 5.229% after reaching its highest level since 2002 this week. The 30-year Treasury bond yield dropped more than 5 basis points to 5.602% after trading around a 24-year high recently.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that more hikes are needed to bring inflation down after around 5-and-a-half years above the central bank's 2% target, but suggested rates did not need to rise immediately.
"The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings," Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul. "But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
His comments initially sent yields higher on the day. However, rates gave back those advances after President Donald Trump said the U.S. won't attack Iran until after the November midterm election . Yields also pulled back after a solid 30-year Treasury bond auction.
The department sold $22 billion in 30-year paper, with indirect bidders — which include central banks — scooping up 72.3% of the sale. That's above a 10-auction average of 68%. Direct bidders, including institutional investors, took 20.9% of the auction, just below an average of 22%. The yield at auction ease 5.618%.
That marks the final auction of the week. The department sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday and another $39 billion in 10-year notes.
Thursday's sale "was decent but nowhere close to as good as the 10 yr auction yesterday," wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of One Point BFG Wealth Partners.
— CNBC's Brianna Bernath contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: New Apple TV 4K vs previous model: Here’s everything new
articles.content_orig:
Apple just launched a new Apple TV 4K, the fourth generation of the product. Here’s how the new Apple TV 4K compares to the previous, third-gen model from 2022.
The new Apple TV 4K has an A19 chip, the same chip that debuted in the iPhone 17 last year.
The third-gen Apple TV 4K from 2022 includes an A15 Bionic chip that first shipped in 2021. So any sort of chip upgrade would have been a big one, but A19 is an especially sizable leap with several years worth of improvements.
Apple says the new chip “delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance,” which results in “greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations.”
A19 also has a new, dedicated AV1 decoder which enables “more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth.”
Siri AI debuts in the new Apple TV 4K, but Apple says it’s also coming to the second and third generation models. Presumably Siri AI will be more responsive on the latest hardware with A19, but it’s great that users won’t have to upgrade just to get the new Siri.
Apple says Siri AI supports features like “personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions.” Some example queries include:
One exclusive upgrade with the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is that it includes a three-microphone array with voice isolation built right into the box itself for hands-free interactions.
This enables you to say “Siri” or “Hey Siri” to interact with the assistant. You’ll no longer have to press the button on the Siri Remote, though that’s still an option too.
The Siri Remote has been upgraded to include Find My support with Precision Finding.
If you’ve ever used Precision Finding to locate a lost AirTag or another device, you’ll know how valuable this experience should prove for the Siri Remote.
When you lose the Siri Remote, you’ll be able to get guided, step-by-step directions to its location. And thanks to a new built-in speaker, you can even play a sound on the remote to help you find it.
You can order the new Siri Remote here for $59 , it’s compatible with older Apple TV 4K models so you won’t have to buy a whole new Apple TV to get it.
If you have several HomePods in your house, or plan to invest deeply in the Apple Home ecosystem, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K has a new surround sound feature.
Using either HomePod mini 2 or HomePod 2, Apple TV 4K will support a four-speaker surround sound experience. Apple says, “The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space.”
You can also mix and match HomePods, as long as they’re in matching pairs. For example, you can use a HomePod 2 front pair and a HomePod mini 2 rear pair—or opt for four of the same model.
Apple used to sell Apple TV 4K in two models: one with 64GB storage and a more expensive 128GB model.
With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, 128GB is the standard storage configuration. There are no options to pay more for higher storage. It’s still unclear how necessary the extra storage is, but perhaps we’ll see tvOS 27’s Smart Downloads feature resurface soon.
I wanted one, upon reading te article I went to the Apple Store to order 1 but then I saw they want € 349, the previous model was around € 189 and then € 229 or so for years. At € 349 I'll pass. I'll seriously doubt it will be success at this price. I mean it is just a box, the subscription to Apple TV comes on top
There are several connectivity improvements with the new Apple TV 4K. On the wireless front, you get the following:
It’s expected that these upgrades are due to the inclusion of Apple’s N1 wireless chip, though that hasn’t officially been confirmed.
Additionally, Gigabit Ethernet is now included standard on all models. Previously, it was excluded from the base 64GB model that most people bought.
Are you planning to upgrade to the new Apple TV 4K? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Hands-on with the Apple Home Collection
articles.title_zh: Hands-on with the Apple Home Collection
articles.content_orig:
A first look at Apple’s new video doorbell, security cameras, thermostats, and more.
A first look at Apple’s new video doorbell, security cameras, thermostats, and more.
We’ve just gotten a closer look at Apple’s new video doorbell, security cameras, door lock, and thermostats following the company’s “Welcome home” event on Tuesday. The six new devices are part of a new Apple Home Collection , which the company codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
The LG smart lock costs $349 and comes with support for Apple Home Key, allowing you to unlock your door hands-free with UWB. You can unlock the door with a PIN code, too, or by using the physical keyhole beneath the keypad.
There’s also a new $249 video doorbell from LG. It comes with two cameras that support up to 2.5K resolution, allowing you to record your visitors as well as see when packages are delivered to your doorstep. The doorbell has a motion-activated light as well.
A pair of LG outdoor and indoor security cameras sport a tubular design that matches the video doorbell. The plug-in indoor camera costs $199 and records videos in up to 2.5K resolution. It moves up and down automatically, and you can set it to face downward when you return home. Meanwhile, Apple is releasing two versions of its wired outdoor camera: a $399 model with motion-activated floodlights and a cheaper $299 model without lights.
Lastly, we got a closer look at Apple’s round LG smart thermostat and a square one from Schneider Electric. They cost $199 and support Matter.
At the center of Apple’s smart home push is Siri AI-enabled HomeView , the company’s first smart home display. You can control each of the new devices with the HomeView or other Apple products, like an iPhone.

articles.title_orig: Two North Carolinians dead from West Nile Virus
articles.title_zh: Two North Carolinians dead from West Nile Virus
articles.content_orig:
Two adults from Central North Carolina have died from the West Nile Virus this year.
The Centers for Disease Control reports 11 more cases in the state this year.
Dr Cameron Wolfe, an infectious disease expert with Duke Health, said if you get West Nile, you probably won't know it.
Possible symptoms the CDC list s are flu-like, such as a fever with headache, body aches, joint pains, vomiting, diarrhea, or rash.
The CDC recommends preventing mosquito bites as the best way to protect yourself and loved ones.
You can also use an insect repellent, wear loose fitting shirts and pants, and avoid being outside between dusk and dawn when the mosquitoes that spread West Nile virus are most active.
